title: Utah Fit Premises Act: Owner and Renter Duties
bodyText:
The Utah Fit Premises Act requires an owner to keep a rental fit for human habitation and in line with local ordinances and board-of-health rules, with working electrical, heating, plumbing and hot and cold water. An owner may not rent premises that are not safe, sanitary and fit, and must keep common areas sanitary and safe, maintain electrical, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water, keep any air conditioning operable, maintain other appliances and facilities the lease covers, and, in buildings of more than two units, provide garbage receptacles and removal unless otherwise agreed.

The Act covers a renter's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals, and does not reach breakage or malfunctions that do not materially affect the ordinary renter's health or safety. Any duty in the Act may be shifted to the other party by an explicit written agreement signed by both.

Renters must follow health rules, keep the unit clean and safe, dispose of garbage properly, use fixtures reasonably, not add occupants without written permission, stay current on payments, follow the lease (including any smoking rule), not damage the unit or disturb others, and not unreasonably refuse entry for repairs. Cities and counties may not adopt rules inconsistent with the Act.

title: Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions
bodyText:
A Utah renter who believes the unit has a deficient condition may give the owner a written notice describing it, stating the corrective period (3 calendar days for a habitability standard, 10 calendar days for a lease requirement), naming the remedy the renter chooses, permitting entry, and served under the eviction-notice methods or as the lease provides.

If the owner does not take substantial action within the period, the renter's chosen remedy applies: rent abatement, under which rent is abated from the date of the notice, the lease ends, the owner must immediately return the whole deposit and a prorated refund of prepaid rent, and the renter must leave within 10 calendar days after the corrective period expires; or repair and deduct, up to two months' rent, with receipts given to the owner within 5 calendar days after the next rental period begins.

A dangerous condition (substantial risk of imminent loss of life or significant physical harm) may be reported by any reasonable means, and the owner must begin remedial action within 24 hours and pursue it diligently. A renter who is not in compliance with all the renter duties is not entitled to either remedy.

If the unit is not fit for occupancy, the owner may instead end the lease by written notice by the end of the corrective period, refund prorated prepaid rent and any deposit due within 10 calendar days, and give at least 10 calendar days to vacate.

The renter may sue after the period; the owner must answer within 3 business days; damages are available if the owner unjustifiably refused or failed to use due diligence; no damages for mental suffering; the court may award costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party.

title: Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Utah caps residential late fees. An owner may not charge a late fee that exceeds the greater of 10% of the rent in the rental agreement or $75. For example, on $1,200 rent the cap is $120; on $600 rent it is $75. The cap applies whether or not the lease mentions it. A late fee must also be included in the lease to be charged, except that on a month-to-month agreement a new charge may be added after 15 days' notice.

title: Fees Must Be in the Lease
bodyText: A Utah owner may not charge a renter a fee, fine, assessment, interest or other cost that is not included in the rental agreement, or in an amount greater than the agreement states. On a month-to-month agreement, a new charge may be added only after 15 days' notice to the renter. Fees allowed by law or stated in the agreement are not otherwise restricted by this rule.

title: Written Disclosures Before Taking an Application Fee
bodyText: Before accepting an application fee or any other payment from a prospective renter, a Utah owner must disclose in writing: a good-faith estimate of the rent and of each fixed non-rent expense in the rental agreement; the type of each use-based non-rent expense; the date the unit is scheduled to be available; the screening criteria (see the screening row); and how the prospective renter can recover money paid. The estimate may be given in a rental application, deposit agreement or written summary. If an amount in the rental agreement differs from the estimate, or the agreement adds an undisclosed type of use-based expense, a prospective renter who has not signed or moved in may demand a refund in writing within 5 business days after receiving the agreement, and the owner must return all money paid within 5 business days after receiving the demand. Utah sets no cap on application fees.

title: Screening Criteria Disclosure
bodyText: Before taking an application fee or other payment, a Utah owner must disclose in writing the criteria it will use to decide eligibility, including criteria about criminal history, credit, income, employment and rental history. Utah fair housing law bars application forms that express a preference based on a protected class, including source of income, but allows decisions based on an applicant's inability to meet the lease's terms, including financial obligations. An eviction record expunged by a court may not be reported or used by a tenant screening agency, and the renter may answer as though the eviction never happened.

title: Move-In Condition Record
bodyText: Before signing a rental agreement, a Utah owner must do one of three things: give the prospective renter a written inventory of the unit's condition (excluding ordinary wear and tear); give the renter a form to document the condition and allow a reasonable time after move-in to complete and return it; or give the prospective renter an opportunity for a walkthrough inspection. Keeping the completed inventory or form helps the owner support deposit deductions later.

title: Copy of Lease and Rules
bodyText: At or before the start of the rental term, a Utah owner must give the renter an executed copy of a written rental agreement and a copy of any rules and regulations that apply to the unit.

title: Deposit Return Penalty Process
bodyText:
Utah deposit rules cover any deposit however it is named. An owner may apply a deposit to rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, other costs and fees the lease provides for, and cleaning, and must return the balance of the deposit and prepaid rent with an itemized notice of deductions within 30 days after the renter vacates and returns possession.

If the owner misses that deadline, the renter may serve a statutory Tenant's Notice to Provide Deposit Disposition at the address in the lease: in person, or, if the owner is absent, by leaving it with a person of suitable age and discretion, or, if no such person is found, by posting it in a conspicuous place; or by registered or certified mail. The owner then has 5 business days to comply.

If the owner still fails, the renter may recover the full deposit, the full prepaid rent and a $100 civil penalty, and the court must award costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party if the other side acted in bad faith. A renter who does not serve the notice gets none of this relief, but either side may still recover other damages.

title: No Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: Utah sets no limit on the amount of a residential security deposit. The only extra deposit limit is for service and support animals, for which no extra deposit or fee may be charged.

title: No Interest on Deposits
bodyText: Utah does not require a landlord to pay interest on security deposits. An owner managing its own rental need not hold deposits in a separate or interest-bearing account. A licensed property manager must keep tenant deposits in a Utah real estate trust account, non-interest-bearing unless the management contract provides otherwise, unless both the management agreement and the lease state that the manager need not; see "How Deposits Must Be Held".

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: Whoever holds the owner's or agent's interest in the property when a tenancy ends is bound by Utah's deposit-return rules. A buyer of a rented property therefore takes on the deposit obligations, and the seller should transfer the deposits or account for them in the sale.

title: Utah Eviction Notices by Tenancy Type
bodyText:
Utah's notices before an unlawful detainer depend on the tenancy and the ground. A fixed-term tenancy ends at the end of its term with no notice. A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy ends at the end of a period if the owner serves notice at least 15 calendar days before that period ends. A tenancy at will ends after a notice of at least 5 calendar days.

For unpaid rent or other amounts due, the notice gives 3 business days to pay or leave. For breach of another lease term, it gives 3 calendar days to comply or leave. For assigning or subletting against the lease, waste, an unlawful business, a nuisance, or a criminal act on the premises, a 3-calendar-day notice to quit applies with no chance to cure.

For the curable grounds, the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the lease or another person interested in it may pay or perform as the notice requires and save the lease from forfeiture; if a breach cannot afterwards be cured, the landlord may use a no-cure notice.

Notices are served in person; by registered or certified mail or an equivalent means; if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the residence; or, if no such person is found there, by posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property.

Tenants after a foreclosure sale have the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act notice, and tenants in properties covered by the federal CARES Act may have its notice to vacate before removal (Utah limits its reach). Agricultural tenants who hold over for 60 days without a demand get another year.

title: Utah Eviction Process
bodyText: A Utah eviction is an unlawful detainer action. The summons gives the tenant 3 business days to respond, and the landlord must serve with it any written lease, the notice served, an itemized calculation of rent, damages, costs and fees, and the factual basis. On either party's request, the court holds an evidentiary hearing within 10 business days after the tenant answers, where it decides who may occupy during the case; a nuisance claim alleging criminal conduct gets a hearing within 10 days of filing on request. If the tenant stays in possession, trial must begin within 60 days of service unless the parties agree otherwise. A landlord may post a possession bond, after which a tenant may pay all rent and costs within 3 calendar days (nonpayment cases), post a counter-bond, or demand a hearing. A judgment for the landlord in a nonpayment or lease-breach case declares the lease forfeited without ending the tenant's liability for rent for the rest of the term (subject to mitigation), awards the rent plus three times the damages assessed, and requires the court to award reasonable attorney fees and costs to the prevailing party. The order of restitution generally gives the tenant 3 calendar days to leave (less if the court orders immediate restitution in a criminal-nuisance or default case, or the parties agree otherwise), after which a sheriff or constable may remove the tenant. Either party may appeal within 10 days (3 days in a private nuisance action). Apart from retaking abandoned premises under the statutory procedure, only a court may remove a tenant.

title: Tenant Property and Animals After an Eviction
bodyText: When a sheriff or constable carries out an eviction order, the officer may remove the tenant's remaining property to safe storage or delegate inventory, moving and storage to the landlord, who must store it in a suitable place and reasonable manner. The tenant may not take the property back until paying removal and storage costs, except that within 5 business days the landlord, sheriff or constable must give reasonable access to retrieve clothing, identification, financial and immigration or employment documents, public-benefits documents, and medical information, medications and equipment. The stored property is then handled as abandoned property. Since September 1, 2026, a pet found at the eviction goes to the tenant if present; otherwise animal control must be notified, must respond within one business day, and the landlord must give animal control the tenant's name and last known contact information.

title: No Lockouts Without a Court Order
bodyText: It is unlawful for a Utah owner to willfully exclude a tenant from the premises in any way except by judicial process. The statute's only exception is removing contents and retaking the premises after the tenant has abandoned them, following the statutory abandonment procedure. Separately, when you install new locks for a crime victim, the law requires you to refuse a key to the perpetrator, even one on the lease (see "New Locks for Crime Victims"). Forcible entry or detainer can also expose the owner to treble damages. A water or sewer special district may not shut off service at your request to collect a debt or to evict a tenant; you may ask for a temporary shutoff only for maintenance.

title: Rent Owed After Abandonment
bodyText: If a Utah tenant abandons the premises, the owner may retake and try to re-rent at a fair rental value. The tenant owes the rent for the rest of the term or, if it is less, the rent accrued while re-renting plus any shortfall between the new fair rental value and the old rent, a reasonable leasing commission and the cost to restore the unit (less normal wear and tear), even if the owner has not re-rented. After an eviction, the lease forfeiture does not end the tenant's liability for rent for the rest of the term, but neither side's duty to mitigate changes.

title: Eviction Record Expungement
bodyText: Utah courts automatically expunge an eviction filed on or after July 1, 2022 if the whole case was dismissed, no appeal is pending and three years have passed, or if the parties file a stipulation to expunge. Any party may petition to expunge an eviction for holding over after the lease ended or for nonpayment once the judgment is satisfied and a satisfaction of judgment is filed; any party's written objection blocks it, and otherwise the court must expunge after 60 days. An expunged eviction is treated as never having happened and may not be reported or used by tenant screening agencies. A landlord who wants to keep an eviction on record may object.

title: Removing Trespassers and Long-Term Guests
bodyText:
Since May 2025, a Utah owner can ask local law enforcement to remove a trespasser immediately by presenting a verified statutory complaint attesting that the person entered unlawfully, the property was not open to the public, the owner told the person to leave, the person is not a current or former tenant under a written lease or an immediate family member, and no litigation is pending. Law enforcement serves a notice to vacate and puts the owner in possession. Wrongful use exposes the owner to actual damages, triple the fair market rent, costs and attorney fees.

Separately, a long-term guest (someone who is not a tenant or an immediate family member of the owner or a tenant, and who stays more than 48 hours without paying or working in exchange) commits criminal trespass by staying after an owner or tenant tells them to leave, unless a separate owner or tenant has expressly let them stay and that permission has not been revoked or voided by drug use, crime or dangerous behavior.

Neither route is for removing a tenant: the trespasser procedure is unavailable against a current or former tenant under a written rental agreement, and tenants are removed by eviction.

title: Nuisance Abatement by Eviction
bodyText: Utah's 2026 nuisance law lets a county attorney, city attorney, county, residents of the county or businesses there sue to abate an 'unsafe building or place' (drug dealing or use, gambling, gang or group crime, frequent disruptive parties, prostitution, weapons offenses, unlawful discharge of firearms, human trafficking) by evicting the tenant. When the conduct is a third party's on the landlord's property, the landlord is a necessary defendant, and a court may issue the eviction order immediately. Costs and attorney fees can be awarded against a landlord only if the landlord had actual notice of the action and willfully failed to act within a reasonable time. A renter bothered by drug fumes drifting from another unit may sue the landlord only after giving written notice and the landlord knowingly letting it continue. Tobacco-smoke claims are covered by the smoking rows.

title: Expedited Hearing for Criminal Conduct
bodyText: When a Utah unlawful detainer claim is for nuisance and alleges criminal conduct (a felony; a crime affecting the health or safety of tenants, the landlord or others on the property; a crime damaging property; drug or gang crime; violence or threats; or other crime directly affecting safety or peaceful enjoyment), the court must hold an evidentiary hearing within 10 days of filing on request. If it finds the act more likely than not occurred, it must issue an order of restitution, and the sheriff or constable returns possession immediately (the court may allow up to 72 hours).

title: Domestic Violence Lease Termination
bodyText: A Utah renter who is a victim of domestic violence may end all future obligations under the lease by giving the owner a court order protecting the renter, or a police report showing the renter is a victim and not the predominant aggressor; a written notice with the move-out date; and a termination fee of one month's rent, paid when notice is given or at move-out, whichever is later. The renter must move out within 15 days and pay rent for that time, and remains liable for amounts owed before the notice. The renter must otherwise be in compliance with the lease, except that a failure to stay current on payments, or a violation of the renter's duties not to damage the unit, disturb other renters or refuse repair access, that occurred in the 30 days before the notice and is due to the domestic violence does not bar termination if the renter gives evidence of it with the notice; the renter stays liable for that noncompliance. The right is not available after an eviction notice is served. Other people on the lease stay bound.

title: New Locks for Crime Victims
bodyText: A Utah renter who is a victim of domestic violence, stalking, a sexual offense (until January 1, 2027, not including enticing a minor, sexual battery, lewdness or lewdness involving a child), burglary or dating violence may require the owner to install a new lock by providing a cohabitant abuse protective order issued after a hearing of which both sides had notice, or a police report, and paying for the lock. The owner may rekey a working lock or replace the whole mechanism with one of equal or better quality, may keep a key, and, regardless of the lease, must refuse a key to the perpetrator. A perpetrator who is on the lease and not barred by a protective order may petition a court within 30 days.

title: Calling Police or Emergency Services
bodyText: A Utah owner may not restrict a renter's ability to ask for help from police, fire, ambulance or similar public safety agencies, and may not penalize or evict a renter for making reasonable requests for help. A city's good landlord program may not penalize an owner for renter or crime-victim calls the owner may not restrict.

title: No General Retaliation Statute
bodyText: Utah has no general statute barring retaliation against residential tenants for complaints or code reports. Three specific protections exist: a landlord may not coerce, threaten or take reprisal against a person for exercising fair housing rights or filing a fair housing complaint, and may not penalize or evict a renter for reasonable calls for police or emergency help. And a mobile home park operator may not refuse to renew, change or unevenly enforce rules, threaten or bring an eviction, or otherwise retaliate based primarily on a resident's complaint to a government agency or good-faith complaint to the operator, lawsuit, or testimony (see "Tenant Organizing").

title: Utah Fair Housing Act
bodyText: The Utah Fair Housing Act bars housing discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, source of income, disability, sexual orientation or gender identity, including in ads and application forms, and requires reasonable accommodations and reasonable modifications. It does not apply to a single-family home rented by its owner if the owner holds fewer than four single-family homes for sale or lease, has not sold two or more non-residence homes in 24 months, uses no broker, and makes no discriminatory statement, notice, ad or application form, or to renting a room in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units (ads still covered). Since May 2026 a private landlord may designate a dormitory, boarding house, shared rental property or other group-living accommodation where residents share a bedroom or bathroom as single-sex by biological sex at birth, unless that would violate federal law or a condition of federal funding. Distinctions based on an applicant's inability to meet the lease's financial terms are allowed. Remedies include actual damages, attorney fees and civil penalties of up to $10,000, $25,000 or $50,000; a private suit may add punitive damages. The Act preempts local fair housing ordinances.

title: Source of Income Protection
bodyText: Utah bars housing discrimination because of source of income, meaning the verifiable condition of receiving federal, state or local assistance, including medical assistance, or of being a tenant receiving government subsidies such as rental assistance. A landlord covered by the Utah Fair Housing Act may not refuse a renter, set different terms, or advertise a preference because the renter uses a voucher or other assistance. The Act's small-owner and owner-occupied exemptions apply.

title: Service and Support Animals Under Utah Law
bodyText: Utah law gives people with disabilities equal access to rental housing and bars an owner or lessor from discriminating over a service animal or support animal, including by charging an extra fee or deposit, though the owner may recover a reasonable repair cost for damage. A 'service animal' is a dog trained, or in training, to do disability-related work; a 'support animal' is any other animal that qualifies as a reasonable accommodation under federal law. It is a class C misdemeanor to knowingly and falsely represent that an animal is a service or support animal, or to misrepresent facts to a health care provider to get documentation. The misrepresentation offense reaches housing because it covers false representation 'to another person'.

title: Penalty for Denying Service Animal Rights
bodyText: Under Utah law, any person, or agent of a person, who denies or interferes with the rights Utah's disability statute gives a person with a disability commits a class C misdemeanor. In rental housing those rights include equal access to housing, being accompanied by a service animal, and freedom from discrimination, extra fees or deposits because of a service animal or support animal.

title: Servicemember Tenant Protections
bodyText: During state military service, a Utah landlord may not evict a servicemember or dependents, or take and hold their property, for unpaid rent on premises renting for less than $2,400 a month without a court order; the court may stay the case for up to three months. Knowingly evicting otherwise is a class B misdemeanor. Federal servicemembers also have the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, including lease termination on qualifying orders.

title: State Preemption of Rent Control and Local Landlord Rules
bodyText: Utah counties, cities and towns may not control rents or fees on private residential property without the Legislature's approval. They may not adopt rules inconsistent with the Utah Fit Premises Act, or use local enforcement to change its repair deadlines or renter remedies. The Utah Fair Housing Act preempts local fair housing ordinances. Cities may license rental dwellings (see the licensing row) but may not interfere with an owner's contract with a tenant about paying utilities or municipal services. Local rules on building, health, zoning and short-term rentals still apply and are not covered here.

title: Local Rental Licensing and Good Landlord Programs
bodyText: A Utah city may require the owner of a rental dwelling (rented a month or longer) to hold a business license or a regulatory business license with an inspection, but no more than one regulatory license for all of an owner's rentals, and it may not charge for the inspection. An owner who receives no compensation can opt out by affidavit. Cities may charge a higher 'disproportionate rental fee' but must reduce it for owners who complete a good landlord training program; an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units is exempt. Counties have no rental-dwelling licensing statute of their own: a county may license businesses in its unincorporated area for regulation and charge fees to recover its costs, and it may not require egress-window or other retrofits beyond those state law lists. Check the city's rules for the property. State business-filing laws can also reach you. If you rent under a name other than your own legal name, you must register that name as a D.B.A. with the Division of Corporations and Commercial Code within 30 days after you start, naming a Utah registered agent, and until you comply you may not bring a lawsuit, an eviction included, as the D.B.A. (Utah Code Ann. §§ 42-2-201, 42-2-205). An out-of-state LLC or corporation may not do business in Utah until it registers with the Division. While it does business here unregistered it may not maintain an action or proceeding in Utah, though its leases stay valid. The statute lists owning real property as something that is not doing business, so whether renting the property out is doing business depends on the facts; get advice before filing an eviction (Utah Code Ann. §§ 16-1a-503, 16-1a-506). If an out-of-state owner doing business here has no Utah registered agent, papers can be served on anyone employed by or acting as an agent for the owner, such as a property manager. And whoever you are, owning, using or possessing Utah real estate lets a Utah court hear claims arising from it, with the papers served on you outside the state (Utah Code Ann. §§ 78B-3-204, 78B-3-205, 78B-3-206).

title: No Rent-Increase Notice Rule
bodyText: Utah has no statute setting notice for a residential rent increase, except for mobile home parks. During a fixed term, rent changes only as the lease allows. On a month-to-month tenancy, the practical route is to end the tenancy with at least 15 calendar days' notice before the end of a period and offer new terms; a new fee (not rent) may be added on 15 days' notice.

title: Landlord's Lien for Rent
bodyText: Utah gives a lessor a lien for rent due on the tenant's nonexempt property brought or kept on the premises while the tenant occupies and for 30 days after. The lien is enforced only through a court: the landlord files a complaint, a sworn affidavit and a bond, and an officer attaches the property. It ranks behind taxes, construction liens, perfected security interests and preferred wage claims. The statute gives the landlord no right to seize property without a court writ. The library offers no lease clause creating a separate contractual lien.

title: Exemption Waivers Are Unenforceable
bodyText: In Utah, a waiver of exemptions signed in favor of an unsecured creditor before a levy on an individual's property is unenforceable. A lease clause waiving a tenant's exemptions from collection would not work, so the library offers none.

title: Stigmatized Property
bodyText: Utah law says an owner is not liable for failing to disclose that property is 'stigmatized': the site or suspected site of a homicide, other felony or suicide; the home of someone infected or suspected of being infected with HIV or another disease that the Department of Health and Human Services determines cannot be transferred by occupying a dwelling; or property found contaminated by an illegal drug operation that the local health department has since found decontaminated. A property that is currently contaminated by methamphetamine must still be disclosed in the lease.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Utah requires no radon testing or disclosure for rentals.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Utah has no statute requiring landlords to disclose or remediate mold as such. Mold that makes a unit unfit falls under the Utah Fit Premises Act's habitability duty.

title: No Bed Bug Rule
bodyText: Utah has no statute on bed bug disclosure, inspection or treatment in rentals. Infestations are handled under the habitability duty and the lease.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Utah has no flood-risk or flood-history disclosure requirement for rentals.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: Utah's landlord-tenant statutes set no smoke or carbon monoxide alarm duty for rentals. Alarm requirements come from the State Construction and Fire Codes adopted under Title 15A and local ordinances. A city may require a plug-in or battery smoke detector in a legal nonconforming rental dwelling even though it may not otherwise require physical changes to it. Utah's version of the fire code requires existing residential (Group R) buildings, including existing apartment buildings and rental homes, to have carbon monoxide detection as the fire code provides, while removing the national fire code's retroactive fire alarm requirements for existing apartment and hotel buildings; the national text itself (IFC Section 915 and Chapter 11) is not in the library's sources.

title: Towing from Rental Property
bodyText: A Utah tow company may tow a vehicle from private property at the owner's request only if the vehicle owner consents, the property has signs meeting state requirements at each entrance, or the owner has placed a written 24-hour warning notice on the driver's side window stating the exact time it was placed. Signs and notice are not required for towing from a detached single-family home or duplex, from places where parking is prohibited by law (fire lanes, near hydrants, disabled spaces without a placard), from places plainly not open to parking, from gated or attended lots, where the vehicle materially interferes with access, or for a legal repossession. A city or county may add requirements.

title: Firearms Stored in Vehicles
bodyText: A Utah landlord may not have a rule prohibiting a person from keeping a lawfully possessed firearm locked in a vehicle, out of plain view, in a parking area, unless the landlord provides free alternative parking nearby or a secured, monitored storage location. Single-family detached homes, owner-occupied or tenant-occupied, are exempt. Utah law also does not change a tenant's lease duties about discharging a firearm.

title: Flag Display
bodyText: A Utah landlord may not prohibit a renter from displaying a United States or Utah flag made of fabric, up to 3 by 5 feet, consistent with federal flag rules, within an area the renter exclusively controls, from a staff, pole or window. The winner of a suit to enforce this right gets costs and attorney fees.

title: HOA and Condominium Rental Rules
bodyText: A Utah homeowners or condominium association may restrict or prohibit rentals only through its recorded declaration (it may set a minimum lease term of six months or less by rule), with exemptions such as military deployment, renting to a close relative, and job relocation. It may not require approval of the renter or the lease, demand the renter's application, credit report or background check (with limited exceptions), charge extra because a unit or lot is rented (except, where at least 35% may be rented, an administrative fee of up to $200 a year after a noticed board vote), or require its own lease form. It may require the owner and renter to sign a lease addendum. If an owner falls behind on assessments, the association may demand that the tenant pay rent to the association instead.

title: Tenants When the Property Is Foreclosed
bodyText: When a trust deed on residential rental property is foreclosed by trustee's sale, the trustee must post the notice of sale on each unit door (fewer than nine units) or in at least three conspicuous places on the property (nine or more units), or mail it to each occupant, with a notice to tenants in at least 14-point type explaining that federal law may let them stay until the lease ends or 90 days after a notice to vacate. If the lender forecloses in court instead, the plaintiff must post or mail a similar 14-point notice to tenants within 20 days after filing the action. A bona fide tenant under the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act may be evicted only after that notice's effective date. A former owner who stays after the sale may be evicted on a notice to quit.

title: No Statute on a Tenant's Death
bodyText: Utah has no statute ending a lease when a tenant dies or setting a process for the tenant's belongings. The only tenant-death rule is in the abandoned-property procedure, which extends the time to reclaim property by up to 15 days when an immediate family member provides a death certificate or obituary.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Utah has no statute giving tenants a right to install electric vehicle charging.

title: Medical Cannabis and Rentals
bodyText: Utah's medical cannabis law gives cardholders no protection against lease terms or landlord decisions in rental housing. A lease smoking or drug policy may restrict cannabis use on the property.

title: City Water and Sewer Bills
bodyText: A Utah city may require the property owner to sign the application for water or sewer service and agree to pay for all service to the property, whether the owner or a tenant occupies it, and may shut off service if the owner does not pay. A lease can make the tenant responsible to the landlord, but the landlord may remain liable to the city.

title: No Sales Tax on Residential Rent
bodyText: Utah sales tax applies to short-term rentals of tourist home, hotel, motel or trailer-court accommodations for less than 30 consecutive days. A residential lease of 30 days or more is not a taxable short-term rental.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Under Utah law the parties to a contract may agree on any interest rate. If the lease states no rate, the legal rate of 10% a year applies to amounts owed under it.

title: Attorney Fees in Utah Landlord-Tenant Cases
bodyText: In a Utah eviction the court must award reasonable attorney fees and costs to the prevailing party. When a written contract lets one party recover attorney fees, a Utah court may award them to either party that prevails. Other statutes add fee awards: to the prevailing party in Fit Premises Act cases (discretionary), in deposit cases when the other side acted in bad faith, and in flag-display cases.

title: Electronic Notices
bodyText: Utah's eviction notices must be served by the statutory methods: in person; by registered or certified mail or an equivalent means; if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the residence; or, if no such person is found, by posting. Email and text are not named, and whether either is an 'equivalent means' to registered or certified mail is unsettled, so the library does not rely on them. A deposit refund and itemized deductions may be sent electronically by a means the renter provided. Utah's electronic-transactions law does not exclude residential notices, so electronic delivery works where a statute or the parties allow it.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Utah does not require cause to end or refuse to renew a residential tenancy. A fixed term ends on its end date without notice, and a periodic tenancy may be ended with the statutory notice. Fair housing and public-safety-call protections still bar ending a tenancy for a prohibited reason.

title: Damage Caused by Tenant
bodyText:
Utah law already covers most of what happens when a tenant, a member of the tenant's family or a guest damages the home, even badly enough to make it unlivable. A renter must not intentionally or negligently destroy, damage or impair any part of the unit, or knowingly let anyone else do so.

At move-out you may apply the deposit to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear and recover the rest from the tenant. If the damage is waste, or a breach that cannot afterwards be cured, you may serve a 3-calendar-day notice to quit with no chance to cure; in the eviction judgment the court must award three times the damages it assesses, including waste damages you allege and prove. A separate lawsuit for waste may also include treble damages, though that statute names tenants 'for life or years', so a month-to-month tenant may not be covered.

The tenant's repair remedies do not apply: a condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, a guest or invitee, or by a use that breaks the lease or the law is not a 'deficient condition', so the renter can neither abate rent and end the lease nor repair and deduct, and a renter who is not meeting the renter's own duties gets neither remedy anyway. No Utah statute lets a tenant walk away after a fire or flood the tenant's side caused, and Utah has no procedure for a renter to pay rent into court.

A tenant who abandons owes the rent for the rest of the term or, if less, the rent for the time reasonably needed to re-rent at a fair rental value plus any shortfall, a reasonable leasing commission and restoration costs beyond normal wear and tear, even if you have not re-rented. An eviction judgment for unpaid rent, or for a breach the tenant did not fix after a notice to comply, ends the lease without ending the tenant's liability for rent for the rest of the term; the statute does not say whether the same applies after a no-cure eviction for waste. The statute leaves any duty to mitigate unchanged; how far you must try to re-rent is case law.

What the statutes do not say is that rent keeps running while you repair, or that you recover lost rent when the lease ends some other way; the optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause says both.

One exception: unless an eviction notice has already been served, a domestic violence victim who meets the statute's conditions may end future obligations under the lease even if damage that was due to the domestic violence happened in the 30 days before the notice; the renter stays liable for that damage. The optional Fire or Other Casualty clause already excludes a casualty caused by the tenant, an occupant, or a guest or invitee.

title: Holdover Damages in Utah
bodyText:
Utah's eviction statute says a fixed term ends at its end without any notice, and a tenant who stays on is in unlawful detainer. But the statute's definitions describe unlawful detainer as staying after a notice to quit, so it is unsettled (a question of case law) whether you can file, or claim tripled damages, without first serving a written notice to quit; serving one avoids the question.

A month-to-month or other periodic tenant is in unlawful detainer after staying past a notice served at least 15 calendar days before the period ends, and a tenant at will after a notice of at least 5 calendar days.

In the eviction case the court assesses your damages from the unlawful detainer and any amounts due under the lease, and must enter judgment for the rent plus three times those damages, with reasonable attorney fees and costs to the prevailing party. The statute does not say the holdover must be willful, but it sets no figure for your loss, and the tripling applies only in an eviction case.

Outside an eviction case, for example when a tenant leaves a few days late and you do not sue, you recover your actual damages as the lease's Holdover section describes. The optional Holdover Charge clause sets a daily figure for those days. Under it you agree not to claim the charge in an eviction case, so it is never part of what a court triples; because it is a charge set out in the lease you may take it from the deposit or sue for it separately, crediting it if you later win an eviction judgment for the same days. In an eviction case you claim your actual damages instead. Whether a separate suit for the charge is barred once an eviction case has been decided is case law.

An agricultural tenant who stays more than 60 days after the term without any demand for possession or notice to quit is treated as renewing for another full year.

title: Waiving Habitability in Utah
bodyText: Utah's Fit Premises Act lets you and your tenant shift a duty under the Act to the other party, but only by an explicit written agreement signed by both of you. That moves who does the work; the Act does not say a lease may remove a habitability standard itself. You still may not rent a unit that is not safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, and the unit must have electrical systems, heating, plumbing and hot and cold water. The Act has no sentence voiding a waiver, so whether a court would enforce a lease term giving up habitability is a question of case law. The cautious course is never to waive habitability: list any specific task the tenant takes over in the library's tenant-performed duties clause. The Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals, and it does not reach minor breakage that does not materially affect the ordinary renter's health or safety.

title: Habitability Terms the Lease May Change
bodyText: A few of the Fit Premises Act's owner duties are written so that the rental agreement can change them. Appliances and facilities beyond the basics are yours to maintain only as the agreement specifically provides. In buildings with more than two units, garbage receptacles and removal are yours except to the extent you and the tenant agree otherwise. The 24-hour notice before you enter applies except as the rental agreement provides otherwise. Any other duty under the Act may be shifted to the tenant only by an explicit written agreement signed by both of you. The core standards have no such wording: the unit must be safe, sanitary and fit, and you must maintain the common areas, electrical systems, plumbing, heating, hot and cold water and any air conditioning. The general rule letting a signed written agreement shift any duty still reaches them on its face, but whether a court would enforce shifting a core duty is case law, so don't shift one (see "Waiving Habitability in Utah"). Your lease may also set a method your tenant may use to deliver a notice of a deficient condition to you; the tenant may instead serve it by a method the eviction statute provides, so treat a notice served either way as valid. Every unit the Act covers must have hot and cold water, whatever the source; the Utah Code has no separate rule on how a rental's water is supplied, and drinking-water and well rules sit in the Utah Administrative Code and local board of health rules. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: No General Non-Waiver Rule for Utah Rentals
bodyText: Unlike states with a uniform landlord-tenant act, Utah has no statute declaring that a tenant's rights under its rental laws cannot be waived. No sentence in the Utah Code or Constitution voids a waiver in a residential rental agreement under the Fit Premises Act, the deposit statute or the eviction statute; Utah's express non-waiver rule for tenancies is in the Mobile Home Park Residency Act, which covers mobile home lots, not the homes this library serves. That does not make waivers safe. Several rules apply whatever the lease says: for example, whatever the rental agreement says, if you install a new lock at a crime victim's request you must refuse to give a copy of the key to the person who committed the act (a Fit Premises Act rule, which covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals); and if a court treats a residential lease as a consumer transaction under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act, including in the lease a waiver of the tenant's rights under that Act is a deceptive act. Whether a court would enforce a lease waiver of any other statutory protection is case law, so the library's leases waive none.

title: No Deposit Non-Waiver Statute in Utah
bodyText: Utah's deposit statute has no sentence saying a tenant cannot waive it, and no statute makes such a waiver void. Its rules still bind you as written: return the deposit or give a written explanation at the end of the tenancy, return the balance of the deposit and any prepaid rent, with an itemized written notice of any deductions, within 30 days after the tenant vacates and returns possession; state any nonrefundable part in writing when you take the deposit; and, if you still don't comply within five business days after a proper tenant notice, owe the full deposit (if you didn't return its balance), the full prepaid rent (if you didn't return its balance) and a $100 civil penalty; in a suit, the court awards costs and attorney fees to the winner if it finds the other side acted in bad faith. Whether a court would enforce a lease term giving up these rules is case law, so the library's leases waive none of them.

title: Jury Waivers in Utah Leases
bodyText: In a Utah eviction, the judge decides the case unless a party asks for a jury. Utah's Constitution says a jury in a civil case is waived unless demanded, and the eviction statute has the jury or, if there is no jury, the court assess damages. So a lease jury waiver would mainly stop a tenant from demanding one. No Utah statute allows or forbids a jury waiver in a residential lease, and whether a court would enforce one signed before any dispute is a question of case law. The library does not offer a jury waiver for Utah. How and when a party demands a jury is set by court rule.

title: Clauses Limiting Your Liability
bodyText: No Utah statute addresses a residential lease clause that releases you from liability, makes the tenant hold you harmless, or limits what you owe for your own negligence. Utah voids indemnity clauses only in other settings, such as construction, motor carrier and design-professional contracts and product sales contracts (a buyer indemnifying a manufacturer for a defective product). Whether a court would enforce such a clause in a lease is decided by case law. A general release does not by itself shift your duties under the Fit Premises Act (which covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals): the Act lets a duty move to the tenant only by an explicit written agreement signed by both parties, and whether a release clause could do that is case law (see "Habitability Terms the Lease May Change"), and if the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act reaches leases, a clause that misstates the tenant's rights could be a deceptive act. The library's leases do not excuse you from your own negligence.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms in Utah
bodyText: No Utah statute written for residential leases lets a court strike an unconscionable term; Utah's unconscionability statutes for leases cover leases of goods. The Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act makes it a violation for a supplier to commit an unconscionable act or practice in connection with a consumer transaction, before, during or after it. A court decides unconscionability as a question of law, after hearing evidence of the term's setting, purpose and effect, and considers what the supplier knew or had reason to know. If the Act applies, a tenant may sue for a declaration, an injunction and actual damages, and the Division of Consumer Protection may bring its own action; only in a class action the division brings for consumers, on the division's motion and where the supplier appears to be hiding or disposing of assets, may the court also strike or limit an unconscionable clause. Whether a residential lease is a consumer transaction under the Act, and the general contract doctrine for real property leases, are matters of case law. The cautious course is to keep every term one you could explain as fair for its purpose.

title: Charging the Tenant for an Eviction
bodyText:
No Utah statute bans a lease charge for evicting a tenant, but two rules shape one. Any fee or other cost must be in the rental agreement and cannot exceed the amount it states; on a month-to-month agreement a new charge may be added after 15 days' notice. And in an eviction case the court must award reasonable attorney fees and costs to the prevailing party, so you recover those through the court, not a lease charge. Whether a fixed eviction charge beyond your real cost is an unenforceable penalty is case law.

The cautious course is to state any charge in the lease as a fixed amount that is a reasonable estimate of your real cost, as the library's notice-service fee clause does, and never to charge for costs a court awards you.

title: Agreed Damages in a Utah Lease
bodyText:
Utah has no general statute on liquidated damages that reaches a residential lease. Statutes allow agreed damages only in particular settings, such as sales of goods, leases of goods and certain cooperative and partnership contracts.

For a real property lease, whether a fixed charge for a breach is enforceable or is a penalty is decided by case law. Any such charge must also be stated in the rental agreement (on a month-to-month agreement, a charge the agreement does not include needs 15 days' notice).

The library's holdover charge says its figure is a reasonable estimate of a loss that is hard to measure in advance, which is the cautious course; that sentence is common drafting, not a guarantee.

The early termination fee is drafted as a price the tenant chooses to pay for leaving early, not damages for a breach; whether a court would see it that way is case law, which is why the fee is a flat one month's Rent. (The fee rule is in the Fit Premises Act, which covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.)

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText: No Utah statute decides whether accepting rent after you serve a notice, or after you learn of a breach, gives up the notice or the breach. Utah's only rule of this kind is in the Mobile Home Park Residency Act, which covers mobile home lots, not these homes. So the answer rests on case law. The cautious course: after serving a notice for anything other than unpaid rent, don't accept rent, or return it promptly, unless you mean to keep the tenancy. After a notice to pay rent or leave, the tenant is in unlawful detainer only if the notice goes uncomplied with for three business days after service; the statute also lets the tenant (or a subtenant or anyone else interested in the lease) pay all rent and other amounts due and save the lease from forfeiture after the notice period, and how late that may be done is case law. Whether accepting only part of what is due gives up the notice is also case law not read; the cautious course is to refuse a partial payment, or to serve a new notice for the balance after accepting one.

title: Lease Terms Utah Law Bars or Overrides
bodyText: Utah has no single list of banned lease terms and no general statute voiding terms that waive a tenant's rights. Specific statutes bar or override certain terms instead. You may not charge a fee, fine or other cost more than the rental agreement states, or one it does not include unless the agreement is month-to-month and you give 15 days' notice of the charge (a cost allowed by law is not barred), and a late fee may not exceed the greater of 10% of the rent or $75. A waiver of exemptions from collection signed in favor of an unsecured creditor before a levy is unenforceable. You may not restrict a tenant's ability to ask police or other public safety agencies for help, or penalize or evict a tenant for reasonable requests. A crime victim's lock-change right and a domestic violence victim's termination right apply as the statute sets them. A lease of more than one year must be in writing signed by the landlord or by an agent the landlord authorized in writing. The fee, late-fee and public-safety rules come from the Fit Premises Act, which covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals. If a court treats a residential lease as a consumer transaction under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act, a confession of judgment or a waiver of the tenant's rights under that Act in the lease is a deceptive act, which can bring damages, fines and attorney fees; whether the Act reaches leases is case law, so the library's leases include neither.

title: No Penalty for Using a Barred Lease Term
bodyText: Utah's rental statutes impose no money penalty on a landlord for knowingly putting a prohibited or unenforceable term in a lease. The nearest rule is in the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act: if a residential lease is a consumer transaction, including a confession of judgment or a waiver of the tenant's rights under that Act is a deceptive act, for which a tenant may recover actual damages and costs and the state's consumer protection division may impose fines of up to $2,500 per violation. Whether the Act reaches leases is case law. Charging a fee the lease does not include is separately barred.

title: Waiving or Shortening Eviction Notices
bodyText: No Utah statute lets a lease waive or shorten the notices that come before an eviction, and none says in words that it cannot. The notices are built into what an unlawful detainer is: a tenant is in unlawful detainer only after the notice the statute names for that ground has been served and has run (for example, three business days to pay rent or leave, or 15 calendar days before the end of a month-to-month period). A fixed term needs no notice at its end. Whether a court would enforce a lease term shortening a statutory notice is case law, so the cautious course is to give every notice in full, and the library offers no waiver.

title: Confession of Judgment Clauses
bodyText: Utah's general statute lets parties sign an agreement to confess judgment before a default, except in an employment contract or a consumer credit contract, where one signed before the default is void. A residential lease is neither of those by its terms. But the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act makes it a deceptive act to include any confession of judgment in the written documents of a consumer transaction, and whether a residential lease is a consumer transaction is case law. Utah also bans confessions of judgment in rental-purchase agreements for goods. The cautious course is to leave a confession of judgment out of the lease; the library offers none.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Terms in Utah
bodyText:
Utah has no casualty statute for residential leases, so the lease decides (see the library's optional casualty clause, "Fire or Other Casualty" clause), but the Fit Premises Act still applies: if a casualty the tenant's household or guests did not cause leaves a deficient condition, a tenant who is meeting the tenant's own duties under the Act may give a written notice and, if you don't act within the corrective period, choose rent abatement (which ends the lease) or repair and deduct; and if the unit is not fit for occupancy, you may answer that notice by deciding not to repair and ending the lease by written notice before the corrective period ends, paying the prorated prepaid rent and any deposit due within 10 calendar days and giving at least 10 calendar days to move out.

The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

On mitigation, the eviction statute says a judgment ending the lease does not change any duty either side has to mitigate damages, and the abandonment statute sets how much rent an abandoning tenant owes. No Utah statute says whether a lease may waive your duty to mitigate; that, and how far the duty goes, is case law. The cautious course is not to waive mitigation and to try to re-rent promptly.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Utah Leases
bodyText: Utah's Uniform Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate a later dispute valid and enforceable, except on a ground that would let a court revoke any contract, and it has no exception for consumer or residential leases. A party cannot give up, before a dispute arises, the right to be represented by a lawyer in the arbitration. The library still does not offer an arbitration clause for Utah. Under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act it is a deceptive act, with damages, attorney fees and state fines of up to $2,500 per violation, to include in a consumer transaction's documents a waiver of the rights the Act gives a consumer, which include suing in court and class actions; whether a residential lease is a consumer transaction, and whether an arbitration clause is such a waiver, are questions of case law. Under the library's rule, a clause whose use could carry a statutory penalty, or whose safety turns only on case law, is not offered.

title: Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and Leases
bodyText: The Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act covers a sale or lease of goods, services or other property to a person for primarily personal, family or household purposes, and it treats a lessor who regularly enters into such transactions as a supplier. Whether that reaches a residential lease of a home is a question of case law, so the cautious course is to act as if it does. Under the Act a supplier may not commit a deceptive or unconscionable act before, during or after a transaction. Deceptive acts include putting a confession of judgment, or a waiver of the consumer's rights under the Act, in the contract; charging for something the consumer did not agree to; and falsely describing a consumer's rights, remedies or obligations. A consumer who suffers a loss may recover actual damages and court costs, seek a declaration or an injunction, and may be awarded attorney fees; the state's consumer protection division may sue and impose fines of up to $2,500 per violation. The Act does not apply to an act or practice that state or federal law requires or specifically permits. Utah's statutes don't list blank spaces at signing as a violation.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Statement in Utah
bodyText: Utah has no truth-in-renting law. No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires you to give a tenant a state statement of tenant and landlord rights, or to print in the lease a notice that it must comply with state law. Utah does require written disclosures of other kinds, such as the owner's or manager's name, address and phone number at or before the start of the tenancy and pre-application disclosures before you take an application fee.

title: No Blank-Space Rule for Utah Leases
bodyText: No Utah statute says a lease must have every blank filled in before signing, or makes a blank space a breach. Utah does require you, at or before the start of the term, to give the tenant an executed copy of a written rental agreement and a copy of any rules. The cautious course is to complete or strike every blank before the tenant signs, so the copy you hand over is the agreement.

title: What a Utah Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Utah prescribes no layout for a residential lease and no rule that the start and end dates appear on the first page. Several rules still depend on what the lease says. A fee, fine or other cost may be charged only up to the amount the rental agreement states, and one the agreement does not include may be charged only on a month-to-month agreement after you give 15 days' notice of the charge (a cost allowed by law is not barred). If you have a written agreement, any part of a deposit that is nonrefundable must be stated in writing when you take the deposit. The tenant may not add occupants beyond the number the rental agreement specifies without your written permission, so state that number. A managing or leasing agent is treated as the owner for notices unless the agent says otherwise in writing in the rental agreement. The Fit Premises Act rules here cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals. A shift of a Fit Premises Act duty to the tenant needs an explicit written agreement signed by both of you. A lease for more than one year must be in writing, signed by the landlord or an agent authorized in writing. At or before the start of the term you must disclose in writing the name, address and phone number of the owner or of a person authorized to manage or receive notices, and give the tenant an executed copy of a written agreement and a copy of any rules.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law in Utah
bodyText: Utah has no plain-language law for consumer contracts or residential leases: no statute sets a readability test, requires a lease to be divided and captioned by sections, or sets a type size for a lease. Utah's plain-language rules cover other documents, such as guardianship notices and insurer directories. Writing the lease clearly is still the best protection when a term is disputed.

title: No Consumer-Restrictions Statement Required
bodyText: No Utah statute requires a lease to carry a front-page statement listing the terms that limit the tenant's rights or every waiver the lease contains, or offers a state preapproval of lease forms. Utah has no plain-language consumer contract statute of that kind.

title: Forms Utah Prescribes for Rentals
bodyText: Utah prescribes no form for the lease itself. Its statutes set out the wording of a few side documents. A tenant who has not received the deposit balance and itemization within 30 days may serve you a Tenant's Notice to Provide Deposit Disposition in substantially the statutory form, after which you have five business days to comply. A lender that files a court foreclosure on residential rental property must, within 20 days after filing, post or mail a 14-point notice to the tenants in substantially the form the statute gives. An owner asking police to remove a trespasser who was never a tenant under a written rental agreement uses a verified complaint in substantially the statutory form. Court forms for evictions are published by the courts.

title: Utah Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Several Utah rental notices must be written. Yours: the pre-application disclosures before you accept an application fee; the owner and manager disclosure at or before the start of the tenancy; a statement in writing, when you take a deposit, of any part that is nonrefundable; a written notice explaining why a refundable deposit is retained, and the itemized written notice of deductions within 30 days after the tenant vacates and returns possession; a posted and mailed notice that property left by a tenant who abandoned the home is considered abandoned; a notice to pay rent or leave, or to comply with a lease term or leave; and, if you decide not to correct a deficient condition in a unit that is unfit, written notice to the tenant by the end of the corrective period.

The tenant's: a notice of a deficient condition, termination for your failure to deliver possession, a domestic violence victim's notice of termination, a written dispute of your declaration of abandonment within 24 hours, and a written demand for abandoned property.

You also give your written permission, which the tenant needs before adding occupants beyond the number the rental agreement specifies.

No Utah statute addresses whether a lease may let these notices be oral; since the statute requires writing, give them in writing.

title: No Rule Requiring Initials on Lease Terms
bodyText: No Utah statute requires a tenant to initial a particular lease term, such as a notice period longer than the statute's, for that term to bind the tenant; where a statute requires a signature, it is a signature on the agreement, not initials beside a term (for example, shifting a Fit Premises Act duty needs a written agreement signed by both of you; the Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals). Initials next to an unusual term are still good evidence that the tenant saw it.

title: Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be Written
bodyText: Under Utah's statute of frauds, a lease for longer than one year is void unless the lease, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing signed by the landlord or by an agent the landlord authorized in writing. A lease of one year or less is exempt. The statute does not limit a court's power to order specific performance of an agreement that has been partly performed; when that saves an unwritten long lease is case law, so put every lease over one year in writing. A lease or memorandum you want recorded needs a notarial certificate, usually a notary's acknowledgment of the signature, before the county recorder will accept it. A written lease of more than one year is a recordable document, and an unrecorded document is void against a later buyer of the property who buys in good faith, for value, and records first; record a long lease, or a memorandum of it, if you need it to bind a future buyer.

title: Lease Length and Who Must Sign
bodyText: No Utah statute caps how long a residential lease may run or requires a seal or notarization to sign one. A lease longer than one year must be in writing signed by the landlord or a written-authorized agent. If you are married and the property has been recorded as your homestead, Utah says no conveyance of it is valid unless both spouses join; whether a lease counts as a conveyance is case law, so have both spouses sign any written lease of a recorded homestead. No Utah statute requires a seal or notarization for a lease to be valid between you and the tenant. A lease you want to record needs a notarial certificate, usually a notary's acknowledgment; an unrecorded lease of more than one year does not bind a later good-faith buyer who records first (see "Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be Written"). Agricultural land is different: a tenant who holds over more than 60 days with no demand for possession is treated as renewing for a year.

title: Preset Cleaning and Repair Charges
bodyText:
When a Utah tenancy ends, you may apply a deposit to unpaid rent, to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, to other costs and fees the lease provides for, and to cleaning of the unit. No Utah statute requires or forbids a lease schedule of preset cleaning, carpet or repair charges, requires a special notice for one, or limits cleaning charges to professional cleaning that is reasonably necessary.

If you want to deduct a preset charge, list it in the lease with its amount: a Utah owner may not charge a fee or cost more than the amount the rental agreement states, or one it does not include unless the agreement is month-to-month and the owner gives 15 days' notice of the charge. Set each amount at a reasonable estimate of your real cost, and apply repair charges only to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear.

Every deduction, preset or not, goes in the itemized notice you must mail or deliver within 30 days after the tenant vacates and returns possession.

The fee rule covers a residential rental unit that is the tenant's principal residence; it does not cover a boarding or rooming house, a mobile home lot or recreational property rented occasionally. The library's optional clause for a preset list is "Preset Move-Out Charges" clause.

title: No Carpet-Cleaning Statute
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution lets you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out as a matter of law, forbids a lease term that requires it, or limits carpet or paint deductions by the carpet's age or condition.

What Utah law does say: when the tenancy ends you may apply the deposit to cleaning of the unit and to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, and you must itemize each deduction in the notice you send within 30 days after the tenant vacates and returns possession. A tenant of a residential rental unit must keep the premises clean and safe and must comply with the requirements of the rental agreement, so a lease term requiring carpet cleaning at move-out is an ordinary contract term.

Put any carpet-cleaning duty or charge in the lease: a Utah owner may not charge a fee or cost the rental agreement does not include (except, on a month-to-month agreement, after 15 days' notice of the charge). These Fit Premises Act rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

The library offers two optional clauses: "Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out" clause (for carpets professionally cleaned just before the tenancy: the tenant has them professionally cleaned at move-out, and if the tenant doesn't, you may deduct what a third-party carpet cleaner bills you, with no markup) and "Preset Move-Out Charges" clause (a stated carpet-cleaning charge).

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A deposit balance or refund you owe a former tenant but cannot deliver, including a refund check the tenant never cashes, is unclaimed property under Utah's Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, which names security deposits and refunds as property. As the person who owes it, you are the holder if you owe it in the course of a business; whether an individual who rents out one home does is not settled, so treat the refund as reportable. Utah sets no special period for tenant deposits: a refund owed by a business is presumed abandoned three years after the obligation to pay arises, and a refund owed by anyone else three years after the tenant could first demand it or the obligation arose, whichever is earlier. An indication of interest in the money from the tenant, as the act defines it, restarts the period. Once the money is presumed abandoned and is worth $50 or more, mail the tenant a notice with the heading the law prescribes (and email it too if the tenant agreed to email) 60 to 180 days before you report. File the report online before November 1 each year, covering the 12 months before July 1, pay the money to the state with it, and keep the records for five years. Paying in good faith after substantially following the notice rules ends your liability to the tenant for that amount. Late reporting or payment can cost interest and a penalty of up to $200 a day, capped at $5,000; a contract made to evade the act, or a willful failure, can cost up to $1,000 a day, capped at $25,000, plus 25% of the amount. A lease clause cannot make an unclaimed refund yours: the money must be reported even if the tenant never asks for it, and a contractual deadline on the tenant's claim does not stop it being presumed abandoned. You may deduct a dormancy charge only if a valid contract with the tenant authorizes it for failing to claim within a set time, you regularly impose it and do not reverse it, and the amount is not unconscionable. Surplus from selling a tenant's abandoned belongings is handled under the same act when you cannot locate the tenant.

title: No Deposit Installment Right
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives a tenant a right to pay a security deposit in installments or requires you to offer a payment plan for a deposit or other move-in money. You may agree to one. If you do, put the amounts and due dates in the lease or a signed addendum so the schedule is part of the rental agreement; any fee or interest for paying in installments must also be stated there, because a Utah owner may not charge a fee or cost the rental agreement does not include (on a month-to-month agreement, only after 15 days' notice of the charge); that rule is in the Fit Premises Act, which covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals. If you have a written agreement and any part of the deposit is nonrefundable, state that in writing when you take the deposit, including any installment. Utah sets no limit on the amount of a residential security deposit.

title: Last Month's Rent and Prepaid Rent
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution limits collecting last month's rent in advance, and none gives a tenant a right to use the security deposit as the last month's rent or forbids it.

What Utah law does say: when the tenancy ends you may apply the deposit toward unpaid rent, so a tenant who does not pay the last month still owes it, and you may deduct it in the itemized notice.

Money you collect as prepaid rent, such as last month's rent paid at signing, is handled alongside the deposit: within 30 days after the tenant vacates and returns possession you must mail or deliver the balance of any prepaid rent with the deposit balance, and itemize any deduction from either. If you then miss the tenant's 5-business-day demand, the tenant may recover the full prepaid rent (if you didn't return its balance), the full deposit (if you didn't return its balance) and a $100 penalty.

Prepaid rent must also be refunded if you fail to deliver possession and the tenant ends the agreement, and, under the Fit Premises Act, when a tenant's rent-abatement remedy ends the lease or you end it rather than repair a unit that is unfit for occupancy (the Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals).

Label each move-in payment in the lease as deposit or prepaid rent. The library's default deposit clause says the deposit does not relieve the tenant of rent due before the lease ends.

title: No Move-Out Notice Condition on Deposit Refunds
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution lets you make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, returning keys by a deadline or giving a forwarding address. Utah's deposit statute sets the duty without any such condition: within 30 days after the tenant vacates and returns possession, mail or deliver the deposit balance, any prepaid rent balance and the itemized notice of deductions to the tenant's last known address, or electronically by a means the tenant gave you. Chapter 17 has no provision on whether a lease may add a condition, and no court decisions were read, so the cautious course is not to make the refund depend on notice. What you can do: ask the tenant in the lease for a forwarding address (the library's return clause does), and if a month-to-month tenant leaves without the notice your lease requires (Utah law sets none for the tenant; see "Notice to End a Month-to-Month Tenancy" clause), or abandons the unit, deduct the rent the tenant owes under the lease or the abandonment statute from the deposit and itemize it.

title: How Deposits Must Be Held
bodyText:
If you own the rental and manage it yourself, Utah sets no rule on how you hold a security deposit: no escrow, separate or interest-bearing account, no interest, no notice of where the money is held and no bond.

A licensed property manager is different. Utah's property manager license begins January 1, 2027 (see "Property Manager License from 2027"); until then, anyone who manages your rental for pay must hold a broker or sales agent license, and the trust-account rules for that licensee are Real Estate Commission rules; from then a property manager, meaning an individual licensed or required to be licensed to manage real estate owned by someone else for pay, must associate with at least one real estate trust account at a bank or credit union in Utah that is used to secure tenant security deposits, rent and an owner's reserve money, unless the management contract provides otherwise.

The account must be non-interest-bearing unless the parties to the management contract agree in writing to an interest-bearing account and name who receives the interest.

A property manager who is not affiliated with a principal broker may skip the trust account only if the property management agreement says so and the lease states that the property manager is not required to hold property management client funds in a trust account; the library's optional clause for that statement is "Property Manager Trust Account Exemption" clause. A property manager affiliated with a principal broker must keep the funds in the principal broker's trust account, following the Real Estate Commission's rules and the broker's requirements.

A licensee who mixes money belonging to others with the licensee's own money, or fails to account for or remit it within a reasonable time, faces discipline.

An individual owner or lessor managing real estate that individual owns or leases, and an individual in the owner's immediate family, needs no license; whether an entity owner's own staff need one is not settled by the text (Real Estate Commission rules not held), so check before relying on it.

title: No Deposit-Standards Posting Rule
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires you to post, or give applicants, the standards you use to set security deposit amounts, whatever the number of units you own, or to use a single standard. Two related rules apply. Before you accept an application fee or any other payment from a prospective renter of a residential rental unit, you must give a written good-faith estimate of the rent and of each fixed non-rent expense in the rental agreement, and your screening criteria; Utah does not say whether a refundable deposit is a non-rent expense, so include the deposit amount in that estimate. And, unless one of the Utah Fair Housing Act's narrow exemptions applies (see "Utah Fair Housing Act"), you may not set different deposit terms because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, source of income, disability, sexual orientation or gender identity. Keep written deposit standards and apply them the same way to every applicant.

title: Nonrefundable Deposits: No Separate Notice Required
bodyText: Utah does not require a separate document, a special form, bold type or the tenant's initials to make part of a deposit nonrefundable. What Utah does require: where there is a written agreement and any part of a deposit is to be nonrefundable, you must state that in writing to the tenant at the time you take the deposit. A statement in the lease works when the deposit is paid at signing; if you take a deposit earlier, for example under a deposit agreement or with the application, put the nonrefundable part in that writing then.
