Any part not stated as nonrefundable is refundable under the deposit-return rules. The library's clause for the statement is "Nonrefundable Deposits" clause.

title: Holding Deposits and Money Taken Before the Lease
bodyText: Utah has no statute written for holding deposits, but its rule on money taken before the lease covers them. Before you accept an application fee, a holding deposit or any other payment from a prospective renter of a residential rental unit, you must give a written disclosure: a good-faith estimate of the rent and of each fixed non-rent expense, the type of each use-based expense, the date the unit should be available, your screening criteria, and how the prospective renter can get money back. A rental application, deposit agreement or written summary can carry the estimate. If the rental agreement you then offer has a different amount than your estimate, or a use-based expense you did not disclose, a prospective renter who has not signed or moved in may demand a refund in writing within 5 business days after receiving the agreement, and you must return all money paid within 5 business days after receiving the demand. Outside that rule, no Utah statute requires you to refund a holding deposit when the applicant backs out, or to pay back double if you back out: the deposit agreement governs, so say in it when the money is credited to the deposit or rent, when it is refunded and when it is kept. State in writing, when you take it, any part that is nonrefundable. If you sign the lease but cannot deliver possession on the agreed date, the tenant may end the agreement and you must promptly return all prepaid rent and any security deposit. The full disclosure rule is in "Written Disclosures Before Taking an Application Fee".

title: No Rule on Fees in Lieu of a Deposit
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution regulates a fee charged in place of a security deposit or a deposit-alternative program, requires you to offer one to every applicant, or gives the tenant a right to switch to a regular deposit. If you offer one, the general rules apply. Put the fee and its amount in the rental agreement, because a Utah owner may not charge a fee the agreement does not include. Utah's deposit statute covers deposits however they are named, so if your program collects money you can later apply to rent or damage, treat it as a deposit: return any balance with an itemized notice within 30 days after the tenant vacates and returns possession, and state in writing when you take it any part that is nonrefundable. Utah sets no cap on deposits, so calling the fee a deposit does not limit its amount. If you or your program report a tenant's unpaid damage claim to a credit bureau, Utah's negative-credit-report notice applies to creditors who regularly extend consumer credit; whether a lease or an unpaid damage claim is consumer credit is case law, and a creditor who owes the notice and skips it is liable for the tenant's actual damages (and the winner of any suit over it gets court costs and attorney fees), so give the written notice it describes, no more than 30 days after the report, as a low-cost precaution.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution sets up a procedure for a tenant to ask for an early or expedited deposit disposition, or a fee for one. You may always return a deposit sooner than the law requires. The ordinary deadline is 30 days after the tenant vacates and returns possession. If you miss it, the tenant may serve the statutory notice and you then have 5 business days to comply before the penalty applies. Shorter deadlines apply in three Fit Premises Act situations for a residential rental unit: if a tenant ends the agreement because you did not deliver possession on time, return all prepaid rent and any security deposit as promptly as reasonable; if a tenant's rent-abatement remedy ends the agreement after you fail to fix a deficient condition, pay the entire security deposit and prorated prepaid rent immediately; and if you end the agreement because the unit is unfit and you choose not to repair, pay any deposit due and prorated prepaid rent within 10 calendar days. Any fee for faster handling would have to be stated in the lease.

title: Utility Deposits You Hold
bodyText: Utah has no separate category of landlord-held utility deposit and no special refund deadline for one. Money you collect from a tenant to secure utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease is a deposit under Utah's deposit statute, which covers deposits however they are named. When the tenancy ends you may apply it to utility charges the lease provides for, and you must return the balance, with an itemized notice of any deduction, within 30 days after the tenant vacates and returns possession, together with any other deposit. The tenant's demand notice, the 5-business-day cure period and the penalty apply to it as to any deposit. State in writing when you take it any part that is nonrefundable, and put any utility charge you bill the tenant in the lease with its amount or the method for calculating it. In a mobile home park, service charges for utilities may not bring the park more over a year than the actual cost of providing the service. A deposit a utility company takes from your tenant is between the tenant and the utility.

title: Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Utah caps late fees on a residential rental unit that is the tenant's principal residence. You may not charge a late fee that exceeds the greater of 10% of the rent agreed to in the rental agreement or $75. On $1,200 rent the most you may charge is $120; on $600 rent it is $75. A lease figure above the cap does not let you charge more than the cap, and the late fee must also be in the lease to be charged at all, except that on a month-to-month agreement you may add a new charge after giving 15 days' notice. Utah does not say whether daily late fees for one late payment are added together; keep the total of all late fees for one late payment within the cap. The cap does not reach a boarding or rooming house, a mobile home lot or recreational property rented occasionally. For a lot in a mobile home park, Utah sets no late-fee cap, but the park lease must disclose all rent, service charges and other fees charged on a periodic basis, a fee increase in a periodic tenancy is unenforceable until 60 days after notice is mailed, and the park and resident may not waive the Mobile Home Park Residency Act. The full rule is in "Late Fee Limit".

title: Fee Disclosure Rules
bodyText:
Utah's fee-disclosure rules for a residential rental unit come at two points. Before you accept an application fee or any other payment, give the prospective renter a written good-faith estimate of the rent and of each fixed non-rent expense in the rental agreement, and the type of each use-based expense, such as metered utilities. If the agreement you then offer has a different amount, or a use-based expense you did not disclose, a prospective renter who has not signed or moved in may demand a full refund within 5 business days after receiving it.

Then the lease itself: you may not charge a fee, fine, assessment, interest or other cost the rental agreement does not include, or more than the amount it states, except that on a month-to-month agreement you may add a charge after 15 days' notice.

Utah has no all-in rent rule, no first-page fee box, no required wording and no total-price rule for rental advertising. Utah's Consumer Sales Practices Act, which may apply to a residential lease, lists charging a consumer for something not previously agreed to as deceptive; following the lease rule above keeps you clear of it. Utah's automatic-renewal notice law does not apply to leases.

For a mobile home park lot, the lease must fully disclose all rent, service charges and other fees and how utility charges are calculated. The library's optional clause listing every fee in one place is "Fees and Charges" clause.

For a fee that passes on a cost you incur, state it as the amount a third party bills you, with no markup, labor charge or added fee, and say you will give the tenant a copy of the bill.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution specifically bars charging a tenant a fee for a service you do not actually provide. Several rules still make the practice risky. Every fee must be in the rental agreement with its amount (on a month-to-month agreement you may add one after 15 days' notice), so a fee is collectible only for what the lease or that notice says it pays for. These Fit Premises Act rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals. If the rental agreement specifically promises appliances or facilities, you must maintain them, and a failure to meet a requirement of the rental agreement can be a deficient condition: a tenant who is complying with the tenant duties, and did not cause the problem, may give you a written notice naming the remedy chosen and, if you take no substantial action toward correcting it within 10 calendar days, use the rent-abatement or repair-and-deduct remedy. Utah's Consumer Sales Practices Act, which may apply to a residential lease, lists as deceptive indicating that something was supplied as represented when it was not, and failing to furnish services that were paid for within the time represented. In a mobile home park, service charges over a year may not exceed the park's actual cost of providing the services. Charge only for services you actually deliver, and say in the lease what happens to the fee if a service stops.

title: Are Fees Rent?
bodyText: Utah's landlord-tenant and eviction statutes do not define rent, and no Utah statute makes a fee rent because the lease calls it additional rent, except in mobile home parks. For eviction you do not need the label: a 3-business-day notice to pay or vacate may demand the rent and other amounts due, the complaint states the rent or other amounts due, and in an eviction based only on nonpayment where you file a possession bond, the tenant can keep the tenancy by paying, within three calendar days of service of the bond notice, accrued rent, all other amounts due, and other costs, including attorney fees as the rental agreement provides. So an unpaid fee the lease requires can go in the notice either way. Utah's other rules treat fees and rent as different things. The late-fee cap is figured on the rent agreed to in the rental agreement, and the domestic violence termination statute lists rent and fees separately. Whether a court would let a lease that labels fees as additional rent raise the late-fee base, or change how eviction damages are calculated, is case law; the cautious course is to figure the late-fee cap on base rent alone. In a mobile home park, rent may include service charges and fees, and a park's cure costs billed under a 15-day notice are treated as additional rent. If your lease lets you recover attorney fees, a court may award them to whichever side prevails in a suit on the lease, and in an eviction the prevailing party recovers fees and costs anyway.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText:
A refundable pet deposit is a deposit under Utah's deposit statute, which covers deposits however they are named. When the tenancy ends you may apply it like any deposit, and you must return the balance with an itemized notice within 30 days after the tenant vacates and returns possession. If any part is nonrefundable, state that in writing when you take it.

Utah sets no cap on pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent and does not require pet money to be folded into one capped deposit. Put pet rent and any pet fee in the lease with its amount: for a residential rental unit you may not charge a fee the rental agreement does not include, except that on a month-to-month agreement you may add one after 15 days' notice.

You may not charge any extra fee or deposit for a service animal or a support animal, though you may recover a reasonable cost to repair damage the animal causes.

In a mobile home park, charges for pets are fees that the park lease must disclose, and an increase in a periodic tenancy takes effect only 60 days after notice is mailed.

title: Utah Money Limits for Rentals
bodyText:
Utah sets few dollar limits on residential rentals. No cap applies to rent, the security deposit or an application fee, though you may charge no extra fee or deposit for a service or support animal. The limits that do apply:
- Late fee: no more than the greater of 10% of the rent in the rental agreement or $75 (residential rental unit that is the tenant's principal residence).
- Other fees: only fees the rental agreement includes, in the amount it states; on a month-to-month agreement a new charge needs 15 days' notice.
- Dishonored check: a $20 service charge, not collectible if a redeposited check clears; collection costs of up to $35 if the check is not paid within 15 calendar days after a written notice is mailed; if the check is still unpaid 30 calendar days after the notice is mailed, you may offer not to sue if the issuer pays the check amount, the $20 charge and the collection costs plus the greater of $50 or triple the check amount (capped at the check amount plus $250), and, if you retained an attorney, attorney fees of up to $50; in a suit filed no sooner than 31 days after the notice, damages of the greater of $100 or triple the check amount, capped at the check amount plus $500, plus interest, costs and reasonable attorney fees.
- Collection fee: if the lease provides for it and you assign the debt to a registered agency or licensed attorney, no more than the lesser of what you must pay them or 40% of the principal.
- Interest: any rate the lease states; the legal rate is 10% a year where a contract states none, but because the Fit Premises Act bars charging interest the rental agreement does not include (except on a month-to-month agreement after 15 days' notice), state any interest rate in the lease (whether the legal rate counts as allowed by law without a lease term is case law).

Amounts the law sets for the other side: the deposit penalty is the full deposit and prepaid rent plus $100; a tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy is capped at two months' rent; a domestic violence victim's termination fee is one month of rent; an eviction judgment includes the rent and three times the damages assessed; and you may not evict a servicemember's household for nonpayment during state military service where rent is under $2,400 a month without a court order.

Mobile home parks: no entrance, exit or installation fee; yearly service-charge income no more than actual cost; a reasonable initial security deposit; an abandoning resident owes rent for no more than 90 days.

Associations, which bind you as an owner: a rental fee of up to $200 once every 12 months where at least 35% of units may be rented, and a cost of up to $25 when an association collects your tenant's rent.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText:
Utah lets you pass a city's rental license fee or disproportionate rental fee on to your tenant: a city may not prohibit a residential landlord from passing the license or disproportionate fee on to the tenant, and may not interfere with your ability to contract with a tenant over paying the cost of a utility or municipal service. A city may not charge a fee for inspecting a rental dwelling, so there is no inspection fee to pass on. No Utah statute bars passing other government fees to a tenant.

The fee rule controls how you do it for a residential rental unit: the reimbursement must be in the rental agreement, and you may not charge more than the amount it states. Name the fee in the lease and fix how the tenant's share is figured, such as all or a stated percentage of the government's bill with a copy given and no markup, because a fixed-term lease cannot add a new charge mid-term; on a month-to-month agreement you may add a charge after 15 days' notice.

Court filing and service costs in an eviction are recovered through the court's award to the prevailing party, not as a lease reimbursement. In a mobile home park, the park may pass through increases or decreases in electricity rates when service charges are not included in rent. The library's optional clause is "Government Fee Reimbursement" clause.

title: Receipts for Rent
bodyText: Utah's landlord-tenant statutes say nothing about rent receipts, but a general Utah statute does: a person who pays money is entitled to a receipt from the person to whom the payment is made, and may demand a properly signed receipt as a condition of paying. So a tenant who pays you rent, in cash or any other way, may ask for a signed receipt, and may make the payment conditional on getting one. Give a signed receipt whenever a tenant asks, and give one for every cash or money-order payment as a matter of practice. Utah does not say whether an electronic payment confirmation counts as a receipt, so sign and send one on request. No Utah statute makes a missing receipt a defense to eviction or sets a penalty for it, and no Utah statute presumes that earlier rent was paid because the tenant holds a receipt for a later month; how a court weighs receipts as evidence is a matter of court rules and case law.

title: No Rule Tying Rent to the Repair Duty
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution contains the uniform landlord-tenant act's rule that a lease, assignment, deed, trust deed or security instrument may not let anyone receive rent free of the duty to maintain the unit. Utah's Fit Premises Act is not that uniform act and has no purposes section. What Utah law does say: each owner and owner's agent renting a residential rental unit must keep it fit for human habitation, and owner includes the lessor and any sublessor, so whoever rents the unit to the tenant carries the duty. Any duty in the Act may be shifted to a different party, such as the tenant, only by an explicit written agreement signed by the parties. If your lender enforces an assignment of rents and collects rent from your tenant, it need not spend the rent on maintenance, but its right to collect is subject to the lease and to the tenant's claims and defenses from your nonperformance, unless the tenant agreed otherwise, and the tenant may ask a court for a receiver if unpaid maintenance threatens the tenant's interest. If a condominium association collects rent from your tenant because you did not pay assessments, you must credit those payments as rent paid to you.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Utah has no opt-in lockout for unpaid rent. It is unlawful for an owner to willfully exclude a tenant from the tenant's premises in any manner except by judicial process, and willful exclusion means preventing the tenant from entering with intent to deprive the tenant of entry. A lease clause allowing a lockout, a lock change or a seizure of belongings for late rent therefore cannot make one lawful under that statute. For unpaid rent, serve a 3-business-day notice to pay rent and other amounts due or vacate, and if the tenant does not comply, file an unlawful detainer action; the court can award damages, which it trebles, plus attorney fees and costs. Your landlord's lien for rent on the tenant's nonexempt property on the premises (while the tenant occupies and for 30 days after) is enforced through a court writ of attachment; the statute gives no self-help route, and whether taking the property yourself is lawful is case law, so don't (see "No Lockouts Without a Court Order"). The statute lets you retake the unit without a court only after the tenant abandons it, following the abandonment rules. During state military service, evicting a servicemember's household or taking its property for nonpayment where rent is under $2,400 a month needs a court order, and doing it otherwise is a misdemeanor.

title: Charges for Alarm Tampering
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code authorizes, sets or caps a fee for a tenant who removes or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and Utah's landlord-tenant statutes set no alarm rule of their own.

Utah's general rules decide what you may charge. A tenant of a residential rental unit may not intentionally or negligently damage, impair or remove any part of the unit, so a disabled, damaged or missing alarm is tenant-caused damage, and you may apply the deposit to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear.

Any charge must be in the lease: a stated amount, or the amount a third party bills you or the price of parts, with no markup, labor charge or added fee and a copy of the bill. Whether a fixed tampering fee above your real cost could be enforced is case law, so the library's clause charges the documented repair cost.

The State Fire Code adopts the International Fire Code, 2024 edition, whose own text, including any rule on tampering with fire protection equipment, is not in this library's sources; check it, and any city ordinance, before relying on a fine or a code violation. The library's optional clause is "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms" clause; the alarm duties themselves are in "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms".

title: Late Fees in Subsidized Tenancies
bodyText: Utah has no separate late-fee rule for subsidized tenancies, so Utah's general cap applies: for a residential rental unit, a late fee may not exceed the greater of 10% of the rent agreed to in the rental agreement or $75, and must be in the lease. For a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, federal rules say the family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing assistance payment covers, and the housing authority's failure to pay it is not a lease violation. So charge a late fee only when the tenant's own share is late, never because the housing authority paid late. Utah does not say whether the 10% is figured on the full contract rent in the lease or on the tenant's share; the cautious course is to figure it on the tenant's share. Treating voucher holders or other assisted tenants differently on late fees can be discrimination in the terms of a rental, because Utah's Fair Housing Act protects source of income. Federal program rules for public housing, project-based Section 8 and the voucher tenancy addendum may limit late fees further; those rules are not in this library's sources, so check the program's lease or addendum before setting a fee.

title: No Rent Concession Rule
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution regulates rent concessions, free-rent periods or move-in specials, or taking a concession back when a tenant leaves early.

Three general rules touch them. Before you take an application fee or other payment, your written good-faith estimate of the rent should reflect any concession, because a prospective renter who receives a lease with a different amount may demand a full refund within 5 business days. The late-fee cap is figured on the rent agreed to in the rental agreement; Utah does not say whether that is the full rent or the discounted rent during a concession, so the cautious course is the discounted rent. And if you want to recover a concession when the tenant breaks the lease, the lease must say so and state the amount, because you may not charge a cost the rental agreement does not include; whether recovering it on top of your other damages can be enforced is case law.

State each concession, its value and the rental periods it covers in the lease; the library's clause for that is "Rent Concessions" clause.

title: No Domestic Violence Confidentiality Rule
bodyText: Utah has no statute on how you must handle the information or papers a tenant gives you about domestic violence. When a renter uses Utah's domestic violence termination right or a crime victim asks you for a new lock (see "Domestic Violence Lease Termination" and "New Locks for Crime Victims"; both rights cover a renter's principal residence, not a boarding or rooming house, a mobile home lot or occasional recreational rental), the law lists the court order or police report the renter gives you, but no section of the Utah Code or Constitution tells an owner to keep those papers confidential, limits who you may share them with, or sets a penalty for sharing them. The cautious course is still to treat them as confidential: keep them apart from the general tenant file, let only the staff who need them see them, and never share them with the person named as the abuser, with other tenants, or in a reference or screening reply. A tenant may tell you that he or she is enrolled in Utah's Safe at Home address program and send you its notification form. The program's rules on using the substitute address bind state and local government offices, not private landlords, but anyone who knowingly or intentionally obtains a participant's actual address from the program or a government office without authorization commits a misdemeanor. If your property is in a federally covered housing program (for example public housing, Section 8 assistance or a low income housing tax credit property), federal law does set a rule: information a tenant or applicant gives you to claim protection as a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking, including the fact of being a victim, must be kept in confidence, may not go into a shared database, and may not be disclosed to anyone unless the tenant asks for or consents to it in writing, it is needed in an eviction proceeding under the federal rule, or other law requires it.

title: Deposits After a Domestic Violence Termination
bodyText: Utah has no special deposit rule for a renter who ends the lease under Utah's domestic violence termination right ("Domestic Violence Lease Termination"; that right covers a renter's principal residence, not a boarding or rooming house, a mobile home lot or occasional recreational rental). The ordinary deposit law applies ("Deposit Return Penalty Process"): within 30 days after a renter vacates and returns possession, you must send the balance of the deposit and of any prepaid rent, with a written notice itemizing and explaining each deduction. The renter owes you a termination fee of one month's rent and rent for any days he or she stays during the 15 days after giving notice. The deposit law lets you apply a deposit to rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, cleaning and other costs and fees provided for in the lease; it does not say whether the statutory termination fee is one of them, so the cautious course is to collect the fee separately when it falls due. When other renters stay, the termination ends only the departing renter's future obligations and the lease continues for the others. Utah law does not say whether the 30-day clock then starts when the departing renter leaves or waits for the tenancy to end; it ties the deadline to the day a renter vacates and returns possession, and it separately requires you, at the end of a tenancy, either to return a deposit or to give written notice explaining why it is being kept. No case law was read on the point. The cautious course: within 30 days after the departing renter moves out, either refund any part of the deposit that you and all the renters agree in writing belongs to the departing renter, or give the departing renter written notice that the deposit stays in place for the continuing tenancy and will be accounted for when it ends; then send the final accounting to every renter, including the departing renter at the address or electronic means he or she gives you.

title: Evicting a Domestic Violence Victim
bodyText: Utah has two eviction-related rules that touch domestic violence. The first protects every renter's calls for help: you may not restrict a renter's ability to ask police, fire, ambulance or similar public safety agencies for help, and you may not penalize or evict a renter for making reasonable requests for that help ("Calling Police or Emergency Services"). That rule is in the Fit Premises Act, so it covers a renter's principal residence, not a boarding or rooming house, a mobile home lot or occasional recreational rental. Second, belongings removed and stored when an eviction order is carried out are treated as abandoned property, as are belongings a tenant leaves behind; you must give a tenant who provides a police report or protection order for domestic violence up to 15 more calendar days to recover them ("Handling of Property Left Behind" clause). Beyond that, no section of the Utah Code or Constitution bars you from evicting a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, or gives a victim a defense in an eviction case: the ordinary grounds (unpaid rent, lease breach, nuisance, a criminal act on the premises) apply with no victim exception. Two related rules: a victim's right to end the lease early ("Domestic Violence Lease Termination") is lost once you serve an eviction notice; and if you change the locks for a crime victim ("New Locks for Crime Victims"), you must refuse a key to the perpetrator, who if a renter on the lease may go to court. A court's protective order can exclude the abuser from the victim's residence; follow it. The cautious course is to act on the abuser's conduct rather than the victim's status: whether evicting a victim for an abuser's acts could be sex discrimination under fair housing law is a question for case law. If your property is in a federally covered housing program (for example public housing, Section 8 assistance or a low income housing tax credit property), federal law goes further: you may not deny admission to or evict an applicant or tenant because he or she is or has been a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking; an incident of that violence is not a serious or repeated lease violation or good cause to end the victim's tenancy; and you may split the lease to evict the abuser without penalizing the victim. You may still evict for a lease violation not based on that violence, if you hold the victim to no more demanding standard than other tenants, or where you can show an actual and imminent threat to other tenants or staff.

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations
bodyText: Utah's domestic violence rental rules borrow their definitions from the protective order chapter and the criminal code. As of November 8, 2026, every cross-reference they use points to a section that exists, including after Utah's 2026 recodification of the criminal code and criminal procedure titles (in force July 1, 2026). That covers the termination right ("Domestic Violence Lease Termination"), the crime victim lock change ("New Locks for Crime Victims"), the limit on penalizing calls for help ("Calling Police or Emergency Services") and the extra time a domestic violence victim gets to collect abandoned belongings ("Handling of Property Left Behind" clause). For termination, a qualifying court order is a civil protective order issued after a hearing with notice to both sides (child, dating violence, sexual violence, cohabitant abuse or workplace violence orders), a civil stalking injunction, a criminal protective order or a criminal stalking injunction, but not an ex parte protective order, or an ex parte stalking injunction for which a hearing has been requested. For a lock change, the order must be a cohabitant abuse protective order issued after a hearing with notice (see "Documents Domestic Violence Victims Give You"). From January 1, 2027, the lock-change list of qualifying crime victims no longer leaves out victims of enticing a minor, sexual battery, lewdness and lewdness involving a child. Three cross-references elsewhere that you may meet are out of date: the eviction statute's nuisance ground, and the 2026 law on off-limits orders for drug offenders (which a court may enter in a nuisance action), both still point to a nuisance section that Utah's 2026 nuisance law replaced with a new chapter ("Nuisance Abatement by Eviction"); and the community association law's definition of the protected areas from which an HOA rule may restrict a sex offender still points to a former registry section, while the condominium law points to the current one. Until the Legislature fixes them, read each as pointing to the current provision, and if a case turns on one, get legal advice; no case law was read.

title: Documents Domestic Violence Victims Give You
bodyText: Three Utah rental rules turn on documents a victim gives you, and each accepts a different list. None sets a time limit: neither the age of the order or report nor the time since the abuse cuts off the right. (1) Ending the lease early ("Domestic Violence Lease Termination"): the renter gives you either a court order protecting the renter from a domestic violence perpetrator, or a copy of a police report showing that the renter is a victim of domestic violence and not the predominant aggressor. A qualifying court order is a civil protective order issued after a hearing of which both sides had notice (a child, dating violence, sexual violence, cohabitant abuse or workplace violence protective order), a civil stalking injunction, a criminal protective order or a criminal stalking injunction; an ex parte protective order does not count, nor does an ex parte stalking injunction for which a hearing has been requested. The renter also gives you a written notice with the move-out date and pays the termination fee. If the renter fell behind on payments, or broke the duties not to damage the unit, disturb other renters or refuse repair access, in the 30 days before the notice because of the violence, the renter must also give you evidence of that with the notice; the law does not say what form that evidence takes. (2) New locks ("New Locks for Crime Victims"): a victim of domestic violence, stalking, a sexual offense (until January 1, 2027, not enticing a minor, sexual battery, lewdness or lewdness involving a child), burglary or dating violence gives you either a cohabitant abuse protective order protecting the renter, issued after a hearing of which both sides had notice, or a copy of a police report documenting the crime. Dating violence, sexual violence and stalking orders are not on this list, so a victim holding one of those uses a police report. (3) Extra time to collect belongings left after an abandonment ("Handling of Property Left Behind" clause): you must extend the 15-day period by up to 15 more calendar days if the tenant gives you a copy of a police report or a protection order for domestic violence; this list has no hearing requirement. These rules (except the third) are in the Fit Premises Act, which covers a renter's principal residence, not a boarding or rooming house, a mobile home lot or occasional recreational rental. In a federally covered housing program (for example public housing, Section 8 assistance or a low income housing tax credit property), a separate federal list applies when a tenant or applicant claims federal victim protection: you may, but need not, ask in writing for a HUD-approved certification form, a statement signed by both the tenant and a victim service provider, attorney, or medical or mental health professional, in which the professional states under penalty of perjury that he or she believes the incident qualifies, a law enforcement, court or administrative agency record, or, at your discretion, the tenant's own statement; the tenant has 14 business days to provide it, and you may extend that. Utah law does not say whether you may ask for more than its own listed documents, and it sets no remedy for a false one. The cautious course is to accept a document that matches the list without asking for more, keep it confidential ("No Domestic Violence Confidentiality Rule"), and get legal advice before refusing one; no case law was read.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText:
Under the Utah Fair Housing Act you may not refuse a reasonable accommodation in a rule, policy, practice or service when it may be necessary to give a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling, and you may not refuse to let a person with a disability make, at that person's own expense, reasonable modifications of the unit the person lives in or will live in when they are necessary for full enjoyment of it. In a rental you may, where it is reasonable, make your permission conditional on the renter agreeing to restore the interior, when reasonable, to its earlier condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted.

Disability means a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits major life activities, including a record of one or being regarded as having one; current illegal use of, or addiction to, a federally controlled substance is not a disability. The Act does not make you exercise a higher degree of care toward a person with a disability, and does not excuse anyone from obligations the written lease places on all tenants. It is a defense that the person's disability, even with reasonable accommodation, poses a serious threat to the health or safety of that person or others; you must prove it.

The Act does not cover a single-family home rented by an owner who holds fewer than four such homes for sale or lease, has not sold two or more non-residence homes in 24 months, uses no broker and makes no discriminatory statement or ad, or a room in a single-family dwelling rented by the owner who lives there, where the dwelling is designed for four or fewer families (the advertising rule still applies) ("Utah Fair Housing Act").

Separately, Utah's disability rights law gives people with disabilities equal access to rental housing and bars charging extra for a service or support animal ("Service and Support Animals Under Utah Law", "Service and Assistance Animals" clause); under the Labor Commission's rule you may verify a disability and the need for an assistance animal when they are not readily apparent. Utah law does not require the restoration condition to appear in the lease, and sets no restoration deposit or escrow.

Federal fair housing rules, where they apply, let you condition permission on a reasonable description of the work and assurances that it will be done in a workmanlike manner with any needed permits, forbid raising the usual security deposit, and, where necessary to make sure restoration money will be there, let you negotiate payments into an interest-bearing escrow account, over a reasonable period, of no more than the restoration cost, with the interest going to the tenant. An optional lease clause is "Disability Modifications and Restoring the Premises" clause.

Buildings of four or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991 must also meet accessible design requirements: every unit if the building has an elevator, and the ground-floor units otherwise.

title: Asking Applicants About Protected Traits
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution, apart from the fair housing ban on discrimination itself, forbids a landlord to ask an applicant or tenant about a protected trait or to keep a record of one. What the Utah Fair Housing Act does bar is any oral or written statement, notice or ad, and any application form, that directly or indirectly expresses a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, source of income, disability, sexual orientation or gender identity. That rule reaches even the small owners and owner-occupants who are otherwise outside the Act. A question on your application about one of those traits may be read as expressing such a preference; no case law was read on the point. Federal fair housing rules, where they apply, go further for disability: you may not ask whether an applicant, a future occupant or anyone associated with them has a disability, or about its nature or severity. You may ask every applicant, disabled or not, whether he or she can meet the requirements of the tenancy, whether he or she qualifies for housing or a priority reserved for people with disabilities, whether he or she currently illegally uses or is addicted to a controlled substance, and whether he or she has been convicted of illegally making or distributing one. The cautious course is to ask only what your written screening criteria need ("Screening Criteria Disclosure"), ask every applicant the same questions, and keep protected traits out of your files unless a housing program requires them. Related: "Utah Fair Housing Act", "Source of Income Protection".

title: Immigration Status and Renting
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution tells a landlord whether to ask about an applicant's or tenant's immigration status, bars you from asking, protects tenants from threats to report their status, or expressly makes renting to someone who is not lawfully present unlawful (the harboring crime below is the nearest rule). Immigration status and citizenship are not on the Utah Fair Housing Act's list of protected traits, but national origin is, and it means the place of birth of a person or of any of his or her ancestors; a status check applied only to some applicants because of where they or their families come from could be national origin discrimination. Utah's harboring crime is aimed at concealment and inducement, not at renting as such (whether it can reach a landlord who knowingly rents to someone unlawfully present is case law, so never hide a tenant from authorities or recruit tenants because they are unlawfully present): it applies to a person who, knowingly and with intent to violate federal immigration law, conceals, harbors or shelters from detection a person illegally present for commercial advantage or private financial gain, knowing or in reckless disregard of that presence, or who encourages or induces such a person to come to, enter or reside in Utah knowing or in reckless disregard that it is unlawful. No case law was read on how it applies to renting. After an eviction, the tenant must be given access within 5 business days to documents including those about immigration or employment status ("Tenant Property and Animals After an Eviction"). The cautious course is to screen every applicant by the same written criteria ("Screening Criteria Disclosure"), accept any reliable proof of identity and income rather than demanding immigration papers, and not threaten or mention a tenant's status.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a landlord to tell a tenant or applicant that a registered sex, kidnap or child abuse offender lives in or near the property, to put a registry notice in the lease, or to check the registry. The registry law says expressly that it creates no duty on anyone to request or obtain offender information.

The state publishes the registry on a public website (the Sex, Kidnap, and Child Abuse Offender Notification and Registration website), searchable by surname and postal code, showing each offender's residence addresses, photograph, vehicles and registrable offenses; users must agree not to use the information to harass or threaten an offender or the offender's family.

A nearby offender is not one of the stigmas Utah's no-liability rule lists (a homicide, other felony or suicide on the site, an occupant's non-transmissible infection, or decontaminated drug contamination; see "Stigmatized Property"), so that rule does not cover it; whether failing to mention an offender you know about could ever create liability is a question for case law.

The cautious course is not to make statements about who does or does not live nearby, and to point tenants to the public website instead; an optional lease notice is "Registered Offender Information" clause. For rules on renting to offenders, see "Renting to Registered Offenders".

title: Renting to Registered Offenders
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution makes it an offense for a landlord to rent to a registered sex offender, and apart from the victim-requested restriction described below, none limits where an offender may live: there is no distance-from-school residency rule, no ban on two or more offenders living together, and no lease statement a landlord must collect. Utah's restriction runs against the offender, not you: a sex offender who committed a registrable offense against someone under 18 may not be in a protected area, which includes a licensed day care or preschool, a school, and a public pool, park or playground, or one maintained, operated or owned by an apartment complex, homeowners' association or condominium project, with exceptions for parental duties and some school and day-care uses (and for a 55-or-older complex's pool or park when no minors are present). An offender under a victim-requested restriction while on probation or parole may also not be within 1,000 feet of the victim's residence. A condominium or homeowners' association may adopt a rule restricting a sex offender from its own protected areas; those statutes name associations only and say nothing about a landlord's own rule for an apartment complex pool or playground (no case law was read). If you screen for criminal history, disclose your criteria in writing before taking an application fee ("Screening Criteria Disclosure") and apply them to everyone. Disclosure questions: "No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty".

title: Protecting Tenant Information
bodyText: No Utah statute bars a landlord in general from sharing a tenant's or applicant's information or sets a consent rule for doing so. Utah's general data law does reach you: anyone who does business in Utah and keeps a person's name together with a Social Security number, a driver license or state ID number, or a financial account or card number with the code that opens it must keep reasonable procedures to prevent unlawful use or disclosure of that information, and must destroy records of it that won't be kept by shredding, erasing or otherwise making the information unreadable. If such computer data is breached, you must promptly investigate and, if misuse for identity theft or fraud has occurred or is reasonably likely, notify each affected Utah resident (and the Attorney General and the Utah Cyber Center at 500 or more residents, and the national credit bureaus at 1,000 or more); a waiver of the breach rule is void. The Attorney General enforces these rules with civil penalties of up to $2,500 per consumer and $100,000 for related violations; the act gives no private right to sue but leaves contract and tort claims open. A written cybersecurity program that meets Utah's standards, in place at the time of a breach, gives you an affirmative defense to claims about the breach. You may not display a Social Security number where it is likely to be open to public view. Utah's notice rule for selling personal information does not apply to transactions related to real property, and its consumer privacy act reaches only businesses with annual revenue of $25 million or more that handle data of 100,000 or more consumers (or 25,000 with most revenue from selling data). A city's good landlord program may not collect from you a tenant's credit report, criminal history or lease unless you agree and the law allows it, and a condominium or homeowners' association generally may not make you hand over a renter's application, credit report, background check or age documents. For victims' papers see "No Domestic Violence Confidentiality Rule"; for expunged evictions see "Eviction Record Expungement". Federal rules also require anyone who holds consumer report information for a business purpose to dispose of it with reasonable measures against unauthorized access.

title: Tenant Records and Rent Ledgers
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a residential landlord to keep a rent ledger, give rent receipts, include a payment history in a nonpayment notice, or answer a tenant's request for records. The written records Utah does require are specific: the pre-application disclosures and screening criteria ("Screening Criteria Disclosure"), the move-in condition record or walkthrough, an executed copy of a written lease and the rules ("Copy of Lease and Rules"), and the itemized deposit accounting within 30 days after move-out ("Deposit Return Penalty Process"). Most of these are in the Fit Premises Act, which covers a renter's principal residence, not a boarding or rooming house, a mobile home lot or occasional recreational rental. Utah's general data security law does reach a landlord who holds applicants' Social Security numbers, driver license numbers or bank and card account data: you must keep reasonable procedures to prevent unlawful use or disclosure, destroy records you won't keep by shredding, erasing or making them unreadable, and investigate and give notice of a breach; details are in "Protecting Tenant Information". The cautious course is to keep a dated ledger of every charge and payment anyway, since you will need it to prove amounts owed in an eviction or deposit dispute.

title: Screening Property Management Staff
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a landlord to run background checks on apartment or rental-property employees, such as managers, leasing agents or maintenance staff who hold keys. The state does screen one group through licensing: an individual may not engage in property management for others for consideration (advertising or arranging rentals, collecting rent, or signing leases or addenda with tenants for real estate owned by another person) unless licensed as a principal broker, associate broker, sales agent, dual broker or property manager (managing others' property for pay is already a principal broker's act; the separate property manager license begins January 1, 2027), and license applicants, including every property manager applicant from January 1, 2027, must submit fingerprints and consent to a state and FBI criminal background check, with ongoing monitoring. No license is needed by an owner or lessor managing his or her own property, the owner's immediate family managing the owner's property, an unlicensed or remote assistant of a property manager, someone who only does maintenance and repairs or bookkeeping and accounting, or a regional manager or corporate official of a rental agency who does none of the management acts. If you screen employees yourself using consumer reports, federal credit reporting rules on employment screening apply. The cautious course for staff with key access is a written, consistently applied hiring screen.

title: No Work Cards for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires staff of a 55-or-older or other senior housing community to hold a work card or permit, or requires the landlord to screen them. What Utah law says about senior housing for landlords is that the Utah Fair Housing Act's familial-status rules do not apply to a complex, condominium or other development designated as housing for older persons under the federal fair housing law ("Utah Fair Housing Act", "Children and Occupancy Limits"). Staff who manage property for others for pay need a real estate license now (a separate property manager license becomes available from January 1, 2027), with a fingerprint background check; assistants of a licensed manager and staff who only do maintenance, repairs or bookkeeping are exempt ("Screening Property Management Staff"). Licensed assisted living or nursing facilities are governed by health facility licensing law.

title: Reporting Rent to Credit Bureaus
bodyText:
Utah has no state rent-reporting program, does not require any landlord to offer tenants positive rent reporting, and does not bar you from requiring or offering it.

Utah does have a notice rule for negative credit reports: a creditor may submit a negative credit report (information about late or irregular payment, delinquency or default that would be expected to hurt the person's ability to get credit) only if it notifies the person in writing, in person, by first-class mail to the last-known address or, with consent, by email, no more than 30 days after it submits the report; one notice covers later reports on the same obligation.

A notice substantially in the statute's form is enough, and it may be part of a default notice or other letter. A creditor who fails to give it is liable for actual damages, the winner of the suit gets costs and attorney fees, and a willful violation can bring punitive damages of up to twice actual damages, unless the creditor kept reasonable procedures to comply.

The rule is in Utah's Consumer Credit Code and covers creditors that regularly extend consumer credit; whether a landlord reporting unpaid rent is such a creditor is not settled by the statute, so the cautious course is to give the notice whenever you or a collection agency will report unpaid rent (optional clause "Credit Reporting of Unpaid Amounts").

Federal credit reporting law also bars anyone from furnishing information about a consumer to a credit bureau if the furnisher knows or has reasonable cause to believe it is inaccurate. A city's good landlord program may not collect a tenant's consumer report from you unless you agree and the law allows it ("Protecting Tenant Information").

title: Rent-Setting Software
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution specifically addresses landlords who set rents or lease terms using pricing software or an algorithm. Utah's general antitrust law still applies to rental housing as to any trade: every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade is illegal, and so is monopolizing, attempting to monopolize, or combining or conspiring to monopolize any part of trade. A Utah citizen or resident injured, or threatened with injury, in business or property (including a tenant who dealt with you only indirectly) may sue for an injunction and three times the damages, plus costs and attorney fees, and the Utah Constitution states the same free-market policy. The Legislature has told Utah courts to follow federal court readings of comparable federal antitrust law. Whether sharing confidential rent or occupancy data with competing landlords through a common pricing tool, or following its recommendations, amounts to an agreement in restraint of trade is a question of case law. The cautious course is to set your own rents, not to share nonpublic rent, vacancy or lease-term data with competitors (directly or through a vendor), and to treat any software recommendation as advice you are free to reject. Utah also preempts local rent control ("State Preemption of Rent Control and Local Landlord Rules").

title: Children and Occupancy Limits
bodyText:
Utah does not require a lease to say anything about children, but the Utah Fair Housing Act bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, or advertising a preference because of familial status: having one or more children under 18 living with a parent, legal custodian or the custodian's written designee, and also being pregnant, being in the process of getting legal custody of a child, or being single.

The Act allows any reasonable local, state or federal restriction on the maximum number of occupants of a dwelling, and its familial-status rules do not apply to a development designated as housing for older persons under the federal fair housing law. The small-owner and owner-occupant exemptions apply ("Utah Fair Housing Act"), though even exempt owners may not advertise a preference.

Under the Fit Premises Act (a renter's principal residence, not a boarding or rooming house, mobile home lot or occasional recreational rental), a renter may not increase the number of occupants above the number in the rental agreement without your written permission ("Permitted Occupants" clause).

Utah has no statute on a child born or adopted during the tenancy; whether enforcing an occupancy figure against a household that grows by a child is familial-status discrimination is a question for case law.

The cautious course is to base any occupancy limit on a reasonable government standard rather than a stricter number of your own, count children like adults, and give a growing family a reasonable chance to move to a larger unit or the end of the term rather than an immediate notice.

title: No Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives a landlord a tax credit, grant or other incentive for renting to a veteran or servicemember, requires you to give them a rent preference, or makes veteran or military status a protected class in housing. Utah's veteran property tax exemption applies to property owned by qualifying veterans, not to landlords who rent to them, and the state's homeless-to-housing account may fund programs that serve veterans among other groups, which is a government program rather than a landlord duty. You may offer your own concession to veterans if you apply it consistently and it does not work as a preference based on a protected trait such as disability or familial status ("Utah Fair Housing Act"). Servicemember tenants have eviction protections during state military service and federal lease rights ("Servicemember Tenant Protections").

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives a renter a right to display religious or cultural items on a door, doorframe or elsewhere at a rental, or limits a landlord's rules on such displays. Utah's display protections for religious and holiday signs, symbols and decorations bind condominium and homeowners' associations and protect unit and lot owners: an association rule may not abridge a condominium unit owner's right to display them inside the unit, or a lot owner's right to display them on the lot, the dwelling's exterior or front yard (subject in each case to reasonable time, place and manner limits on displays visible from outside). Those rules protect owners, not their tenants, and do not bind a landlord's own rules; if your rental is in an association, its rules may still limit what your tenant may put up. The Utah Fair Housing Act bars discrimination in the terms of a rental because of religion, so a display rule must be neutral and applied the same way to every faith. The only display right Utah gives renters directly is for United States and Utah flags ("Flag Display").

title: Political Signs, Canvassing and Candidate Access
bodyText: For apartments and other ordinary rentals, no section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a landlord to let candidates, canvassers or petition circulators into a building, or gives a renter a right to post political signs; your rules on these must not treat tenants differently because of race, religion or another trait the fair housing law protects ("Utah Fair Housing Act"). Mobile home parks are different. A park operator must permit a resident association's meetings in the park for manufactured home living or social or educational purposes, including forums for or speeches by public officials or candidates for public office, and, except for reasonable time, place and manner limits, may not prohibit or adopt a rule prohibiting a resident or a resident advocacy group from exercising free expression for noncommercial purposes in the park, including peacefully organizing, assembling, canvassing, petitioning, leafleting or distributing written noncommercial material ("Tenant Organizing"). Condominium and homeowners' associations may not prohibit an owner from displaying a political sign or flag in a window (and in a homeowners' association, on the lot, exterior or front yard) or regulate its content except to restrict obscene, profane or commercial content; those rules protect owners, not tenants. Renters may display United States and Utah flags ("Flag Display").

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: For apartments, houses and other ordinary rentals, no section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives tenants a right to organize or form a tenant association, or bars a landlord from interfering with one; the only related protection is the fair housing ban on coercion, threats, interference or reprisal against a person who exercises, or helps another exercise, fair housing rights, or who opposes a discriminatory practice or takes part in a fair housing complaint ("Utah Fair Housing Act", "No General Retaliation Statute"). Mobile home parks have a full statute. Residents (people who lease or rent a space in the park) may form a resident association and join regional, state or national resident or advocacy groups, and residents may attend association meetings whether or not they are members. A park operator, including its employees, agents and contractors, may not be a member, may not attend a meeting without an officer's written invitation, may not unlawfully interfere with the association's operation, harass or threaten it, or interfere with a resident's right to complain to a health department, municipality or other group about health and safety conditions. The operator must permit association meetings in the park (including forums with public officials or candidates), must let the association schedule the park's common facilities free of charge (the operator may limit use to no less than once a week), may not charge more than the usual uniform deposit for that use, and may require liability insurance only where alcohol is to be served under park rules that allow it. Except for reasonable time, place and manner limits, the operator may not bar residents or resident advocacy groups from noncommercial free expression in the park, including organizing, assembling, canvassing, petitioning and leafleting. The operator also may not alter or refuse to renew a rental agreement, change or unevenly enforce rules, threaten or bring an eviction, or take other action in retaliation based primarily on a resident's complaint to a government agency or to the operator in good faith, lawsuit, or testimony. The operator need recognize only the primary (largest) association when there is more than one, and may still evict for the causes the Mobile Home Park Residency Act allows.

title: Guests and Visitors
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives a tenant a statutory right to receive guests, caregivers or suppliers, bars a guest fee, or limits a landlord's guest rules, so guest terms are a matter for the lease ("Guest Policy" clause, "Guest Policy (14-Day Limit)" clause); any fee for guests must be stated in the lease ("Fees Must Be in the Lease") and guest rules must be applied the same way to everyone ("Utah Fair Housing Act").

Utah does treat guests in a few places. Under the Fit Premises Act (a renter's principal residence, not a boarding or rooming house, mobile home lot or occasional recreational rental), a condition the renter's guest or invitee causes is not one you must repair under the renter-remedy process ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions").

In a mobile home park, behavior by a resident's invited guest or visitor that threatens the safety or health of others in the park, or damages park property, is a cause to terminate the lease, and the park may not make residents buy exterior materials or tie-down equipment from a supplier it designates.

A long-term guest (not a tenant or immediate family member, staying more than 48 hours without paying or working for the stay) who remains after the owner or a tenant tells him or her to leave commits criminal trespass, unless another owner or tenant has given express permission to stay that has not been revoked or voided ("Removing Trespassers and Long-Term Guests").

title: Reporting Duties and Police Cooperation
bodyText: Several Utah reporting duties bind every person, so they bind you and your staff when you learn something on the job. If you have reason to believe a child is or has been abused or neglected, or see a child in conditions that would reasonably result in abuse or neglect, you must immediately report it to the Division of Child and Family Services or the nearest peace officer or law enforcement agency. If you have reason to believe a vulnerable adult is or has been abused, neglected or exploited, you must immediately report it to Adult Protective Services or the nearest peace officer or law enforcement agency. Willfully failing to make either report is a class B misdemeanor. If you find, or have custody of, a body where the death appears to be by violence, gunshot, suicide or accident, was sudden in apparent good health, was unattended, or occurred in suspicious or unusual circumstances (among other listed cases), you must immediately notify the nearest law enforcement agency; for an unattended death, the person with custody of the body must notify the medical examiner. If a court authorizes a wiretap, pen register or trap and trace device, a landlord asked by the authorized officers must furnish the information, facilities and technical assistance needed, and is paid reasonable expenses; the statute also bars suits over assistance given under such an order against the communications provider and other specified persons. Utah has no crime-free housing statute: no law requires a crime-free lease addendum, and a city may not require a landlord to deny tenancy because of an applicant's criminal history unless a facility housing released parolees or probation violators is located in the city. A city's good landlord program may, however, offer a fee reduction to landlords who implement crime-reduction measures its ordinance or policy specifies. You may not restrict a renter's calls for police or emergency help or penalize reasonable calls ("Calling Police or Emergency Services"), and eviction for criminal acts and nuisances follows the ordinary process ("Expedited Hearing for Criminal Conduct", "Nuisance Abatement by Eviction").

title: Drug-Free Housing Terms
bodyText:
Utah does not require a drug-free housing addendum, but you may use one (optional clause "Controlled Substances and Cannabis"), and Utah law gives you reasons to. An owner or other person in control of a building, room or other place who knowingly and intentionally lets someone occupy it while the person is unlawfully making, possessing, using or distributing a controlled substance there commits a crime (a class B misdemeanor the first time, rising to a felony on a third conviction). Knowingly renting or making premises available for the purpose of unlawful drug manufacture, storage, distribution or use is a second degree felony, and any dwelling or place where people resort to use controlled substances, or that is used to keep or sell them, is a common nuisance that no one may open, keep or maintain.

A tenant's breach of a drug-free covenant can be enforced by a three-day notice to comply or quit; drug crimes on the premises and drug nuisances can also be pursued as a criminal-act eviction, a nuisance eviction, or a private nuisance action by neighbors, with a fast hearing for criminal conduct ("Expedited Hearing for Criminal Conduct", "Nuisance Abatement by Eviction"). Mobile home parks may terminate for use or distribution of illegal drugs that threatens others in the park.

Utah gives medical cannabis cardholders no housing protection, so your lease may bar cannabis ("Medical Cannabis and Rentals"); say expressly whether medical cannabis is allowed. A property contaminated by methamphetamine must be disclosed ("Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure" clause). You may not restrict a tenant's calls for police or emergency help ("Calling Police or Emergency Services"). Federally assisted housing has its own addendum and rules.

title: Government Inspections of Utah Rentals
bodyText:
Utah has no statewide rental inspection program. A city or town may, by ordinance, require the owner of a rental dwelling (a home available or built to be rented for a month or longer) to hold a regulatory business license and to allow inspections as a condition of that license.

The city may not charge a fee for the inspection, may not make an owner of several rentals hold more than one regulatory license, and once an inspection approves the dwelling it may not inspect again except as the good landlord statute allows. No city or town may make you submit to a random building inspection without cause and notice. An owner who gets no compensation from the dwelling can opt out of the license by signed affidavit.

Counties have no rental-dwelling licensing statute of their own; a county may license businesses in its unincorporated area. State law does not let a local or state health inspector, or a fire officer, enter a private dwelling for a routine inspection.

No Utah statute makes a tenant admit a government inspector or lets a lease give that consent for the tenant. Your tenant's own duty is not to unreasonably refuse you, your agent or manager entry to make repairs, and you must give 24 hours' notice of entry unless the lease says otherwise.

Whether a lease term can count as the tenant's consent to an inspector's entry is a constitutional question for the courts, so do not rely on one: arrange inspections with your tenant, or use the optional cooperation clause ("Government Inspections" clause). Check your city's ordinance for its licensing and inspection rules.

title: Local Health Department Rules for Rentals
bodyText: Utah's Fit Premises Act makes you keep a rental fit for human habitation and in line with local ordinances and the rules of the local board of health for the area, and it makes your tenant follow that board's rules that materially affect health and safety. Each county's local health department enforces state health laws and its own board's regulations in every city and unincorporated area it serves, may investigate and inspect, may issue notices and orders, and may abate a nuisance and bill the owner or person in charge. Whoever controls the property, owner or tenant, must remove or abate a nuisance, health hazard or sanitation violation within the time the health department orders, not more than 30 days; violating a health order is a misdemeanor and the violator pays the abatement cost. The health department's routine-inspection entry power does not extend to private dwellings. A person affected by a health department action can ask for a hearing. No Utah statute requires you to give a tenant the health department's rental rules on request or to refer a tenant to the health department; the only statutory protection for contacting a health department is for mobile home park residents. The content of each local board's housing or sanitation regulations is not in this library, so check the regulations of the health department serving your county. These Fit Premises Act duties cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Owner-Occupancy Limits on Renting Homes
bodyText: No Utah statute bars renting a house in a single-family zone unless the owner lives on the lot, and Utah has no state lot-split or two-unit program with an owner-occupancy condition. Owner occupancy matters in three places. First, an internal accessory dwelling unit (an apartment created inside the footprint of a detached single-family home that the owner of record lives in) is a permitted use in residential zones, but the city or county may prohibit renting it if the home is not the owner's primary residence, may prohibit renting it for less than 30 consecutive days, and may require a rental permit or license. Second, a larger city that must allow detached accessory dwelling units on lots of 11,000 square feet or more may require the owner to live in the house or the detached unit, and may bar renting the detached unit for less than 90 consecutive days. Third, where a city or county grants a density bonus for affordable single-family homes, it may require that at least 60% of the homes be deed-restricted to owner occupancy for at least five years, and a state first home village must keep at least 25% of its homes owner occupied for 25 years; check the deed and plat before you buy such a home to rent. A city may not regulate a co-owned home differently from other homes. Separately, a homeowners' or condominium association may restrict or prohibit rentals in its recorded declaration, with exemptions that turn partly on who lives in the home ("HOA and Condominium Rental Rules"). Local zoning may still limit rentals in ways not covered here; check the city's or county's ordinance.

title: No Good-Cause Notice in Utah
bodyText: Utah has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law for houses and apartments, so there is no notice telling a tenant whether such a law covers the unit and nothing of that kind to put in the lease. A fixed term ends on its end date without notice, and you may end a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy by serving notice at least 15 calendar days before the end of a rental period without giving a reason ("No Just-Cause Eviction Rule", "Utah Eviction Notices by Tenancy Type"). The shorter eviction notices are tied to what the tenant did: a notice for unpaid rent must demand the rent or possession, and a notice for another lease breach must demand performance or possession, so write the default into the notice. Two exceptions sit outside ordinary rentals. Mobile home park space leases may be ended only by agreement or for causes the Mobile Home Park Residency Act lists. And if your tenant has a federal Housing Choice Voucher, during the lease term you may end the tenancy only for a serious or repeated lease violation, a violation of law tied to the occupancy, or other good cause, and you must give the tenant a written notice stating the grounds, with a copy of any eviction notice to the housing authority.

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: No Utah statute requires you to give a tenant a statement or summary of tenant rights prepared by a state agency, to attach one to the lease or put it on the first page, to get the tenant's signed acknowledgment, or to provide one before you can sue. Utah also has no truth-in-renting statement ("No Truth-in-Renting Statement in Utah"). What Utah does require in writing is set out in "Utah Notices That Must Be in Writing": the pre-application disclosures before you take an application fee, the owner and manager contact disclosure at or before the start of the tenancy, and an executed copy of a written lease and any rules ("Copy of Lease and Rules"). The one statutory rights disclosure is for mobile home park space leases, which must conspicuously describe the resident's protection against termination without cause and the resident's rights to end the lease and sell the home, and the park must post a copy of the Mobile Home Park Residency Act; that rule does not reach houses or apartments.

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: No Utah statute requires a state agency to publish a guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, and none requires you to give a tenant such a guide before signing or at renewal or to get a signed acknowledgment. The state fair housing division may run programs to make landlords and others aware of their fair housing rights and responsibilities, but that creates no duty for you to hand anything to a tenant. You still must give an executed copy of a written lease and any rules at or before the start of the tenancy ("Copy of Lease and Rules"); that Fit Premises Act rule covers a renter's principal residence, not a boarding or rooming house, a mobile home lot or occasional recreational rental. See also "No State Tenant Rights Statement" and "No Truth-in-Renting Statement in Utah".

title: Changing Terms of a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText:
Utah has no statute that sets a notice period for changing the rent or other terms of a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, and none that says a term change must be made by a termination notice.

One rule is fixed: you may not charge a fee, fine, assessment, interest or other cost in an amount greater than the amount agreed to in the rental agreement, and that bar has no month-to-month exception. The only notice route in the statute is for a charge that is not in the rental agreement at all: on a month-to-month agreement you may add it after giving the tenant 15 days' notice.

To raise the rent or an agreed fee, or change another term, get the tenant's agreement to the change, ideally a signed written amendment (the law treats any agreement, written or oral, that modifies the terms as part of the rental agreement), or end the tenancy by serving notice at least 15 calendar days before the end of a rental period and offer a new agreement on the new terms ("Notice to End a Month-to-Month Tenancy" clause, "No Rent-Increase Notice Rule"). A tenancy at will can be ended on five calendar days' notice.

Whether a tenant who stays on after your notice of new terms has accepted them is a question for the courts, so do not rely on silence.

Mobile home park space is different: an increase in rent or fees for a periodic tenancy is unenforceable until 60 days after notice is mailed. These Fit Premises Act fee rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Repair Orders and Receivership for Substandard Rentals
bodyText: Utah has no statute that lets a city, county or tenant put a substandard rental building into receivership so a receiver collects the rents and makes repairs, and no special rule for buildings of two or more units. Utah's general receivership law lets a court appoint a receiver over real property, including a rental of one to four units when the owner collects rents, but the grounds are those of a creditor or party with an interest in the property (waste, a judgment, a mortgage default, equitable grounds), not code violations. Code enforcement works through other tools. A city may declare and abate nuisances and fine those who keep them; its nuisance inspector must give written notice and at least 10 days to comply (180 days for a hazardous-materials notice) before abating at your cost and liening the property, and generally may not order work on conditions solely inside a building unless the building is being demolished or was closed for hazardous materials. The local health department may abate a nuisance or health hazard and bill the owner, and you must abate within the time it orders, not more than 30 days. A city or county using a state-approved code may adopt an ordinance requiring removal, demolition or repair of a building, a dangerous building code or a rehabilitation code. A court may also order abatement by eviction of an unsafe building or place, meaning one used for drug dealing, gang crime, prostitution or similar activity, and you are a necessary party when a tenant or third party is the cause. A city's or county's enforcement of an administrative remedy may not change the Fit Premises Act's corrective periods, a tenant's remedies or your habitability duties to the tenant; that Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not a boarding or rooming house, a mobile home lot or occasional recreational rental. Check the local ordinance for any dangerous-building or repair-order procedure.

title: Lead Certificates and the Lease
