bodyText: Utah has no lead-safe certificate for rental units and no state rule requiring a lead inspection or certificate to be attached to a lease. The only lead attachment is federal: for housing built before 1978 (except housing for the elderly or people with disabilities and studio or other zero-bedroom units where no child under 6 lives or is expected to live), each lease must include, as an attachment or within the lease, the federal Lead Warning Statement, your disclosure of any known lead-based paint or hazards (or that you know of none), a list of any lead records or reports you have given the tenant, the tenant's acknowledgment of receiving them and the federal lead pamphlet, any agent's statement, and the signatures and dates. Give the disclosure and pamphlet before the tenant is obligated under the lease, and keep a copy for at least three years from the start of the lease. Use the library's lead-based paint disclosure clause. Utah's own lead law certifies people who do lead inspection, abatement and renovation work; it does not certify rental units.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit in Utah
bodyText:
Utah protects internal accessory dwelling units: an apartment created inside the existing footprint of a detached single-family home that the owner of record lives in, for long-term rental of 30 consecutive days or longer. In any area zoned primarily residential, one internal unit is a permitted use, and the city or county may not restrict it beyond a set list.

From that list, the city or county may require a permit or license to rent it, may prohibit renting it if the home is not the owner's primary residence, may prohibit renting it for less than 30 consecutive days, may bar a separate utility meter, may require an extra parking space, may require that the unit not change the home's single-family appearance, may bar units in zoning districts covering up to a set share of its residential area, and may bar units on lots of 6,000 square feet or less, in homes on failing septic tanks or in mobile homes.

If you break a valid rule, the city or county must give written notice and a chance to cure (at least 14 days for renting for under 30 days, 30 days otherwise) before it can record a lien of up to $100 a day. The unit must meet building, health and fire codes, and the state's protection for existing undersized bedroom windows does not apply to it, so you may have to install an egress window.

Larger cities must also allow detached accessory dwelling units on lots of 11,000 square feet or more, and may require the owner to live in the house or the detached unit and may bar renting the detached unit for less than 90 consecutive days.

A homeowners association may not prohibit building an internal unit or restrict or prohibit renting one that meets land use, building, health and fire codes; the condominium statute has no such rule. A tenant renting the unit as a principal residence has the same Fit Premises Act rights as any other tenant. The optional shared-lot clause ("The Premises Is an Accessory Dwelling Unit" clause) records who lives in the main house and which areas are shared.

title: Utah Lead Notices Beyond the Federal Rule
bodyText:
No Utah statute requires a lead notice, certificate or information packet with a lease beyond the federal lead-based paint disclosure.

For housing built before 1978 the federal rule applies: before your tenant is obligated, give the federal lead pamphlet and disclose any known lead-based paint or hazards and any reports, with the signed certification in or attached to the lease ("Lead Certificates and the Lease", "Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause).

Utah's lead law is about people, not leases: the Air Quality Board certifies lead inspectors, risk assessors, abatement workers and renovators and sets their work practices, and the health department runs a child blood lead program.

If you hire anyone to renovate or repair painted surfaces in a pre-1978 rental, the cautious course is to use a certified renovator; the board's rules and the federal renovation rule may require information to be given to occupants before the work.

No Utah statute requires a landlord notice about lead service lines or lead in a rental's drinking water; the state's lead-in-water testing statute covers schools and child care centers.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: No Utah statute requires you to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy, to give the tenant a copy, or to attach one to the lease, and no Utah statute itself addresses renting a unit that lacks one; whether a unit may be occupied before a certificate issues is set by the building codes Utah adopts by reference, so do not rent a new, converted or altered unit until the building official has issued its certificate of occupancy. The certificate matters before you rent: a city or county may enforce its ordinances by withholding a building permit or certificate of occupancy, and building, altering or changing the use of a building without a building permit is an infraction in a city and unlawful in a county. Once issued, a certificate of occupancy cannot be withdrawn unless later changes that need a building permit are made. A structure finished without a permit, inspections or certificate may face added permitting or inspections if it was completed ten years ago or less or poses a health, life or safety concern. Separately, renting a unit that is not safe, sanitary and fit is barred by the Fit Premises Act ("Utah Fit Premises Act: Owner and Renter Duties"). Check your city's or county's rental licensing rules, which may ask for proof of occupancy approval.

title: Disclosing Inspection and Condemnation Orders
bodyText: Utah has no general rule requiring you to tell a prospective tenant about outstanding code violations, inspection orders or condemnation or vacate orders. One disclosure is required: if you actually know the property is currently contaminated from the use, storage or manufacture of methamphetamine, the lease must disclose it, and a tenant can sue for damages, costs and attorney fees if you do not ("Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure" clause). Once the local health department finds the property decontaminated, that duty ends. A local health department places drug-lab-contaminated properties on a public contamination list and may close a structure to occupancy. Even without a disclosure rule, you may not rent premises that are not safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, and a lease that hides a known unfit condition invites claims. If you receive a city or health department order about the property, deal with it before you rent, and check your city's licensing rules for any local disclosure.

title: No Penalty Tied to Move-In or Move-Out Inspections
bodyText: Utah does not require you to tell a tenant about move-in or move-out inspection rights, and it sets no penalty, such as losing the right to deduct from the deposit, for skipping an inspection. Before signing, you must do one of three things: give a written inventory of the unit's condition, give the tenant a condition form to complete within a reasonable time after moving in, or offer a walkthrough ("Move-In Condition Record"). If you fail to, the tenant cannot use that failure to avoid the lease or to sue you, but you will have a harder time proving damage later. Utah's only deposit penalty is for not returning the deposit balance and itemized deductions: within 30 days after the tenant vacates, and then within five business days after the tenant serves the statutory notice, or you owe the full deposit, any prepaid rent and a $100 civil penalty, plus costs and fees if you acted in bad faith ("Deposit Return Penalty Process"). These Fit Premises Act duties cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Rent for Condemned or Unfit Premises
bodyText: No Utah statute bars collecting rent after a city or health department condemns a rental or orders it vacated, for houses and apartments. The Fit Premises Act does three related things. You may not rent premises that are not safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy. If your tenant serves a written notice of a deficient condition choosing rent abatement and you do not take substantial action within the corrective period, rent is abated from the date of the notice, the lease ends, you must immediately return the whole deposit and prorated prepaid rent, and the tenant must move out within 10 calendar days after the corrective period. And if the unit is not fit for occupancy, you may decide not to repair and end the lease by written notice by the end of the corrective period, prorating rent to that date, refunding prepaid rent and any deposit due within 10 calendar days, and giving the tenant at least 10 calendar days to leave. A local enforcement order may not shorten those periods or reduce the tenant's remedies. Whether rent is owed for a period when a government order bars occupancy is otherwise a contract question for the courts, so do not charge rent for days the tenant cannot lawfully live there. Mobile home parks are different: after notice of a planned closure or condemnation, the park may not raise rent. The fire and casualty clause covers destruction ("Fire or Other Casualty" clause).

title: Code Variances and Tenant Notice
bodyText: No Utah statute requires you to give tenants a copy of a health, sanitary, housing, building or fire code variance or exception for your rental, or to attach one to the lease. Utah has no state sanitary or housing code for rentals: the habitability standards come from the Fit Premises Act, local ordinances and the rules of the local board of health. A zoning variance from a city or county appeal authority runs with the land and carries no tenant-notice rule. Whether a local health department's regulations allow variances and require them to be shared with occupants is in local regulations; check with the health department that granted any variance. A variance does not relax your Fit Premises Act duties to the tenant.

title: Which Code Edition Applies in Utah
bodyText: Utah freezes its building and fire codes at editions the Legislature names in statute; a newer national edition does not apply until the Legislature adopts it. Today the State Construction Code uses the 2024 International Building, Plumbing, Mechanical, Fuel Gas, Energy Conservation, Existing Building and Swimming Pool and Spa Codes, but the 2021 International Residential Code (for one- and two-family homes and townhouses) and the 2023 National Electrical Code, with Utah amendments. The State Fire Code is the 2024 International Fire Code without its appendices, plus named 2024 NFPA standards; separately, cities and counties may adopt the appendices of the 2021 International Fire Code. From January 1, 2027 the 2024 International Wildland-Urban Interface Code replaces the 2006 Utah wildland code. For an existing rental, the construction code applies when you build new or voluntarily repair, remodel, alter or change the use of the building, not merely because a new edition is adopted. A city may not make you retrofit a rental with a safety feature that was not required when it was built, except as the construction code requires for a structural change or under an ordinance adopted before 2008, and in a legal nonconforming rental it may require only listed items such as smoke detectors, GFCI outlets on existing wiring, handrails and, with limits, egress bedroom windows. An existing bedroom window that met the code when the bedroom was finished need not be enlarged in a detached one- to four-family dwelling or qualifying town home if the change would compromise the structure or cannot meet current code, except in an internal accessory dwelling unit. The International Property Maintenance Code is not part of the state code; cities may adopt it locally. Your lease does not change which edition applies.

title: Utah State Fire Code and Rentals
bodyText:
The State Fire Code is the code that cities, counties, fire protection districts and the state must follow; it is the 2024 International Fire Code, without its appendices, with Utah's statewide amendments and three named 2024 NFPA standards, and it changes only when the Legislature adopts a new edition.

Building construction and alteration follow a different set of editions: the 2024 International Building Code for apartment buildings but the 2021 International Residential Code for one- and two-family homes and townhouses ("Which Code Edition Applies in Utah").

A city or county may adopt a stricter fire code to meet a local public safety need, may adopt the fire code appendices and a sprinkler ordinance under state limits, but generally may not, after December 1, 2016, adopt or enforce a fire rule stricter than the State Fire Code for a structure built under the International Residential Code.

A fire chief or officer may enter and inspect a building or premises not used as a private dwelling at any reasonable hour, and the owner, lessee, manager or operator must permit it, so common areas of apartment buildings can be inspected; the statute gives no such entry into a private dwelling ("Government Inspections of Utah Rentals").

For a single-family home, the city or county must provide a review of a fire code compliance inspection within 30 days of notice. Smoke and carbon monoxide alarm duties come from these codes and local ordinances ("Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms"). The optional fire safety clause ("Fire Safety Compliance" clause) puts the tenant's part in the lease.

title: Recording a Lease in Utah
bodyText: Utah has no lease registry, and no statute requires you to record a residential lease or makes any tenant right depend on recording. Recording matters only for a lease longer than one year. A lease for a term not exceeding one year is not a "document" under Utah's recording law. A longer lease, or a memorandum of it, may be recorded with the county recorder; a notary's acknowledgment entitles it to be recorded, and it must contain a legal description of the property; once recorded it gives notice of its contents to everyone. An unrecorded document is void against a later buyer who buys in good faith and for value and records first, so a tenant under an unrecorded long lease risks losing it to such a buyer. Whether a tenant's possession alone puts a buyer or lender on notice is a question of case law. Separately, a lease for longer than one year is void unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the landlord or the landlord's agent authorized in writing ("Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be Written"). If the property is foreclosed, see "Tenants When the Property Is Foreclosed".

title: Size Thresholds in Utah Rental Law
bodyText: Utah's core landlord-tenant duties apply to every landlord regardless of how many units you own; there is no general small-landlord exemption from the Fit Premises Act, the deposit statute or the eviction statute. A few rules turn on size, and the exemptions with several conditions require all of them. Fair housing: the Utah Fair Housing Act does not apply to a single-family home sold or rented by its owner only if the owner does not own an interest in four or more single-family homes held for sale or lease at the same time, has not sold two or more non-residence homes in 24 months, does not use a real estate broker or salesperson, and does not make any discriminatory statement, notice, advertisement or application form of the kind the act's advertising ban covers, whether oral or written; renting a room in a home designed for four or fewer families is exempt only if the owner lives in one of the units, and the advertising ban still applies. Federal fair housing law has its own exemptions ("Utah Fair Housing Act"). Accessible design rules reach buildings of four or more units first occupied after March 13, 1991: every unit if the building has an elevator, otherwise the ground-floor units. Garbage: in a building of more than two units you must provide receptacles and removal unless you and the tenant agree otherwise. City disproportionate rental fees may not be charged on a single building of no more than four units of which one is owner occupied, both conditions being required, and a city may not make an owner of several rentals hold more than one regulatory license. The egress-window protection covers detached one- to four-family dwellings and qualifying town homes. Utah's commercial receivership law reaches a one- to four-unit property when the owner collects rents from others, and asbestos inspection rules treat residential property of four or fewer units differently. Licensing for property management (a real estate license now, or the property manager license available from January 1, 2027) turns on whether you manage property you own, not on size.

title: Student Housing in Utah
bodyText: Utah has no special landlord-tenant rule for student housing: no exemption from the Fit Premises Act, deposit or eviction statutes for renting to students, and no separate duties for privately owned student buildings. Utah's student-housing rules are fair housing exceptions. A nonprofit educational institution may require its single students to live in housing it owns, operates or has under contract, and may segregate that housing by sex or familial status for modesty or privacy or for religious exercise; because the exception reaches housing under contract with the school, a private owner whose building is contracted to a school can fall within it. Separately, any private landlord, lessor or property manager may designate a dormitory, boarding house, shared rental or other group-living accommodation as single-sex housing (shared bedroom or bathroom) and limit it to people whose sex at birth matches the designation, unless that would violate federal law or a federal funding condition; this does not reach housing the state or a city owns or operates. A public college or university's own housing must follow its sex-designation rules. Federal fair housing law has its own terms ("Utah Fair Housing Act"). Whether a school-run dormitory is a residential rental unit under the Fit Premises Act or a boarding or rooming house facility it excludes is a question the statute does not answer; an ordinary apartment rented to students as their principal residence is covered.

title: Tenant Child Care in a Utah Rental
bodyText:
No Utah statute requires you to let a tenant run a family or home child care in your rental, and none sets the conditions (insurance, liability waivers, numbers) on which you must allow one, so the lease decides.

Utah regulates the care itself: residential child care is care provided in the provider's own home, and a provider caring for eight or fewer qualifying children may choose to hold a state Residential Child Care Certificate, with home inspections for sanitation, fire and health hazards; without a certificate or license a provider may not care for more than 10 children at a time, and larger operations need a state license. Cities and counties may not license or regulate how a licensed or certified child care program provides care, but they may require a business license and enforce building, health and fire codes.

If you allow child care, use the optional clause ("Child Care in the Property" clause) to require the state certificate or license, compliance with local rules, notice, a child limit and liability insurance. If you do not, your lease's residential-use terms govern, and the tenant must follow every requirement of the lease.

title: Home Businesses in Utah Rentals
bodyText:
No Utah statute makes a home-based business a right a tenant can use against you, and none stops a lease from restricting or banning business use; the library's residential-use clause ("Residential Use Only" clause) bars commercial use unless you give permission.

Utah's home-business statutes limit local governments, not landlords. A city may not charge a resident a fee to operate a home-based business unless the business and the home together have materially more offsite impact than the home alone, though it may charge an administrative fee to an exempt owner who asks for a license and must tell home-business owners about the exemption; a county may not charge a license fee for a home-based business on the same impact test.

A home-based microschool (a registered business teaching 16 or fewer K-12 students for pay from a residential dwelling, accessory dwelling unit or residential property) is a permitted use in every city zoning district (counties have the same rule), subject to local parking, traffic, noise, hours and business-license rules, and needs no extra occupancy standards beyond a home's, except an escape window for any below-grade floor used for it.

In a homeowners association, rules may not interfere with reasonable activity inside a dwelling that complies with local law, but may bar activity that is not normally residential or that causes costs, danger, excessive noise or traffic, unsightly conditions or annoyance.

If you allow a home business, use the optional permission clause ("Home-Based Business (Landlord's Permission)" clause).

title: No Font or First-Page Lease Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Utah sets no font size, type style or first-page placement for a house or apartment lease or any disclosure in it, and has no required single-family-home notice about squatters or unlawful occupants. The layout rules that exist are narrower. A mobile home park space lease must contain conspicuous disclosures of the resident's protection against termination without cause, the park's termination causes and the resident's rights. Utah's automatic-renewal notice rule, which requires renewal notices to be clearly and conspicuously disclosed, expressly does not apply to a rental agreement. A lender foreclosing on rental property must give tenants a notice in 14-point type ("Forms Utah Prescribes for Rentals"), but that is the lender's notice, not yours. To remove a trespasser who was never your tenant, Utah has a law-enforcement procedure that needs no lease wording ("Removing Trespassers and Long-Term Guests").

title: When a Condition Counts Under the Fit Premises Act
bodyText: Utah's Fit Premises Act draws its own materiality line. The Act does not apply to breakage, malfunctions or other conditions that do not materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter, so a cosmetic flaw or a minor malfunction is outside its duties and its tenant remedies. The measure is the ordinary renter, not one tenant's particular needs. Above that line the Act works in two tiers. A deficient condition is one that breaks a habitability standard or a requirement of the rental agreement and was not caused by the tenant, the tenant's family, guests or invitees or by a use that breaks the lease or the law; the tenant may serve a written notice that starts a corrective period of 3 calendar days for a habitability standard or 10 calendar days for a lease requirement. A dangerous condition is a deficient condition posing a substantial risk of imminent loss of life or significant physical harm; the tenant may report it by any reasonable means, and you must begin fixing it within 24 hours and keep at it diligently until it is done ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions"). Read literally, the materiality line covers the whole Act, including a lease promise about an appliance or amenity, so a failure that does not affect health or safety may not open the statutory remedies even where the lease promised the item; how a court applies that is case law, so keep every promise your lease makes. No other section of the Utah Code or Constitution sets a materiality test for the condition of a rental. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Habitability Presumption in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution creates a presumption about the condition of a rental. Nothing presumes a unit fit or unfit, and nothing presumes you breached a repair duty because a code violation went uncorrected, an inspection failed or a set time passed. The Utah Code does not use the phrase warranty of habitability at all. Your duty is stated directly instead: under the Fit Premises Act you may not rent a unit that is not safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, and you must keep it fit while it is rented ("Utah Fit Premises Act: Owner and Renter Duties"). A tenant who says the unit falls short proves it through the Act's notice process, and if the tenant sues to enforce the chosen remedy, damages beyond that remedy turn on the court finding that you unjustifiably refused to correct the condition or failed to use due diligence ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions"). The only presumptions in Utah's residential landlord-tenant statutes concern a tenant's abandonment of the premises. Whether Utah courts recognize any habitability presumption or implied warranty beyond the statute is case law, so keep records of each repair request and what you did about it. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in a Utah Lease
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires your lease to say that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation, or to repeat the habitability standard in any form. The duty does not depend on the lease: every owner renting a residential rental unit must keep it fit for human habitation and in line with local ordinances and board-of-health rules, with electrical systems, heating, plumbing and hot and cold water, and may not rent it unless it is safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy. That holds for an oral agreement as much as a written one, so leaving the duty out of the lease narrows nothing; only an explicit written agreement signed by both parties can shift a duty to the tenant ("Tenant-Performed Duties" clause). The few things a Utah lease or its paperwork must carry are listed in "What a Utah Lease Must Contain"; the library's existing-condition clause records the condition the tenant accepts, and "Utah Fit Premises Act: Owner and Renter Duties" sets out the duties. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Heat in Utah Rentals
bodyText:
Heat is one of the Fit Premises Act's core duties. Every residential rental unit must have heating, and you must maintain it along with the electrical systems, plumbing and hot and cold water. Heating is a habitability standard, so if the heat fails and the tenant's side did not cause it, the tenant may serve a written notice of deficient condition with a 3-calendar-day corrective period; a failure posing a substantial risk of imminent loss of life or significant physical harm is a dangerous condition, which you must begin fixing within 24 hours of any reasonable notice ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions"). The tenant must use the heating in a reasonable manner.

No section of the Utah Code itself sets an indoor temperature or a heating season. The building codes Utah adopts by reference may set a heating standard for new or altered buildings, and your duty also runs to local ordinances and board-of-health rules, which may set one; check them.

Utah does not confine a shift of the heating duty to separately metered equipment or require extra consideration for it: any Fit Premises Act duty, heat included, may be allocated to the tenant, but only by an explicit written agreement signed by both of you ("Tenant-Performed Duties" clause). Whether a court would enforce a shift of a core habitability duty like heat is case law, so the cautious course is to keep heating repair yours and use the optional freeze-protection clause ("Heat and Freeze Protection" clause) for the tenant's part.

Who pays for gas or electricity is a utilities term. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Stove or Refrigerator Requirement in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires you to supply a stove, oven, range or refrigerator in a rental, and none makes a unit without them unfit. The Fit Premises Act's appliance rule runs the other way: apart from electrical systems, heating, plumbing, hot and cold water and any air conditioning system, you must maintain other appliances only as the rental agreement specifically contracts. So decide what you supply and say it in the lease. List the kitchen appliances you will maintain in the appliances-included clause, and list any item you leave at the unit but will not maintain in the optional exclusion clause ("Appliances Not Supplied by Landlord" clause), because the library's Maintenance & Repairs clause makes you responsible for repairing the appliances located at the property. The electrical systems and plumbing that serve a kitchen stay yours either way. A city or county ordinance or a local board-of-health rule could add kitchen requirements; the library does not hold those, so check the local rules. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText:
Utah's Fit Premises Act ties your appliance duty to the lease. Beyond the core systems, you must maintain other appliances and facilities only as the rental agreement specifically contracts. No Utah statute presumes that an appliance sitting in the unit is one you supply, but none presumes the opposite either, and the library's Maintenance & Repairs clause makes you responsible for repairing the appliances located at the property.

So if you leave an item you will not maintain, such as a refrigerator a prior occupant left or a washer the tenant owns, list it in the optional exclusion clause ("Appliances Not Supplied by Landlord" clause).

Some things can never go on that list. You must maintain the electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water, and any air conditioning system in operable condition, whatever the lease says, unless you and the tenant shift a specific duty in an explicit written agreement both of you sign ("Tenant-Performed Duties" clause). The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Special Rules for Furnished Rentals
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution sets rules for a furnished rental. Nothing requires a furniture inventory, presumes that furniture left in the unit is included, sets a condition standard for furnishings, limits or specially regulates a deposit for them (Utah sets no deposit cap, so you may take a larger deposit for a furnished unit if the lease states it; see "No Security Deposit Limit"), or requires you to maintain them.

A furnished unit is governed by the same rules as an unfurnished one. Two of those rules do the work. Your tenant may not intentionally or negligently damage or remove any part of the unit, or knowingly let anyone else do so, and at move-out you may apply the deposit to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear.

Because nothing is presumed, list what you provide and its condition in the optional furnishings clause, alongside your move-in condition record. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Shifting Repair Duties to the Tenant
bodyText:
Utah lets you shift Fit Premises Act duties to your tenant with fewer conditions than most states set. Any duty in the Act may be allocated to a different party, but only by an explicit written agreement signed by the parties. The Act adds nothing more: no extra consideration or rent credit, no rule that the work be done in lieu of rent, no limit to single-family homes, no separate-document or conspicuous-print rule, and no list of duties that may or may not move.

Two duties are written to be set by agreement in any case: you maintain appliances and facilities beyond the core systems only as the rental agreement specifically contracts, and in a building with more than two units the garbage receptacles and removal are yours except to the extent you and the tenant agree otherwise.

Use the tenant-performed duties clause, which names each duty, is in writing and is signed with the lease, so it meets the strictest of these standards; keep each duty specific.

The Act does not say whether a shift of a core habitability duty (a safe, sanitary and fit unit, the common areas, electrical systems, plumbing, heating, hot and cold water, any air conditioning) will be enforced against the tenant; that is case law, so the cautious course is to shift only defined tasks and keep the core systems yours ("Waiving Habitability in Utah", "Habitability Terms the Lease May Change"). The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Promises to Repair or Improve
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires your promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed.

That does not make a loose promise safe. Under the Fit Premises Act a rental agreement includes any agreement, written or oral, that sets or changes the terms of the tenancy, so a promise your leasing agent makes can become a requirement of the rental agreement.

If a promised item is not done, the tenant may serve a notice of deficient condition with a 10-calendar-day corrective period, and if you take no substantial action in that time the tenant's chosen remedy applies: rent abatement, which ends the lease, or repair and deduct up to two months' rent ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions").

The Act does not reach a condition that does not materially affect the ordinary renter's health or safety, so whether a purely cosmetic promise opens those remedies is case law; it may still be enforced as a contract term. A promise about an appliance or amenity can also become something you have specifically contracted to maintain for the whole term.

Put every promise in the lease with a date, and say which items are one-time work, using the optional promised-work clause ("Promised Cleaning, Repairs or Improvements" clause). Utah's Consumer Sales Practices Act may apply to a misleading promise; whether it reaches leases is case law ("Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and Leases"). The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Repair Notices Under the Fit Premises Act
bodyText: Utah's Fit Premises Act sets two kinds of repair notice. To use a statutory remedy, the tenant must give you a written notice of deficient condition that describes each condition, states the corrective period in days (3 calendar days for a habitability standard, 10 for a lease requirement), states the remedy the tenant has chosen (rent abatement or repair and deduct), gives you permission to enter to fix it, and is served either by the methods used for eviction notices or as the rental agreement provides. The eviction-notice methods are personal delivery, registered or certified mail or an equivalent means, leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion, or, if no such person is found, posting a copy on the leased property. An oral report never starts the corrective period, and a text or email starts it only if it is served by a method the statute or the lease allows ("Electronic Notices"). A dangerous condition, one posing a substantial risk of imminent loss of life or significant physical harm, is different: the tenant may tell you by any means reasonable in the circumstances, and your duty to begin remedial action within 24 hours runs from that report. Such a report starts a corrective period only if it also meets the written-notice requirements. A lease term requiring all repair requests in writing cannot be relied on to delay the 24-hour duty: the Act gives the reasonable-means right without exception, and whether a lease can narrow it is case law. The lease may add a service method for the written notice, but the eviction-notice methods stay open to the tenant; the library's notices clause deliberately names no alternative method, so give your notice address in the owner disclosure ("Owner and Manager Disclosure" clause). A managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager is treated as the owner for notices unless the agent or manager says otherwise in writing in the rental agreement, so a notice to your manager is notice to you. Ask for routine repair requests in writing for your records ("Maintenance & Repairs" clause), and act on every report. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Ending the Lease Instead of Repairing
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution lets you refuse a repair because its cost is unreasonable, exceeds the rent or exceeds what the unit is worth. Cost is not the test. What Utah gives you instead is an exit when the unit is not fit for occupancy. If a tenant serves a notice of deficient condition and the unit is not fit for occupancy, you may decide not to correct the condition and end the rental agreement. You must tell the tenant in writing no later than the end of the corrective period, rent is prorated to the date you end the agreement, and within 10 calendar days after you end it you must pay the tenant any prepaid rent, prorated, and any deposit due. You may not require the tenant to leave sooner than 10 calendar days after your notice. The Act does not define not fit for occupancy, so whether a particular condition qualifies is case law; if the unit is still fit to live in, the repair is yours whatever it costs ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions"). For fire or other casualty, the optional casualty clause gives either side a contract right to end the lease. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Small-Landlord Exemption Notice in Utah
bodyText: There is nothing for a Utah landlord to give notice of here. No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives a residential tenant a rent-escrow or rent-withholding remedy, and none exempts a landlord from the tenant's repair remedies because of how many units the landlord owns or rents, so there is no exemption statement to put in the lease. The Fit Premises Act's remedies, rent abatement or repair and deduct after a written notice of deficient condition, apply to every owner of a covered unit ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions"). The Act sorts by kind of housing, not by landlord size: it covers a tenant's principal residence and leaves out boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots and recreational property rented occasionally. Its only unit-count rule is that in a building with more than two units you must provide garbage receptacles and removal unless you and the tenant agree otherwise. A city's good landlord program may define an exempt landlord for its own licensing purposes; that changes nothing about a tenant's remedies ("Local Rental Licensing and Good Landlord Programs").

title: No Statutory Self-Cure Right for Utah Landlords
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives the landlord of a house or apartment a right to do work the tenant failed to do and bill the cost back, or to treat that cost as rent. The only statutory self-cure right is for mobile home parks, which may, after a 15-day written notice, enter the resident's space, cure the default and bill the cost as additional rent.

For other rentals your statutory tools are these. A tenant who breaks a lease covenant can be served a written notice to perform it or leave within three calendar days, and the tenancy is saved if the tenant performs. The tenant must not damage the unit and must not unreasonably refuse you entry to make repairs, and you give 24 hours' notice of entry unless the lease says otherwise. At move-out you may apply the deposit to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear.

If you want to do the work yourself and recover the cost during the tenancy, that right has to come from the lease: use the optional self-cure clause ("Landlord's Right to Remedy Tenant's Breach" clause), which fixes how the amount is figured, because Utah lets you charge only amounts the rental agreement states. An unpaid amount due under the lease can be included in a notice to pay or quit as an amount due without being called rent ("Are Fees Rent?").

title: Tenant Remedies When the Landlord Breaches
bodyText: Utah gives a residential tenant a short set of statutory remedies against you; deposit violations have their own penalty ("Deposit Return Penalty Process") and discrimination claims their own remedies ("Utah Fair Housing Act"). For the unit's condition, the Fit Premises Act is the route: after a written notice of deficient condition and an uncorrected corrective period, the tenant's chosen remedy applies, either rent abatement, which ends the lease and requires you to refund the whole deposit and prepaid rent at once, or repair and deduct up to two months' rent. The tenant may then sue to enforce that remedy; the summons requires you to answer within 3 business days, the tenant also gets damages if the court finds you unjustifiably refused or failed to use due diligence to correct the condition, no damages are allowed for mental suffering or anguish, and the court may award costs and attorney fees to whoever prevails. You may counterclaim that the condition does not break the lease. None of this is available to a tenant who is not meeting the tenant's own statutory duties ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions"). If you fail to deliver possession on the date the lease sets, the tenant may end the lease by written notice, and you must return all prepaid rent and any deposit as promptly as reasonable; if the tenant keeps the lease, rent abates until you deliver possession. A failure to give the entry notice, the pre-application or move-in disclosures, the condition inventory or option, or the copies of the lease and rules does not let the tenant withhold performance or sue you. Removing a tenant without a court order is unlawful ("No Lockouts Without a Court Order"), and you may not restrict or punish a tenant's reasonable calls for police or emergency help ("Calling Police or Emergency Services"). No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives a residential tenant any other rent-withholding right or a constructive-eviction remedy. Claims for breach of other lease promises, and constructive eviction, are case law. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Who Does the Repairs
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires you to name a repair person or contractor, or limits whom you may name, and the Fit Premises Act does not say who must do the work when a tenant uses its repair-and-deduct remedy.

That remedy opens only after a written notice of deficient condition and a corrective period in which you took no substantial action; the tenant may then correct the condition and deduct the cost from future rent, up to two months' rent, and must keep the receipts and give you copies within five calendar days after the next rental period begins ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions").

Outside that remedy the tenant has no statutory right to repair at your expense, so you may require in the lease that repairs at your cost be made only with your written consent by someone you approve, and tell the tenant where to send repair requests ("Repair Contact and Approved Repairers" clause).

Whether a lease may also restrict whom the tenant hires under the statutory remedy is case law, so the library's clause leaves that remedy as the Act states it. Contractor licensing law may limit who may do some trades. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Rent Into Court and Counterclaims in Utah Evictions
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution makes a house or apartment tenant pay rent into court to defend an eviction, to get a jury or to get a continuance. The one exception is a mobile home park: a resident who contests an eviction must pay the rents, fees and service charges falling due into court on the park's schedule, and failing to pay may justify summary judgment for the park. For other rentals the possession bond does the work. Any time before final judgment you may file a possession bond in the amount the court approves and serve notice of it, telling the tenant of the alternatives. The tenant may then (1) in a case based only on unpaid rent or other amounts due, keep the lease and end the case by paying, within 3 calendar days after service, the accrued rent, all other amounts due and costs, including attorney fees as the rental agreement provides; (2) stay in possession by filing a counter bond within 3 business days after service or within 24 hours after the court sets the amount, whichever is later (the court may allow up to 72 hours), with prepaid rent counted toward it; or (3) demand a hearing within 3 days, to be held within 3 days of the demand. If the tenant does none of these in time, the court grants you an order of restitution on ex parte motion. Once an order of restitution issues, a tenant's request for a hearing does not stay it unless the tenant posts a bond and the court orders a stay. On counterclaims, the statutes let an unlawful detainer claim be brought as a counterclaim, served under the Utah Rules of Civil Procedure with responses due on the eviction's 3-business-day timeline, and in a tenant's Fit Premises Act suit you may counterclaim that a condition does not violate the lease. Whether a tenant must raise claims against you as a counterclaim in the eviction is set by the Utah Rules of Civil Procedure, court rules the library does not hold ("Utah Eviction Process").

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives a tenant extra time to pay rent, protection from late fees, or a stay of eviction because a federal, state or local government shutdown has interrupted the tenant's pay. Rent is due when the lease says, the late-fee cap is the usual one ("Late Fee Limit"), and the ordinary 3-business-day notice to pay or quit applies. A different rule protects servicemembers: a household in state military service has protections that are not tied to a shutdown ("Servicemember Tenant Protections"). You may always agree in writing to defer rent for a furloughed tenant; state the deferred amount, the new due dates and whether a late fee is waived, because Utah lets you charge only the fees and amounts the rental agreement includes ("Fees Must Be in the Lease").

title: Subsidized Rent When a Unit Has Defects
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution says how a housing subsidy figures in when rent is abated or prorated because of a unit's condition. Utah's only condition-based rent rule is the Fit Premises Act's rent abatement remedy: if the tenant chooses it in a notice of deficient condition and you take no substantial action within the corrective period, rent is abated from the date of the notice, the lease ends, you must immediately refund the whole deposit and a prorated refund of prepaid rent, including rent paid for the period after the notice, and the tenant must move out within 10 calendar days after the corrective period ends ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions"). The Act does not say whether that abatement and refund reach a housing authority's payments. For a federal Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, federal rules cover the subsidy side. The family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing assistance payment covers. Once the housing authority notifies you in writing of a deficiency found on inspection it may withhold its payments (unless it finds the family or its guests caused the deficiency and waives your duty to fix it, in which case it may neither withhold nor abate them), and it must abate them if you do not fix a life-threatening deficiency within 24 hours or another deficiency within 30 days (or an approved extension); withheld payments are paid back if you fix the deficiency in time, but abated payments are never made up. You may not end the family's tenancy because assistance is withheld or abated, though the family may end it during abatement by notifying you and the housing authority, and if the unit is not repaired within 60 days of the abatement notice (or a longer period the housing authority sets) the housing assistance contract is terminated. These federal rules apply to contracts signed or renewed on or after June 6, 2024. Whether a Utah statutory abatement reduces the tenant's share, the subsidy or both is case law; the cautious course is to refund the tenant what the tenant paid and ask the housing authority how its contract treats its payments for the same period. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Inspections in Subsidized Tenancies
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution deals with inspections of a subsidized or voucher unit. Nothing gives you a special remedy when a subsidized tenant refuses an inspection, nothing makes a tenant admit a housing authority's inspector, and nothing addresses a landlord who refuses the program's inspection. Utah's general rules apply: your tenant may not unreasonably deny you, your agent or manager entry to make repairs, and you give 24 hours' notice of entry unless the lease says otherwise; no Utah statute makes a tenant admit a government inspector ("Government Inspections of Utah Rentals"), so ask for cooperation in the lease. Under the federal Housing Choice Voucher rules you must keep the unit to the program's housing quality standards, and a unit fails them when an authorized inspector finds deficiencies on inspection, notifies you in writing and they are not fixed in time; a deficiency the family, a household member or guest caused may lead the housing authority to waive your duty to fix it and to end the family's assistance. The federal rules on the inspections themselves and on a family's duty to allow them are not in the library's sources yet. Refusing a voucher tenant because of the program's inspection requirement may raise Utah's source-of-income protection.

title: No Alternate-Housing Duty in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a private landlord to provide or pay for alternate, temporary or substitute housing for a tenant, whether during repairs, after a fire or flood, or when a unit is unfit, and nothing lets a tenant trigger such a duty by request. What the Fit Premises Act gives the tenant instead is an exit. If the tenant chooses rent abatement in a notice of deficient condition and you take no substantial action within the corrective period, the lease ends, you refund the whole deposit and prorated prepaid rent at once, and the tenant has 10 calendar days after the corrective period to move. If the unit is not fit for occupancy you may end the lease yourself instead of repairing, giving at least 10 calendar days to move ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions", "Ending the Lease Instead of Repairing"). Utah's relocation-assistance law binds government agencies, and others using eminent domain, that displace people by acquiring property or by code enforcement under a federal or state assisted program; it does not bind a private landlord renting its own units, and a city may use certain tax revenue to help residents displaced from a closing mobile home park. For a federal Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, the housing authority, not you, handles a family's move when a contract ends for uncorrected deficiencies ("Subsidized Rent When a Unit Has Defects"). You may still offer a tenant another unit or a hotel stay by written agreement. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Shared Facilities and Building Equipment
bodyText: Under the Fit Premises Act the unit you rent includes the grounds and facilities you hold out for your tenants' general use and any other area or facility the lease provides, so a laundry room, storage area or yard you offer is part of what you rent. You must keep common areas sanitary and safe, and in a building of more than two units you must provide garbage receptacles and removal unless you and the tenant agree otherwise. Beyond the core systems (electrical, plumbing, heating, hot and cold water and any air conditioning) you must maintain other appliances and facilities only as the rental agreement specifically contracts, so say in the lease which amenities you provide and keep up ("Appliances You Do Not Supply"). Two state safety laws reach building equipment whoever owns it. An elevator or escalator, other than one in a single-family dwelling, may not operate without a current state inspection certificate, renewed every two years, and its owner or operator pays the inspection fees. Boilers and pressure vessels are regulated by the Labor Commission, which the building code says excludes those in private residences and in apartment houses of fewer than five family units. No section of the Utah Code or Constitution puts a product-safety duty on a landlord for an automatic garage door opener, a playground or a laundry machine. Pool and spa rules are local board-of-health and state health rules the library does not hold. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Statutory Quiet-Enjoyment Covenant in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution states a covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession running from a landlord to a residential tenant. Utah's statutory quiet-possession words belong to other settings: a warranty deed's covenants on a sale of land, and a defense in a forcible entry case for someone who has held the property in quiet possession for a full year. The Fit Premises Act's peaceful-enjoyment rule runs the other way: your tenant must not interfere with another renter's peaceful enjoyment of that renter's unit. Your tenant's possession is protected instead by specific rules. You must deliver possession on the date the lease sets, or the tenant may end the lease or have rent abate until you do. You give 24 hours' notice before entering unless the lease says otherwise. You may not exclude the tenant except by court process, apart from retaking abandoned premises under the statutory procedure, and turning out a person in actual possession by force, threats or menacing conduct is a forcible entry, for which damages are trebled ("No Lockouts Without a Court Order", "Tenant Remedies When the Landlord Breaches"). Whether Utah courts imply a covenant of quiet enjoyment into a lease, and what breaches it, is case law, so treat those rules as the floor.

title: Your Tenant's Duties Under Utah Law
Habitability Rules Utah Does Not Have
bodyText: Utah's habitability law is the Fit Premises Act, and it is shorter than the uniform codes many form leases assume. No section of the Utah Code or Constitution supplies any of the following: a presumption that a unit is fit or unfit, or that you breached a duty; a required habitability statement in the lease; an indoor temperature standard (the building codes Utah adopts by reference, local ordinances and board-of-health rules may set one); a duty to supply a stove or refrigerator; rules for furnished units; extra conditions, such as consideration or a separate document, on shifting a duty to the tenant beyond an explicit written agreement both of you sign; a writing or completion-date rule for repair promises; a rule on who performs repairs; a right to refuse a repair because it costs too much; rent escrow, rent withholding outside the Act's two remedies, or a small-landlord exemption; a landlord's right to cure a tenant's breach and bill it as rent (mobile home parks aside); a constructive-eviction statute; rent paid into court to defend an eviction (mobile home parks aside); shutdown protection for government workers; a rule on how a housing subsidy figures in a rent abatement or on subsidized inspections; a duty to provide alternate housing; a landlord duty for garage door openers, playgrounds or laundry equipment; and a statutory covenant of quiet enjoyment. Utah also has no general rule voiding waivers of these rights ("No General Non-Waiver Rule for Utah Rentals") and no general retaliation statute. Where Utah is silent, case law may still apply, and city ordinances and health rules may add duties. What Utah does have is in "Utah Fit Premises Act: Owner and Renter Duties", "Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions" and "When a Condition Counts Under the Fit Premises Act".

title: Fire Sprinklers in Utah Rentals
bodyText: No Utah landlord-tenant statute requires you to install fire sprinklers in a rental or to retrofit an existing rental with them. Sprinkler duties come from the State Fire Code and the State Construction Code, which bind owners by law, not through the lease. Utah's version of the fire code requires an automatic sprinkler system throughout a building with a Group R (residential) fire area, such as a new apartment building, but exempts detached one- and two-family homes and townhouses built under the International Residential Code. For a home or townhouse built under that code, a city, county or fire district may require sprinklers only by ordinance and only in listed situations: certain wildland-interface lots, no public water system with hydrants, a steep sole access road, a home over 10,000 square feet, or a home twice the average size of unsprinklered homes in the subdivision. A city may not make you retrofit a rental dwelling with a safety feature that was not required when it was built, unless the construction code requires it for a structural change or an ordinance adopted before 2008 requires it; and the construction code applies to an existing building when you voluntarily repair, remodel or alter it or change its use in a way that adds load or risk. Where a building has sprinklers, only a person certified by the state fire marshal may inspect and test them, and apartments sprinklered under the NFPA 13R standard that are not required to have a building fire alarm system must have a waterflow alarm inside each unit. The national code text that sets the base Group R rule, the maintenance and testing schedule and any retroactive rule for existing buildings is not in the library's sources, so check with your local fire code official before relying on an exemption. Your lease can make the tenant keep sprinkler heads clear and unobstructed ("Fire Safety Compliance" clause).

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Rule in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires you to tell a tenant, in the lease or a separate notice, whether the building has fire sprinklers, whether they work or when they were last inspected. The Code also offers no state grant, loan or tax credit for adding sprinklers to an existing rental. Whether a building must have sprinklers is a fire and building code question, not a disclosure rule ("Fire Sprinklers in Utah Rentals"). Don't describe a unit as sprinklered, or a system as working, unless it is true: Utah's Consumer Sales Practices Act may apply to a misstatement in a lease. Local ordinances can add requirements; check yours.

title: Hot Water and Water Heater Settings
bodyText: Utah requires every residential rental unit to have hot and cold water, and you must maintain the plumbing and the hot and cold water supply. No Utah statute sets a maximum or minimum water heater temperature, and none requires you to reset a water heater before a new tenant moves in. The plumbing codes Utah adopts for new work (the 2024 International Plumbing Code and the plumbing chapters of the 2021 International Residential Code) govern how water heaters and fixtures are installed and may limit how hot water can be delivered at showers and tubs; their text is not in the library's sources, and local board of health rules can also set hot water standards. When you replace a water heater, Utah's amendments require it to be strapped against earthquake movement, and in the areas that miss federal ozone or fine-particle standards a new natural gas water heater must meet a nitrogen oxide emission limit. Checking the setting at each turnover is a sensible safety step. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Window Guards, Bars and Egress Windows
bodyText: No Utah statute requires you to install window guards or other child fall-protection devices, to give a window-guard notice in the lease, or to tell a tenant how security or burglar bars release. Window rules come from the building codes. Utah's version of the residential code (for one- and two-family homes and townhouses) deletes Section R312.2 of the national code outright; what that section required, and what the codes say about bars or grilles over a bedroom escape window, is national code text the library does not hold, so check with your building official before adding bars or relying on an exemption. For an existing rental, a city or county ordinance may not require physical changes to a legal nonconforming rental except listed items, which include an egress bedroom window where the existing one is smaller than the current code requires and hand or guard rails. Utah's version of the residential code itself says an existing bedroom escape window that met the code when the bedroom was finished need not be enlarged if doing so would compromise the structure or could not be done within the code. A city or county may not require you to enlarge an existing bedroom window that met the code when the bedroom was finished in a detached one- to four-family dwelling or a town home of up to three stories with its own exit, if the change would compromise the structure or could not be done within the current code; that relief does not apply to an internal accessory dwelling unit. A city or county may still require an existing bedroom window to be fully openable, or forbid making it smaller, where its opening is below current code. Never block or bar an escape window in a way that stops it opening from inside. Local ordinances may say more.

title: No Steam Radiator Cover Rule in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution mentions radiators or steam heat, so Utah has no statute requiring you to cover steam radiators, to offer covers on request or to add a radiator rider to the lease. Your general duties still apply: every residential rental unit must have heating, and you must keep it safe and maintained ("Heat in Utah Rentals", "Utah Fit Premises Act: Owner and Renter Duties"). If your building has exposed steam radiators and young children live there, covering hot surfaces is a sensible safety step. Local ordinances and the adopted mechanical code may say more. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Pool and Spa Safety Rules in Utah
bodyText:
No Utah landlord-tenant statute requires a pool fence, a pool safety notice at lease signing or any other pool term in a lease. Pool rules come from two other sources.

First, Utah adopts only the residential provisions of the 2024 International Swimming Pool and Spa Code as part of the construction code, and its Utah definition of a private residential pool covers a pool, spa or wading pool used only by an individual, family or living-unit members and guests, and not one serving a multiple-unit housing complex of four or more living units.

Second, the state health department sets and enforces sanitation rules for the design, construction, operation and maintenance of public swimming pools and public spas.

So a pool at a house or small multiplex you rent falls under the residential pool code when it is built or altered, while a pool serving a complex of four or more units falls outside that definition and may be regulated as a public pool under the health department's rules. The code's barrier and gate requirements and the health rules' coverage of apartment pools are in texts the library does not hold, so confirm with your building official and local health department.

As owner you must keep common areas, including a shared pool area, sanitary and safe. (This duty is in Utah's Fit Premises Act, which covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.) A registered sex offender whose offense was against a minor may not be at a pool an apartment complex or association operates, except as the statute allows. An optional pool use clause is "Pool and Spa Use" clause.

title: Locks and Security Devices in Utah Rentals
bodyText:
No Utah statute lists security devices a rental must have (deadbolts, door viewers, window or sliding-door locks), requires you to rekey between tenants or sets a deadline to repair a lock.

Your general duty still applies: you may not rent a residential rental unit unless it is safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy. Whether that duty requires working exterior locks, or rekeying at turnover, is case law; the cautious course is to provide working locks on every exterior door and to rekey or change credentials between tenants.

Utah does set three lock rules. A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, stalking, a sexual offense, burglary or dating violence may require you to install a new lock on giving you a qualifying protective order or a police report and paying for the lock; you may rekey a working lock or replace the mechanism with one of equal or better quality, may keep a key, and must refuse a key to the perpetrator whatever the lease says ("New Locks for Crime Victims"; from January 1, 2027 the list of sexual offenses that qualify widens). You may never change the locks or otherwise exclude a tenant without a court order, except after the tenant abandons the unit ("No Lockouts Without a Court Order").

Locks on exit doors must meet the fire and building codes. Charges for lost keys and rekeying: "Keys" clause. An optional clause on tenant lock changes is "Locks and Keys" clause. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Smart Lock Law in Utah
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution regulates smart locks, keypads, key fobs, app-based entry or biometric entry systems in rentals, and none gives a tenant the right to a physical key instead, sets rules for entry records or limits a landlord's use of them.

The ordinary rules still apply to an electronic system. Under Utah's Fit Premises Act you must give 24 hours' notice before entering the unit unless the lease provides otherwise; no statute says whether unlocking the door remotely is entry, so the cautious course is to treat it as entry. The Act, which also holds the crime-victim lock rule below, covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

You may never use the system to lock a tenant out without a court order, except after the tenant abandons the unit ("No Lockouts Without a Court Order"). A crime victim who gives you a qualifying protective order or police report and pays the cost may require a new lock, and you must refuse access to the perpetrator ("New Locks for Crime Victims"); for an electronic lock, the cautious course is to issue new credentials and delete the perpetrator's.

Utah's consumer privacy act, which covers biometric data, reaches only large businesses ("Protecting Tenant Information"). An optional clause for an electronic entry system is "Electronic Entry System" clause.

title: No Key-Control Policy Rule in Utah
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a landlord or an apartment complex of any size to adopt a key-control policy, to log who holds master or unit keys, or to run background checks on employees who have key access.

Two nearby rules exist. Where access to a building is restricted and the fire code official requires it after consulting the owner, you must install a key box with the keys the fire department needs; the fire jurisdiction, not you, must have a process to account for those keys. And a person who manages rental property for others for pay must, with some exemptions (including assistants of a licensed property manager and staff who only do maintenance or bookkeeping), hold a real estate license (a separate property manager license is available from January 1, 2027), and license applicants must submit fingerprints and consent to a state and FBI background check ("Screening Property Management Staff").

The cautious course is still a written key policy: keep keys and codes secured and logged, limit them to staff who need them, and rekey or reset at turnover. A crime victim may require a new lock, and you must refuse its key to the perpetrator ("New Locks for Crime Victims"). An optional clause on tenant lock changes is "Lock Changes" clause (tagged for Utah).

title: Lighting in Shared Areas
bodyText:
No Utah statute sets a lighting standard for hallways, stairways, entries, parking areas or other shared areas of a rental, and none bars or regulates putting shared-area lights on a tenant's electric meter. Your general duty is to keep the common areas of a residential rental unit in a sanitary and safe condition and to maintain the electrical system; whether adequate lighting is part of that duty is case law, so keep shared areas lit.

Exit-route lighting and emergency lighting in apartment buildings are fire and building code subjects; the International Property Maintenance Code is not part of the state code, though a city may adopt it.

If shared-area lights are wired to a tenant's meter, say so in the lease: a city may not interfere with your contract with the tenant about who pays a utility, and before you take an application fee you must tell an applicant in writing the type of each use-based charge the lease will include ("Written Disclosures Before Taking an Application Fee"). An optional clause for tenant-metered shared lights is "Common-Area Lighting on Tenant's Meter" clause (tagged for Utah). The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires you to have balconies, decks, elevated walkways or other exterior elevated elements of a rental inspected on a schedule, to hire an engineer or inspector to do it, or to report the results to a city or to tenants. Utah's state construction code governs balconies and decks when they are built, repaired or altered, and its residential code amendment exempts from a permit only a deck that is no more than 30 inches above grade, needs no guardrail and does not serve a required exit door. The International Property Maintenance Code is not part of the state code, though a city may adopt it. For a legal nonconforming rental, a city or county may require you to install hand or guard rails. Your general duties remain: you may not rent premises that are not safe, and you must keep common areas sanitary and safe, so inspect and repair balconies, railings and stairs you provide. Local ordinances may require more. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Asbestos in Utah Rentals
bodyText: No Utah statute requires you to inspect a rental for asbestos, to tell a tenant that a building contains asbestos, or to put an asbestos notice in the lease. Utah regulates asbestos work instead. The state Air Quality Board sets certification and work-practice rules for anyone who contracts for hire to do demolition, renovation, salvage or encapsulation involving friable asbestos-containing material, or to do asbestos inspections. For a residential property of four or fewer units those rules apply only where a tested sample contained more than 1% asbestos; the board may not require an asbestos inspection of such a property finished on or after January 1, 1992, may require one before renovation, demolition or disposal work at such a property finished before 1981, and for one finished from 1981 through 1991 may require one only before work on listed materials (sprayed-on textured ceilings, asbestos cement siding or roofing, resilient flooring and mastic, duct or furnace insulation or tape, and vermiculite insulation). Larger buildings are covered without those limits. Breaking the rules can bring civil penalties of up to $10,000 a day, and knowingly handling or disposing of asbestos against the rules is a felony. The rules themselves, and the federal emission standard they implement, are not in the library's sources, so before renovating an older building have the materials tested by a certified inspector and use certified contractors. Your duty not to rent unsafe premises still applies; if you know of damaged asbestos material, the cautious course is to tell tenants and fix it. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Tenant Cooperation with Pest Treatment
bodyText:
No Utah statute mentions bed bugs or sets a specific duty for a tenant to report pests, prepare a unit for treatment or allow a pest inspection ("No Bed Bug Rule").

The tenant's general duties under the Fit Premises Act cover much of the same ground: the tenant must follow board of health rules that materially affect health and safety, keep the unit clean and safe, dispose of garbage in a clean and safe manner, follow the lease's rules, and not unreasonably refuse you entry to make repairs.

You must keep the unit fit and follow local ordinances and board of health rules, and a tenant's statutory repair remedies do not reach a condition the tenant, the tenant's family, guests or invitees caused. The state health department makes rules to control pests by eliminating insanitary conditions, and local health departments may have their own.

Because the statute is general, put the specific duties in the lease with "Pest Reporting and Treatment" clause. When a unit is abandoned you need not store abandoned items that are pests or hazardous. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Notice Before Pesticide Treatment
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code requires you to tell a tenant before pesticide is applied in or around a rental, to post a warning, or to give a pest-control notice in the lease. Any such rule would sit in the Department of Agriculture and Food's pesticide rules or the health department's pest rules.

What the Code does say: a person must hold a state license before applying a restricted use pesticide, or any general use pesticide for hire, so a pest control company you hire must be licensed and a pesticide applicator business must be registered; every pesticide must carry a label with any warning needed to protect health, and the applicator must follow it.

Until the rules are checked, the cautious course is to give tenants written notice before a treatment, with the date, the area, the product and any preparation or re-entry instructions, and to give it with the entry notice your lease requires (24 hours by default).

The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Waterbed Rule in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution mentions waterbeds, flotation bedding or liquid-filled furniture. Utah does not require you to allow a waterbed, does not stop you from refusing one, and sets no waterbed deposit, insurance requirement or notice. Whether to allow one is your choice, and the lease is where to say it: the tenant must follow the lease's rules and use the unit's facilities reasonably, and may not negligently damage the unit. If you charge anything for a waterbed, put the amount in the lease; a charge the lease does not include is allowed only on a month-to-month tenancy after 15 days' notice ("Fees Must Be in the Lease"). An optional clause is "Waterbeds and Liquid-Filled Furniture" clause (tagged for Utah). The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Air Conditioning and Portable Cooling Units
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives a tenant a right to install a portable, window or evaporative cooling unit, or requires a lease that restricts them to say so; whether to allow one is your choice.

Utah does not require you to supply air conditioning, but if the unit has an air conditioning system you must keep it in operable condition. That duty is a habitability standard, so a tenant can give you written notice of a failed system and you have three calendar days to start correcting it before the tenant's statutory remedies open ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions"); a duty can be moved to the tenant only by an explicit written agreement both of you sign ("Tenant-Performed Duties" clause).

If a tenant with a disability needs a cooling unit, fair housing law may require you to allow it as a reasonable accommodation or modification ("Disability Accommodations and Modifications"). An optional clause is "Cooling Equipment and Portable Units" clause. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Tenant Security Cameras and Video Doorbells
