bodyText: No Utah landlord-tenant statute gives a tenant a right to install a security camera or video doorbell, or limits what your lease may say about one, so you may require consent before a tenant attaches a camera to the property ("Locks and Keys" clause). Utah's community association acts protect owners, not tenants: a condominium or homeowners association rule generally may not stop a unit or lot owner from installing a personal security camera right next to the entry, a window or another outside entry point of the owner's unit, though a condominium may bar owner cameras in common areas not connected to the unit. Two general laws bind anyone who installs a camera, tenant or landlord. It is a crime, without the consent of the people entitled to privacy there, to install a device that observes, photographs or records in a private place, or to use one outside that captures sounds or events inside a private place that would not ordinarily be audible or visible outside; the injured person may also sue for an injunction, damages and attorney fees. And recording a conversation is lawful only for a party to it or with one party's prior consent, so a doorbell camera that records audio of passers-by who expect privacy can create liability. You should not place cameras inside a tenant's unit, and should aim any camera you install in common areas away from units' windows and doors. Police generally may not tamper with or redirect a person's surveillance camera on that person's private property without permission, a court order or exigent circumstances.

title: Rentals Served by a Private Well
bodyText: No Utah statute requires you to test a private well that serves a rental, to give a tenant well water test results, or to say in the lease that the water comes from a well. Two rules still matter. First, if your well system provides water for human consumption and other domestic uses to at least 15 service connections, or serves an average of 25 people daily for at least 60 days a year (a larger apartment complex, a mobile home park or a cluster of rentals on one well), it is a public water system and you are its supplier: the state Drinking Water Board's rules on contaminant limits, monitoring, reporting and operation apply, and if you receive a variance or exemption or are found to have violated the drinking water law you must give public notice as the board's rules require. One that serves residents year-round is a community water system. Second, every residential rental unit must have hot and cold water and plumbing kept in line with local ordinances and board of health rules, and local health departments may regulate smaller private wells. The drinking water rules and local health rules are not in the library's sources. For a single-family rental on its own well, the cautious course is to test it regularly and share the latest results with the tenant. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Contaminated Property and Environmental Covenants
bodyText:
**Methamphetamine.** If you have actual knowledge that the property is currently contaminated from the use, storage or manufacture of methamphetamine, you must disclose that in the lease ("Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure" clause); a person may sue to enforce that duty and the court may award damages, costs and attorney fees. Once the local health department finds the property decontaminated, it counts as stigmatized and you are not liable for not disclosing it ("Stigmatized Property").

**Drug-lab sites.** Police who see clandestine drug-lab paraphernalia must report the location to the local health department, which decides whether the property is contaminated and, if so, puts it on a public contamination list and notifies the owner of record with the clean-up requirements and a deadline to say how the owner will address it. The property comes off the list only after the health department documents that decontamination standards are met or a certified decontamination specialist reports it decontaminated; you need not use a certified specialist, but the result must meet the standards, and no government agency may stop you from decontaminating.

The drug-lab statute itself does not say you must tell a tenant or bar renting before clean-up, but contamination is defined as pollution that makes property unfit for human habitation or use, and you may not rent a residential rental unit that is not safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, so do not rent a listed property until it is decontaminated and removed from the list. A city may regulate removal of hazardous materials from a structure closed to occupancy by the health department and may require a certified decontamination specialist.

**Environmental covenants.** A recorded environmental covenant (or, for one created before May 1, 2006, an environmental institutional control) from an environmental clean-up runs with the land and can restrict how the property, its soil or groundwater are used. A copy must be provided, as the approving agency requires, to each person in possession of the property, which includes a tenant, and the covenant itself may require notice when an interest is transferred.

No statute requires you to describe a covenant in a lease, but a tenant's use must comply with it, and the agency and others may sue to enforce it. An optional clause is "Environmental Covenant Notice" clause. No other Utah statute requires a lease disclosure of hazardous-substance contamination, a cleanup site or a brownfield.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure Rule in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires you to disclose defective, corrosive or imported drywall to a tenant or a buyer, or sets any remediation standard for it. Drywall appears in Utah's statutes only as a building material in construction, energy-code, manufactured-home and condominium sections. Your general duties still apply: you may not rent premises that are not safe, sanitary and fit, and you must maintain the electrical system, plumbing and heating, and any appliances your lease says you will maintain; if you know of drywall that is corroding wiring or fixtures or affecting health, the cautious course is to tell the tenant and fix it. Don't describe a unit as free of a defect you know about: Utah's Consumer Sales Practices Act may apply to a misstatement in a lease. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule in Utah
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warning for rental housing is California law and does not apply to Utah rentals. No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a landlord to post or give a warning about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, or a formaldehyde notice for new building materials. Utah's lease disclosures on hazards are narrower: methamphetamine contamination you know about ("Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure" clause; "Contaminated Property and Environmental Covenants") and, under federal law, lead-based paint in pre-1978 housing ("Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause). If you manage property in both states, keep the California warning out of Utah leases unless you choose to give it.

title: No Military or Airport Zone Lease Disclosure in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a landlord to disclose in a lease, or before signing, that a rental is near a military installation, in an air installation noise or accident-potential zone, or near an airport, and none gives a tenant a right to end the lease on learning it. Utah handles these areas through land use and recording instead. Cities and counties must keep compatible use plans for land within 5,000 feet of listed military land (including Hill Air Force Base, Camp Williams, Dugway Proving Ground, Tooele Army Depot and the Utah Test and Training Range) and notify the state before approving land use applications there. Within an airport influence area (land within 5,000 feet of a runway, or 500 feet of a public vertiport), the city or county must tell a person building or developing the land, in writing, about aircraft overflights and noise, and may require an avigation easement. Near a significant private airport, the city or county records a notice against residential parcels within 2,500 feet of the runway, so it appears in the county records. If a tenant asks about aircraft noise, answer truthfully; a misstatement in a lease may fall under Utah's Consumer Sales Practices Act.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared Meter Disclosures
bodyText: Ordnance. No Utah statute requires you to tell a tenant about a former military ordnance or munitions site near the rental; land near listed military land is handled through local compatible use plans ("No Military or Airport Zone Lease Disclosure in Utah"). Demolition. No Utah statute requires you to tell a prospective or current tenant that you have applied for, or received, a permit to demolish the building; ending a tenancy for demolition follows the ordinary notice rules ("Utah Eviction Notices by Tenancy Type"). Shared meters. Utah has no general rule requiring you to disclose that a unit's gas or electric meter also serves another unit or a common area; say so in the lease if it does ("Common-Area Lighting on Tenant's Meter" clause, tagged for Utah). A city or county may prohibit a separate utility meter for an internal accessory dwelling unit, so an ADU may share the main home's meters, and the lease should say how those costs are split. Mobile home parks are different: a park's written lease of a space must fully disclose every cost it charges for public utility services and how each resident's bill is calculated, including costs allocated from a master-metered bill and submetered costs; the park must, at least once a year, give each resident a conspicuous disclosure of how utility charges were calculated over the past twelve months, or post one in a prominent place in the park and keep it current; and a park using a single-service meter must show the resident's utility charges on the resident's bill. Before taking an application fee for any rental, you must disclose the type of each use-based charge in the lease ("Written Disclosures Before Taking an Application Fee").

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a landlord to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, about public rights of access along a lake shore, river bank or beach, about sovereign land boundaries, or about public rights of way to the water. If a rental adjoins a river or stream, be aware of one public right a tenant may notice: the public may float on public water wide, deep and flowing enough for the vessel, may incidentally touch private property for safe passage, portage around a dangerous obstruction by the most direct, least invasive route closest to the water, and fish while floating, but must enter and leave the water on public property or with the owner's permission and may not stop on private property. Boundaries between private land and state sovereign land under navigable lakes and streams can be settled by agreement with the state. If your lease or listing describes water frontage or access, describe it accurately.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a landlord to benchmark a building's energy use, lets a lease term authorize a utility to release a tenant's usage data to the landlord, or sets rules for a landlord's use of that data. If the electric, gas or water account is in the tenant's name and you want the usage history, the practical route is the tenant's own consent on the utility's release form; a lease term can require the tenant to sign it ("Energy Usage Data Authorization" clause, tagged for Utah). Utah's consumer privacy act reaches only large businesses ("Protecting Tenant Information"). Utility commission rules on customer information are not in the library's sources; follow the utility's own release process.

title: No Recycling Notice Rule in Utah
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires a landlord to offer recycling, to tell tenants where and how to recycle on the property, or to give a recycling notice in the lease. The state's recycling laws regulate haulers, facilities, tires, used oil and electronics, and cities and other public entities may regulate the collection of solid waste in their area, so a local ordinance or your hauler contract may set recycling rules (check locally). What the Fit Premises Act does require: in a building with more than two residential rental units you must provide and maintain appropriate receptacles for garbage and other waste and arrange for its removal, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise, and the tenant must dispose of garbage and waste in a clean and safe manner. If you provide recycling, put the rules in the lease or your written rules and give the tenant a copy. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Cure Rights and Eviction Grounds in Utah
bodyText:
Utah's eviction statute gives your tenant two chances to cure and lists other grounds with no cure.

For unpaid rent or other amounts due, your written notice gives the tenant 3 business days after service to pay or leave; you may serve it any time after the rent is due. For a breach of any other condition or covenant of the lease, your written notice gives 3 calendar days after service to perform or leave, and you serve it on the tenant and on any subtenant actually living there.

The tenant, a subtenant in occupation, a mortgagee of the lease or anyone else with an interest in keeping it may pay or perform and so save the lease. The statute's wording leaves unclear whether that chance ends when the notice period runs out, so don't refuse a full cure offered before judgment without legal advice.

If the breach cannot afterwards be cured, you may instead serve a 3-calendar-day notice to quit. That no-cure notice is also the notice for subletting or assigning against the lease, waste, an unlawful business on the premises, a nuisance, and a criminal act on the premises.

The statute does not say the breached term must be material: any lease covenant can support a perform-or-quit notice. Whether a court would end a tenancy over a trivial breach is case law.

No Utah statute lets the lease set its own cure period or its own way of serving these notices, so give the full statutory period and serve by a statutory method: in person; by registered or certified mail or an equivalent; if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the home; or, if no such person is there, by posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property.

These rules cover every tenant holding for a term less than life, residential or commercial. Mobile home park lots follow the Mobile Home Park Residency Act, with its own causes and cure periods. See "Utah Eviction Notices by Tenancy Type", "Default by Tenant" clause and "Waiving or Shortening Eviction Notices".

title: Notice to Pay Rent or Vacate
bodyText:
Before you file an eviction for unpaid rent in Utah, serve your tenant a written notice that requires, in the alternative, payment of the rent and other amounts due or surrender of the premises. You may serve it any time after the rent becomes due. If the tenant neither pays nor leaves within 3 business days after service, the tenant is in unlawful detainer and you may file.

The notice may demand other amounts due under the lease along with the rent; your complaint must then state the amount of rent and other amounts due. Utah prescribes no wording, no state form and no type size for this notice, and requires no mediation or agency form first. Because the notice is served after the rent falls due, the lease itself cannot stand in for it.

Serve it by a statutory method: personal delivery; registered or certified mail or an equivalent; if the tenant is absent, leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the home; or, if no such person is there, posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property.

The statute does not add days for a mailed notice or say when mailed service is complete, and Part 8 does not define business days. The cautious course is to serve in person or by leaving or posting a copy, to count the 3 business days from the day after service, and to leave out Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays.

Utah does not limit how often a tenant may cure by paying, and no statute lets the lease waive, shorten or replace the notice ("Waiving or Shortening Eviction Notices").

After you file, if you post a possession bond, a tenant sued only for nonpayment can still keep the lease by paying the accrued rent, all other amounts due and costs, including attorney fees as the lease provides, within 3 calendar days after service of the bond notice ("Rent Into Court and Counterclaims in Utah Evictions").

On a property covered by the federal CARES Act, Utah's statute says the federal 30-day notice to vacate does not give the tenant more than 3 business days to pay, applies only to the time before the tenant can be removed under an order of restitution, and reaches a nonpayment notice only for rent that accrued during the 2020 moratorium. A state statute cannot narrow a federal law and courts disagree about the federal notice's reach, so on a covered property follow the cautious course in "Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties". A notice-service fee may be charged only as the lease states it. Mobile home park lots follow the Mobile Home Park Residency Act. See also "Utah Eviction Notices by Tenancy Type".

title: Crime at the Rental: Grounds, Void Leases and Owner Liability
bodyText:
Utah gives you several routes when crime happens at your rental, and makes an owner who allows some crimes on the property criminally liable. If your tenant commits a criminal act on the premises, a 3-calendar-day notice to quit ends the tenant's right to stay, with no chance to cure. The same no-cure notice applies to an unlawful business on the premises and to a nuisance there. The statute supplies these grounds whether or not your lease mentions crime. If your eviction claim is for nuisance and alleges criminal conduct, the court must hold an evidentiary hearing on request within 10 days of filing ("Expedited Hearing for Criminal Conduct").

For crime by household members or guests, or near rather than on the premises, the route is breach of a lease covenant: a notice giving 3 calendar days to perform or leave, or a no-cure notice where the breach cannot afterwards be cured. So a criminal-activity term in your lease is useful (optional clause "Criminal Activity"), and the Fit Premises Act separately requires a renter to comply with every requirement of the rental agreement.

Two statutes void a lease outright. If a tenant or occupant, or their employee, is convicted under Utah's pornographic and harmful materials chapter for an activity on the property, the conviction makes the lease void at your option once all direct appeals are over; possession reverts to you 10 days after your written notice, and a tenant who does not leave within those 10 days commits a class A misdemeanor. If a tenant uses the premises to maintain an alcohol nuisance, or knowingly lets another do so, the lease is void and the right to possession reverts to you, with the court remedy the law gives for forcible detention of premises; which eviction action fits is not settled by statute, so the cautious course is to serve a notice to quit and file under Utah's eviction statute with legal advice.

You can be liable too. You commit a class A misdemeanor if, after a tenant's earlier conviction for such an offense on the property, you knowingly let the property be used again for pornographic purposes and do not void the lease within 10 days after written notice from the county or city attorney. You are guilty of assisting an alcohol nuisance if you knowingly let a building you own or lease be used for one, or if, after written notice from a prosecutor or other citizen, you fail to take all proper measures to abate it or remove the people involved. Knowingly and intentionally letting someone occupy a place while unlawfully making, possessing, using or distributing a controlled substance there is a crime for an owner, and renting premises for drug activity is a felony ("Drug-Free Housing Terms"). Knowingly permitting gambling on property you own or rent is a class B misdemeanor, and owning or keeping a place of prostitution is a third degree felony.

A county or city attorney, the county, residents or businesses in the county may also sue to abate an unsafe building or place, such as one used for drug activity, gang crime, prostitution, gambling, weapons offenses or human trafficking, by evicting the tenant; you are a necessary defendant when the conduct is a third party's, and costs and fees can be awarded against you only if you had actual notice and willfully failed to act within a reasonable time ("Nuisance Abatement by Eviction").

If you rent to a family using a federal Housing Choice Voucher, federal rules require the lease to make drug-related crime on or near the premises, and crime threatening other residents or neighbors, grounds for ending the tenancy, and let you act on your own finding without an arrest or conviction.

No Utah statute requires you to evict for crime in general, requires or authorizes a crime-free lease addendum, requires your lease to state any of these rights, or gives you a safe harbor for filing an eviction. A city may not generally require you to deny tenancy for criminal history ("Reporting Duties and Police Cooperation").

Act on the offender's conduct, not on a victim's status, and never penalize a tenant for reasonable calls for police help ("Calling Police or Emergency Services", "Evicting a Domestic Violence Victim"). Mobile home park lots have their own causes under the Mobile Home Park Residency Act.

title: Your Remedies When a Tenancy Ends for Default
bodyText: When your tenant defaults, Utah lets you recover possession and money in one eviction case, or sue for money alone. In an eviction (unlawful detainer) case, a judgment for you includes an order of restitution of the premises; in a case for unpaid rent or breach of a lease covenant it also declares the lease forfeited. Forfeiture does not release the tenant from paying under the lease for the rest of its term, and it does not change any duty either side has to mitigate damages. The court assesses your damages from the unlawful detainer, from waste (if you plead and prove it), from amounts due under the lease and from any nuisance abatement, and enters judgment for the rent plus three times those damages. How far the trebling reaches amounts due under the lease, as opposed to damages for holding over, is case law; claim the amounts and let the court apply the multiplier, and don't threaten a tenant with a trebled figure ("Holdover Damages in Utah"). The court must award reasonable attorney fees and costs to whichever side prevails, and the judgment can be enforced immediately. If more money comes due later, you may ask the court to modify the judgment within 180 days after the earlier of the day the order of restitution is enforced or the day the tenant leaves; the court may allow more time. The tenant must give you and the court a current address within 30 days after the order of restitution issues. If the tenant abandons the property instead, you may retake and re-rent it, and the tenant owes either the rent for the rest of the term or, if less, the rent until you re-rent at fair rental value plus any shortfall in rent, a reasonable commission and restoration costs ("Rent Owed After Abandonment"). To recover money without seeking possession, sue on the lease. Small claims court, a division of the district and justice courts, hears claims for money only, up to $20,000 including attorney fees from 2025 through 2029 and $25,000 from 2030, where the tenant lives or the debt arose; it cannot order possession. Evictions are filed in district court. From January 1, 2027, the Judicial Council may set up a district court division for eviction and debt collection cases, and once it exists every district court must send those cases to it for pretrial and post-judgment processing. No Utah statute addresses rent acceleration clauses in residential leases or makes you choose between possession and rent; whether an acceleration term is enforceable is case law. See "Utah Eviction Process" and "Default by Tenant" clause.

title: Saving the Lease From Forfeiture
bodyText: In Utah a tenant can save the lease from forfeiture only in the ways the eviction statute names. For unpaid rent or other amounts due, and for breach of another lease covenant, the tenant, a subtenant actually living there, a mortgagee of the lease or anyone else interested in keeping it may pay or perform as your notice requires and save the lease. The statute's wording does not make clear whether that chance ends when the notice period runs out, so don't refuse a full cure offered before judgment without legal advice. The no-cure grounds (subletting or assigning against the lease, waste, an unlawful business, a nuisance and a criminal act on the premises) give no chance to save it, and neither does a breach that cannot afterwards be cured. Once the notice period has run, the statute gives one more chance, and only if you post a possession bond: in a case based only on nonpayment, the existing lease stays in force and the case is dismissed if the tenant pays the accrued rent, all other amounts due and costs, including attorney fees as the lease provides, within 3 calendar days after service of the notice of the bond. Otherwise, a judgment for you in a nonpayment or covenant case declares the lease forfeited. No Utah statute lets a court relieve the tenant against that forfeiture or restore the tenancy after judgment because the tenant later pays, and a tenant's request for a hearing does not stay the order of restitution unless the tenant posts a bond the court approves and the court orders a stay. Whether a court could still grant equitable relief from forfeiture is case law. If you accept rent after serving a notice, see "Accepting Rent After a Notice"; for paying to stop an eviction, see "Paying to Stop a Utah Eviction". Mobile home park lots follow the Mobile Home Park Residency Act.

title: Paying to Stop a Utah Eviction
bodyText: Utah gives a tenant behind on rent two statutory chances to pay and keep the tenancy, and no general right to redeem later. First, the tenant may pay the rent and other amounts due within 3 business days after you serve the pay-or-vacate notice ("Notice to Pay Rent or Vacate"). Second, if you file and post a possession bond in a case based only on nonpayment, the lease stays in force and the case is dismissed if the tenant pays the accrued rent, all other amounts due and costs, including attorney fees as the lease provides, within 3 calendar days after service of the notice of the bond. No Utah statute lets a tenant stop the eviction by paying up to a set time before removal, and none says that paying the money judgment stops the order of restitution; a request for a hearing does not stay the order unless the tenant posts a bond the court approves and the court orders a stay. Paying matters later in one way: once a judgment in a nonpayment or end-of-term eviction is satisfied and a satisfaction is filed, either party may petition to expunge the eviction ("Eviction Record Expungement"). Utah prescribes no wording for accepting a partial payment while keeping your rights, and no statute makes you accept rent from a charity, government program or other third party or limits the payment methods you may require for it. Whether accepting part or all of the rent after a notice gives up the notice is case law; the cautious course is in "Accepting Rent After a Notice", and your lease's payment-method terms apply ("Acceptable Forms of Payment" clause). Mobile home park lots follow the Mobile Home Park Residency Act.

title: The Landlord's Possession Bond
bodyText: Utah's possession bond is one you, the landlord, may post after filing an eviction; Utah has no bond a tenant gives at signing to deliver possession at the end of the term. Any time between filing the complaint and final judgment you may file a possession bond (a corporate bond, cash, certified funds, or a property bond signed by two Utah real property owners who are not parties) in the amount the court approves as the likely costs and damages to the tenant if the suit was wrongly brought. You must serve notice of the bond in the same way as the summons and tell the tenant the alternatives. The tenant may then pay all rent, other amounts due and costs within 3 calendar days (nonpayment-only cases), post a counter bond to stay in possession, or demand a hearing within 3 days; if the tenant does none of these in time, the court grants you an order of restitution on ex parte motion ("Rent Into Court and Counterclaims in Utah Evictions", "Utah Eviction Process"). After an order of restitution, the tenant can stay its enforcement only by posting a bond the court approves and getting a court order. A lease term in which the tenant confesses judgment for possession is not offered by the library ("Confession of Judgment Clauses"). Other bonds you may meet: a landlord seeking a writ of attachment to enforce the lessor's lien for rent must file a bond as in other attachment cases ("Landlord's Lien for Rent"), and a plaintiff seeking abatement of a nuisance by eviction may have to give security.

title: Delays and Stays in a Utah Eviction
bodyText: Utah has no eviction moratorium and no statute that lets a court postpone an eviction because of a tenant's hardship, illness, age or children, the weather or season, holidays, or a pending rental-assistance application. Timing comes from the eviction statute. An order of restitution gives the tenant 3 calendar days after service to leave, unless the court ordered immediate restitution after a criminal-nuisance hearing or the tenant's failure to appear, or you and the tenant agree otherwise; after a criminal-nuisance finding the court may allow up to 72 hours. A tenant's request for a hearing or other filing does not stay the order unless the tenant posts a bond the court approves and the court orders a stay. If a hearing the statute requires within a set time cannot be held because no judge is available, it moves to the first date a judge is. After removal, you, the sheriff or the constable must give the tenant reasonable access within 5 business days to retrieve clothing, identification, financial and public-services documents, and medical information, prescription medications and medical equipment. For belongings treated as abandoned, you must allow up to 15 more calendar days to reclaim them if the tenant gives you a domestic violence police report or protective order, verification of an extended hospitalization, or (from an immediate family member) a death certificate or obituary ("Tenant Property and Animals After an Eviction"). Military service is the one statutory stay. During state military service, evicting a servicemember or dependents for nonpayment where rent is under $2,400 a month needs a court order, and the court may stay the case for up to three months. Federal law gives servicemembers in federal military service a court-ordered-eviction rule for homes up to an inflation-adjusted rent limit and a 90-day stay, longer or shorter as the court decides ("Servicemember Tenant Protections"). Either party may appeal within 10 days (3 days in a private nuisance action). Whether an appeal or a post-judgment motion stays enforcement is set by the court rules, which the library does not hold.

title: Who Receives Eviction Papers for Your Tenant
bodyText: No Utah statute lets your lease name a person to receive eviction notices or court papers for your tenant. The notices before an eviction (to pay or vacate, to perform or vacate, to quit) must be served by one of the statute's methods: delivering a copy to the tenant personally; registered or certified mail or an equivalent, addressed to the tenant at the residence or the leased property; if the tenant is absent, leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion there; or, if no such person is found, posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property. A subtenant is served the same way. The summons and complaint are served under the Utah Rules of Civil Procedure, and the court may authorize alternative service under those rules; whether those rules would treat a person your tenant appoints in the lease as an agent to receive process is a court-rule question, so don't rely on a lease designee and serve the tenant by an ordinary method. One statute names a substitute: if your tenant is enrolled in Utah's Safe at Home address-confidentiality program (for victims of abuse, domestic violence, human trafficking, stalking or sexual offenses), the Department of Criminal Justice is the agent authorized to receive process for the tenant, and the tenant's last known address for court papers is the program's assigned address, not the actual address. The statute does not say whether serving the department replaces serving the tenant at the rental, so if you learn your tenant is a participant, serve the department as well as using an ordinary method at the property. Your own side is different: you must disclose in writing who is authorized to receive notices for you, and a managing agent is treated as the owner for notices unless the lease says otherwise ("Owner and Manager Disclosure" clause). Mobile home park leases must name the park's agent for notice and service of process. See "Utah Eviction Notices by Tenancy Type".

title: No Cold-Weather Move-Out Notice Rule
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires your tenant to tell you before moving out or leaving the home empty in cold weather, sets a winter window for such a notice, or gives you a statutory remedy for freeze damage when a tenant leaves without one. If you want that protection, it has to come from the lease: the optional freeze-protection clause ("Heat and Freeze Protection" clause) has the tenant keep the heat on at your chosen minimum during the heating season, tell you before an absence of more than the number of days you choose, and pay a stated, cost-based amount for freeze damage the tenant's failure causes, while leaving heating repair with you. The tenant must already use the heating system reasonably and may not negligently damage the unit, and the heat itself is your duty to maintain ("Heat in Utah Rentals"). An absence notice also matters for abandonment: abandonment is presumed only if the tenant has not told you about an absence ("Tenant Absences and Abandonment"). In a condominium or homeowners association, the association may, if its governing documents allow and after reasonable notice to the unit owner, enter and winterize a unit whose gas or electric service is about to be cut off for nonpayment, and charge the owner the actual and reasonable cost.

title: No Defense for Late Benefit Payments
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives a tenant a defense, a continuance or a right to reinstatement when a Social Security payment, other government benefit or rental-assistance payment arrives late. In Utah the ordinary rules apply: rent that is unpaid after your 3-business-day pay-or-vacate notice supports an eviction, and the tenant can still pay within the notice period or, if you post a possession bond, within 3 calendar days after service of the bond notice ("Paying to Stop a Utah Eviction"). Federal rules for the Housing Choice Voucher program are different: the family does not owe the part of the rent the housing agency's assistance payment covers, the agency's failure to pay you is not a breach of the lease, and during the lease term you may not end the tenancy because the agency's payment is late or missing. Pursue the agency under your contract with it, and evict only for the tenant's own share. You also may not refuse a renter or set different terms because the renter's income comes from government assistance ("Source of Income Protection").

title: When Your Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: Utah's statutes say nothing about evicting a tenant who files for bankruptcy, so federal bankruptcy law controls. The filing creates an automatic stay that generally stops you from starting or continuing an eviction case, enforcing a judgment, or taking any act to obtain possession of property of the bankruptcy estate. Two federal exceptions matter. First, if you obtained a judgment for possession before the tenant filed, the stay does not stop you from continuing the eviction (the statute writes this as an exception to the stay on acts to obtain possession; whether it also frees the court case itself is bankruptcy case law, so confirm with bankruptcy counsel before taking the next step). That exception is delayed only if the tenant files with the petition a certification that state law would let the tenant cure the whole money default after the judgment, and deposits 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy clerk; it is avoided only if, within 30 days, the tenant also certifies having cured the entire money default. You may object, and the court must hold a hearing within 10 days. If the tenant lists your judgment on the petition but files no certification, the exception applies at once. Utah's statutes give a tenant no right to cure after a judgment for possession ("Saving the Lease From Forfeiture"); whether case law does is not something the library has read. Second, for an eviction based on endangering the property or illegal drug use there, the stay stops applying 15 days after you file and serve a certification, under penalty of perjury, that you have filed the eviction or that the tenant endangered the property or used or allowed controlled substances there in the previous 30 days, unless the tenant objects and shows the court the situation did not exist or has been remedied. In any other case, ask the bankruptcy court for relief from the stay before you serve a notice, file or enforce an order of restitution. In a chapter 7 case a residential lease that the trustee does not assume within 60 days after the order for relief (or a longer time the court sets within that period) is deemed rejected. A lease in default can be assumed only if the default is cured or adequately assured, you are compensated for your actual loss, and future performance is adequately assured. A lease term ending the tenancy because the tenant is insolvent or files for bankruptcy cannot be enforced after the case begins. If the tenant is adjudicated bankrupt, your statutory lessor's lien is limited to the rent for 90 days before the adjudication ("Landlord's Lien for Rent"). Get bankruptcy advice before acting.

title: Minors as Tenants and Eviction Defendants
bodyText: In Utah a person is a minor until age 18, and a minor who marries becomes an adult; there is no higher age for signing a lease. A minor is bound by the minor's contracts, a lease included, unless the minor disaffirms the contract before or within a reasonable time after turning 18 and gives back any money or property received under it that the minor still controls; a minor also owes the reasonable value of necessaries. A minor cannot disaffirm if the minor's own misrepresentation of age, or the minor's engaging in business as an adult, gave you good reason to believe the minor could contract. A minor emancipated by court order may enter into contracts and sue or be sued. Whether housing is a necessary, and how much the minor then owes, is case law. The cautious course for an unmarried applicant under 18 who is not emancipated is to have an adult sign as co-tenant or guarantor and to keep the applicant's written statement of age. In an eviction you may name as defendants only the tenant, a lease signer, and any subtenant actually living in the property when you file (a nuisance abatement case is the exception). You need not join anyone else, and everyone who moves in under the tenant after you file is bound by the judgment. So do not name a minor child who is only an occupant. If the tenant or a lease signer is a minor, how the minor is represented in court is set by the court rules, which the library does not hold. No Utah statute otherwise bars filing against a minor or sets special eviction rules for minors.

title: Who May Represent an Entity Landlord in Court
bodyText: If you own your rentals in your own name, you may represent yourself in your own eviction or rent case. The statute protecting self-representation covers only an individual acting for that individual's own interests, in the individual's own right and not as an assignee. If the landlord is a corporation, limited liability company, partnership or trust, plan on a licensed Utah lawyer for an eviction in district court: Utah makes practicing law without a license a class A misdemeanor (a felony in some cases), and a court that finds unauthorized practice before it must award the other side's resulting attorney fees and costs and may strike the filings. What counts as the practice of law, and any exception that lets a non-lawyer such as a licensed paralegal practitioner or a property manager handle an eviction, is set by the Utah Supreme Court's rules, which the library does not hold. Small claims court is the statutory exception: a person or corporation may litigate a small claim (a money claim, not possession) in person or through authorized employees, with or without counsel, and a non-employee non-lawyer may represent it only as the small claims rules allow. An assignee may not file a small claim, so a collection agency that buys your claim cannot use small claims court. See "Your Remedies When a Tenancy Ends for Default".

title: Deadlines for Suing Over Rent and Damage
bodyText: Utah has no limitation period written specifically for rent or leases, so the general periods apply. A claim on a written lease (unpaid rent, other charges, or damages under the lease) must be brought within 6 years. A claim on an oral lease must be brought within 4 years after the last charge is made or the last payment is received. A claim for the value of a holdover's use of the property (mesne profits) also has 6 years. A claim for waste or injury to the property as a wrong rather than under the lease has 3 years, and so does a claim on a liability created by a Utah statute, unless it is a penalty or forfeiture, which an individual must bring within 1 year. Which period fits a particular damage claim, and whether the eviction statute's trebled damages count as a penalty, are case-law questions, so sue well within the shortest period that could apply. Payments and acknowledgments restart the clock: an action to recover a debt may be brought within the applicable period from the date the debt arose, the date the tenant signs a written acknowledgment of the debt or a promise to pay, or the date the tenant makes a payment on it. Time a tenant spends out of state, and not subject to Utah courts, generally does not count. A judgment can be enforced by action for 8 years and can be renewed. Once a claim is barred it cannot be used as a defense either, for example to offset a tenant's claim. For title purposes, a tenant's possession counts as yours until 7 years after the tenancy ends, or, with no written lease, 7 years after the last rent payment.

title: No Bar on Demanding Rent for a Substandard Unit
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution bars you from demanding or collecting rent, raising rent, or serving a pay-or-vacate notice just because the unit has code violations, has been cited, or lacks a local rental license. The limits come through the Fit Premises Act instead. You may not rent a unit unless it is safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, and you must keep it fit and maintain its electrical, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. If your tenant serves a written notice of a deficient condition choosing rent abatement and you do not take substantial action to correct it within the corrective period, rent is abated from the date of the notice, the lease ends, you must immediately refund the whole deposit and prorated prepaid rent, and the tenant must move out within 10 calendar days after the corrective period. If the tenant chose repair and deduct instead, the tenant may fix the condition and deduct the cost from future rent, up to two months' rent. These remedies are not available to a tenant who is not meeting the tenant's own duties under the Act, and the Act covers a renter's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions"). A government order that bars occupancy raises a separate question ("Rent for Condemned or Unfit Premises"). Local rental licensing ordinances may attach their own conditions ("Local Rental Licensing and Good Landlord Programs"). In a mobile home park, the park may not raise rent between its notice of a planned change in land use or condemnation and the date residents must leave.

title: Renting the Same Home Twice
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution forbids renting the same home or room to two tenants for the same period, or says which of two competing tenants wins.

The tenant who loses out has the Fit Premises Act's possession remedy: if you do not deliver possession of the unit on the date the lease gives, the tenant may end the lease by written notice, and you must then return all prepaid rent and any deposit as promptly as reasonable; or the tenant may keep the lease, and rent abates until you deliver possession. That rule covers a renter's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

Beyond it, the losing tenant may have an ordinary breach-of-contract claim, and taking money for a unit you have already let may be a deceptive practice under the Consumer Sales Practices Act, whose reach to residential leases is case law ("Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and Leases").

Keep one signed lease per unit and period, do not take a second application fee or deposit for a unit already promised, and if two leases overlap, refund the second tenant at once. The library's possession-delay clause covers a late start.

title: Barring Non-Tenants Under Trespass Law
bodyText:
You can use Utah's criminal trespass law to keep a person who is not your tenant off your rental property, within limits. A person commits criminal trespass who, knowing the entry or presence is unlawful, enters or remains on property after notice against entering given by personal communication from the owner or someone with apparent authority to act for the owner, by fencing or another enclosure obviously designed to keep intruders out, or by posted signs likely to be seen.

Entering or remaining is unlawful only if, at the time, the place is not open to the public and the person is not otherwise licensed or privileged to be there. Entering or remaining unlawfully with intent to annoy or injure someone, damage property or commit a crime other than theft or a felony, or recklessly causing fear for another's safety, is also trespass.

It is a class B misdemeanor, or class A in a dwelling. It is a defense that the property was open to the public and the person complied with every lawful condition on access, so post or state the conditions for any area open to the public. You may also recover civil damages of three times the damage caused or $500, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees up to $250 and court costs.

For a barred visitor, give the person a written notice not to enter the property, and keep a copy. Whether your tenant's invitation makes that person licensed or privileged to come to the tenant's unit, or through the common areas to it, is case law. So pair the notice with a lease covenant that makes your tenant keep a barred person away, enforceable as a lease breach (optional clause "No Admitting a Barred Person").

None of this removes a tenant or a former tenant under a written rental agreement: that takes an eviction ("No Lockouts Without a Court Order"). The law-enforcement removal procedure is only for people who never had a right to possession, and a long-term guest who has stayed more than 48 hours without paying commits criminal trespass by staying after you or a tenant tells the guest to leave, unless another tenant has expressly allowed the stay ("Removing Trespassers and Long-Term Guests").

title: Tenancies at Will in Utah
bodyText: Utah's statutes mention a tenancy at will in one place: a tenant at will who stays after a notice of at least 5 calendar days is in unlawful detainer, so you end a tenancy at will with a written notice to quit giving at least 5 calendar days. Serve it by a statutory method (in person; registered or certified mail or an equivalent; with a person of suitable age and discretion at the home if the tenant is absent; or by posting it conspicuously if no one is there). The statute does not define a tenancy at will, say how one is created, or set a notice the tenant must give you; those points, and whether a particular arrangement is a tenancy at will or a periodic tenancy, are case law. The difference matters. If rent is reserved by the month or another period, treat the tenancy as periodic and give the notice for that kind of tenancy: at least 15 calendar days before the end of a rental period, ending the tenancy at the end of that period ("Notice to End a Month-to-Month Tenancy" clause). Where the label is uncertain, the cautious course is to give the longer periodic notice. A fixed-term tenancy ends at the end of its term without notice, and Utah has no statute on tenancies at sufferance. Put any at-will arrangement, such as a stay while a lease is negotiated, in writing with its own notice terms, and see "Utah Eviction Notices by Tenancy Type" and "Holdover" clause for holdovers.

title: Seasonal and Short-Term Rentals in Utah
bodyText: Utah has no statute that sets up a special seasonal tenancy, exempts a seasonal lease from the eviction rules, or prescribes a seasonal lease form. A seasonal rental is an ordinary fixed-term tenancy: it ends on its end date without notice, and a tenant who stays is removed by eviction, not lockout. Where seasonal status matters is coverage. The Fit Premises Act (habitability, repair remedies, entry notice, fee limits) does not cover recreational property rented on an occasional basis, because it covers only a renter's principal place of residence. The deposit statute covers deposits from renters of residential dwelling units, with no seasonal exception. Whether a particular seasonal home is occasional recreational property or someone's principal residence is a question of fact, and if your tenant lives there as a primary home for the season, treat the Act as applying. Short stays of fewer than 30 consecutive days are short-term rentals. Cities and counties may require a business license or permit for them and may bar short-term rental of an internal accessory dwelling unit. A city or county may not ban merely listing or offering a short-term rental on a website. Stays of less than 30 days in tourist homes and similar accommodations may be subject to local transient room tax. If you run the property as a lodging establishment (a bed and breakfast, resort, inn or similar place giving temporary sleeping accommodations to the public), Utah's innkeeper law lets you eject a guest for nonpayment, visible intoxication, disorderly conduct causing a public nuisance, or breaking the law or a conspicuously posted rule. Whether a given vacation rental is a lodging establishment or a tenancy is case law, so if in doubt use eviction. Agricultural land has its own rule: a tenant who holds over more than 60 days after the term with no demand or notice to quit is treated as renewing for a year ("Utah Eviction Notices by Tenancy Type"). Check your city or county short-term rental ordinance.

title: Tenant Absences and Abandonment
bodyText:
No Utah statute requires a tenant to tell you before an extended absence, or requires your lease to ask. You may require it in the lease (optional clause "Notice of Extended Absence").

A tenant's absence notice matters most for abandonment. Abandonment is presumed only if the tenant has not told you about an absence and either (1) has not paid rent within 15 days after it was due and nothing other than belongings left behind shows the tenant still lives there, or (2) has not paid rent when due, has removed the belongings, and nothing shows the tenant still lives there.

If you reasonably believe that presumption is met, you may serve a declaration of abandonment in the statutory words; if the tenant does not dispute it in writing within 24 hours (not counting weekends and court holidays), the declaration is evidence that the tenant has abandoned the unit and you may retake possession ("Handling of Property Left Behind" clause, "Rent Owed After Abandonment").

A tenant who has told you of an absence cannot be presumed to have abandoned the unit, so a lease notice term gives you information without taking away that route when no notice comes.

Entering during an absence follows the ordinary rule: at least 24 hours' notice unless the lease provides otherwise (Fit Premises Act units: a renter's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals). Mobile home parks have their own presumption, with a 45-day nonpayment period. See also "No Cold-Weather Move-Out Notice Rule" and "Heat and Freeze Protection" clause for winter absences.

title: A Tenant's Statutory Rights to End the Lease Early
bodyText:
Utah law lets a residential tenant end a lease early on only a few statutory grounds. Your lease's early-termination option is separate and must leave these rights intact.

**Domestic violence:** a renter who is a victim of domestic violence may end all future obligations under the lease by giving you a protective court order or a qualifying police report, a written notice with the move-out date, and a termination fee of one month's rent, if otherwise in compliance with the lease. The renter must leave within 15 days, pays rent for that time and stays liable for amounts owed before the notice. The right is lost once you serve an eviction notice, and co-tenants stay bound ("Domestic Violence Lease Termination").

**Failure to deliver possession:** if you do not deliver the unit on the date the lease gives, the renter may end the lease by written notice, and you must return all prepaid rent and any deposit as promptly as reasonable; or the renter may keep the lease with rent abated until you deliver.

**Unfit conditions:** if the renter serves a notice of deficient condition choosing rent abatement and you take no substantial action within the corrective period, the lease ends, rent abates from the notice date, and you must immediately refund the deposit and prorated prepaid rent ("Renter Remedies for Deficient Conditions").

These three are Fit Premises Act rights, covering a renter's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

**Military service (federal law):** a servicemember may end a residential lease signed before entering military service, or signed while in service and followed by permanent change-of-station orders or deployment orders for at least 90 days, or signed on receipt of such orders and then blocked by a stop-movement order of at least 30 days, by giving you written notice and a copy of the orders. For monthly rent, the lease ends 30 days after the next rent due date following delivery of the notice. You may not charge an early termination fee, rent owed before then is prorated, and you must refund rent paid in advance for later periods within 30 days.

A spouse or dependent may end the lease within a year after a servicemember dies in service, and a servicemember with a catastrophic injury or illness may do so within a year. Utah's own state-military law adds no termination right ("Servicemember Tenant Protections").

No Utah statute lets a tenant end a lease because you misrepresented the property, or because of age, illness, disability or a move into care ("No Early Termination for Age, Illness or Care"), a fire or other casualty ("Fire or Other Casualty" clause is an optional lease term), or a job transfer.

title: No Early Termination for Age, Illness or Care
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution lets a residential tenant end a lease early because of age, illness, disability or incapacity, or because the tenant is moving into a nursing home, assisted living or other care. Utah also has no rule that a month-to-month tenancy ends when a party becomes incapable of contracting, and no statute ending a lease on a tenant's death ("No Statute on a Tenant's Death"). Without a lease term, the tenant's options are the ordinary ones: end a periodic tenancy with the notice the lease sets, use your lease's early-termination option, or negotiate a release. Two related rules: after an eviction or abandonment, you must allow up to 15 extra calendar days to reclaim stored belongings if the tenant gives you verification of an extended hospitalization from a verified medical provider; and federal law lets a servicemember who suffers a catastrophic injury or illness during service end a residential lease within a year ("A Tenant's Statutory Rights to End the Lease Early"). A tenant's request to leave early because of a disability may be a request for a reasonable accommodation under fair housing law; whether releasing the lease is required is case law, so treat the request seriously and respond in writing ("Disability Accommodations and Modifications"). Continuing care retirement contracts are different: by statute the resident may end the contract with or without cause, it ends on the resident's death, and the contract must say what part of the entrance fee is refunded.

title: No Statutory Exit After an Environmental Event
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives you, or your tenant, a right to end a lease because a flood, wildfire, earthquake, contamination, public health emergency, disaster or government vacate order makes the home unusable.

The one statutory exit is narrower. Under the Fit Premises Act, if your tenant serves a notice of a deficient condition and the unit is not fit for occupancy, you may decide not to correct the condition and end the lease, by written notice no later than the end of the corrective period; rent is prorated to that date, you must pay back prepaid rent and any deposit due within 10 calendar days, and the tenant need not leave sooner than 10 calendar days after your notice ("Ending the Lease Instead of Repairing"). That route depends on the tenant's notice and covers only a renter's principal residence (not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals).

If you want a right to end the lease after an environmental event whether or not the tenant has served a notice, it must be in the lease: use the optional fire or casualty clause ("Fire or Other Casualty" clause) and, for contamination, public health emergencies and government orders, the optional environmental event clause.

Separately, if you know the property is currently contaminated by methamphetamine use, storage or manufacture, you must disclose that in the lease ("Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure" clause), and no government agency may stop you from decontaminating your own property. Whether rent is owed while a government order bars occupancy is a contract question for the courts ("Rent for Condemned or Unfit Premises").

title: Ending a Tenancy to Move In
bodyText:
Utah has no statute that gives, limits or conditions ending a tenancy so that you or a family member can move in, and no just-cause rule ("No Just-Cause Eviction Rule"). A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy may be ended for that reason, or any lawful reason, with written notice served at least 15 calendar days before the end of a rental period ("Notice to End a Month-to-Month Tenancy" clause).

A fixed-term lease, though, runs to its end date unless the lease itself reserves an early-termination right; if it says nothing, you have no right to end it early to move in.

If you may want the home back during the term, use the optional owner-occupancy clause, which lets you end a fixed term on written notice of at least the number of days you choose (not less than 30), at the end of a monthly rental period, for occupancy by you or the named family member. Utah sets no minimum period you must then live there, and no relocation payment. If the tenant does not leave, only a court can remove the tenant.

If the tenant uses a federal Housing Choice Voucher, federal rules bar ending the tenancy during the initial lease term because you want the unit for personal or family use, and you must give a written notice stating the grounds. Fair housing rules still bar choosing which tenant to displace for a prohibited reason ("Utah Fair Housing Act").

title: No Automatic-Renewal Rule for Utah Leases
bodyText:
No Utah statute regulates an automatic-renewal clause in a residential lease. Nothing requires larger or bold type, a separate signature or opt-in, a reminder notice before the lease renews, or limits how early you may ask a tenant to decide whether to renew.

Utah has two automatic-renewal laws, and both leave leases out. The Automatic Renewal Contracts Act, which requires a notice 30 to 60 days before a paid term renews and voids a renewal provision that breaks it, does not apply to a rental agreement, and it defines a rental agreement to include any agreement about the use or occupancy of real property for residential purposes. The Service Contracts Act, which requires written notice of an automatic renewal in a contract for service, maintenance or repair of real property, does not cover a contract creating a leasehold interest. A separate paid service or product contract you make with a tenant outside the lease is not covered by either exclusion.

Without a renewal clause, a fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term without notice, and a tenant who stays on without your agreement is holding over ("Holdover Damages in Utah"). If you want the lease to roll over, say so in the lease ("Automatic Renewal" clause), and fix any rent change for a renewal term in the clause or get the tenant's signed agreement to it ("Rent Increases Written Into the Lease").

Agricultural land is different: a tenant who holds over more than 60 days with no demand for possession or notice to quit holds for another full year. Mobile home park spaces follow the Mobile Home Park Residency Act.

title: Lease Guarantors and Co-Signers in Utah
bodyText:
Utah has no statute on lease guarantors or co-signers. Nothing limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires renewal terms to be stated, requires a guaranty to set a maximum amount or an end date, lets a guarantor revoke a continuing guaranty, or caps a deposit you take from a guarantor.

One rule applies: a promise to answer for another person's debt or default is void unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing signed by the guarantor. Have the guarantor sign the lease or a written guaranty.

Whether a guaranty covers a renewal, extension or month-to-month continuation depends on its words, and how a court reads silence is case law, so state it: the library's optional guaranty clause names a maximum and lets you choose whether renewals are covered.

If you release one tenant or co-signer, put an express written reservation of your rights against the others in the same release; without it, Utah's joint obligations law can discharge the others in part. If you take a deposit from a guarantor, the cautious course is to handle it like a tenant's deposit under Utah's deposit-return rules, which speak only of deposits from renters.

title: Paying Rent in Installments
bodyText:
No Utah statute addresses paying rent in installments or says whether a scheduled installment is a partial payment. A lease may set rent in installments, such as half on the 1st and half on the 15th, and each installment is then due on the date the lease sets: the tenant must be current on all payments the rental agreement requires, and a 3-business-day notice to pay or vacate may be served any time after an amount becomes due.

State the schedule in the lease and say that installments paid on schedule are not partial payments. Utah caps a late fee at the greater of 10% of the rent in the rental agreement or $75. How that cap works when one month's rent is split is unsettled, so keep all late fees for one rental period within the cap measured on that period's rent.

Whether taking part of the rent after you serve a notice affects the notice is a question for the courts ("Accepting Rent After a Notice"). These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals. The library's optional clause is "Rent Paid in Installments" clause.

title: Move-Out Forms and Work During a Notice
bodyText: No Utah statute governs a move-out or notice-to-vacate form you ask a tenant to sign, requires a warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain, or sets what a tenant's notice of intent to vacate must say. Utah also has no rule against renovation or other work while a notice to vacate is pending. Two rules still matter. Utah treats any agreement, written or oral, that modifies the terms of the tenancy as part of the rental agreement, so a signed form can change the lease; whether a move-out form does is a question for the courts. And you may not charge a fee or other cost the rental agreement does not include, except by 15 days' notice on a month-to-month agreement. Keep a move-out form to the facts: the move-out date and a forwarding address for the deposit refund. Put any new term in a separate written amendment that says it changes the lease, and do not use the form to add a charge. Until the tenancy ends, your Fit Premises Act duties continue: the unit must stay safe, sanitary and fit, with working electrical, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. You may enter for repairs on 24 hours' notice unless the lease provides otherwise, and the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for repairs. Do not start work that makes the unit unfit while the tenant still lives there. These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Converting a Rental Building
bodyText: Utah has no condominium-conversion statute for rental housing. No Utah law requires notice to tenants before you convert a rented building to condominiums or a cooperative, gives tenants a right to buy their units, requires a conversion statement in the lease, or bars converting rental housing to a hotel or other short-term use. The tenancy rules still apply: a conversion cannot cut short a fixed-term lease, and a month-to-month tenancy ends only on a notice served at least 15 calendar days before the end of a rental period ("Notice to End a Month-to-Month Tenancy" clause). One condominium rule touches tenants: the condominium declaration must be signed by the owners and any lessees of the land, except a lessee whose leasehold does not extend to any part of the common areas. Whether an apartment tenant's lease counts is for the courts, so get legal advice before recording a declaration over occupied units. Mobile home parks are different: an owner planning a change in land use must mail each resident notice at least nine months before the resident must leave, tell new residents before they move in, and may not raise rent in the meantime, and cities and counties may not regulate park closures. Local zoning, short-term rental and conversion ordinances may apply in some cities and are not covered here.

title: No Landlord Foreclosure Disclosure Duty
bodyText: No Utah statute requires you, as the landlord, to tell a tenant or applicant that the property is in default or foreclosure, before or after the lease is signed. The tenant notices Utah requires fall on the foreclosing party. Where the loan's stated purpose was to finance residential rental property, a lender who files a judicial foreclosure must, within 20 days, post a notice on each unit's door (fewer than nine units) or in at least three conspicuous places (nine or more), or mail it to each occupant, in at least 14-point type with a statutory Notice to Tenant. A trustee selling under such a trust deed must post or mail the notice of sale with a similar tenant statement. If the loan was not made to finance rental property, neither tenant notice is required: in a trustee's sale the only notice at the property is the general notice of sale posted in a conspicuous place at least 20 days before the sale, and in a judicial foreclosure no tenant notice is required at all. A missing notice does not invalidate the foreclosure. Your lease and your duties under it continue until the property is sold: keep the unit fit, keep collecting rent, and keep deposits ready for whoever holds the property when the tenancy ends ("Deposits When the Property Is Sold"). What happens to tenants after the sale is covered in "Tenants When the Property Is Foreclosed". Do not misstate the property's status if an applicant asks.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText:
No Utah statute requires you to notify tenants when you sell the property or change managers, and none releases a selling landlord from the lease once notice is given. A sale does not end the lease: a fixed term runs to its end, and the new owner, as your successor, may end a month-to-month tenancy on the usual 15-day notice.

Deposits follow the property: whoever holds the owner's interest when a tenancy ends is bound by Utah's deposit-return rules, so transfer the deposits to the buyer or account for them in the sale ("Deposits When the Property Is Sold").

Utah requires a written disclosure of the owner's or manager's name, address and phone number only at or before the start of the term; when ownership or management changes, the cautious course is to give tenants the new name, address and phone number and where to pay rent, in writing. A manager is treated as the owner for notices unless the lease says otherwise in writing. For showings, give 24 hours' notice unless the lease sets another rule.

If you default on a loan secured by the rents, your lender may notify tenants to pay rent to it. After that notice the tenant must pay the lender, until a court order or the lender's signed cancellation says otherwise; a tenant who does not live in the unit as a primary residence and keeps paying you is not discharged; for a tenant who lives there as a primary residence the statute does not apply that rule, and whether payment to you discharges the tenant is case law. The tenant gets a short grace period, and the lender takes subject to the lease and the tenant's defenses.

A court-appointed receiver may not reject the unexpired lease of a tenant who lives in the unit as a primary residence. Foreclosure is covered in "Tenants When the Property Is Foreclosed".

title: Notices About Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText:
Utah has no general rule requiring you to tell tenants or applicants that the property faces a lawsuit, foreclosure, tax sale, condemnation or code-enforcement case, and no rule requiring a tenant to tell you when the tenant receives such a notice.

Tenants often hear from others instead: a foreclosing lender or trustee must post or mail a notice to the tenants of residential rental property ("No Landlord Foreclosure Disclosure Duty"), and before a tax sale the county auditor mails notice to the occupant of any improved property.

Two disclosures you do owe sit elsewhere: methamphetamine contamination you know of ("Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure" clause), and, for a mobile home park, mailed notice to every resident at least nine months before residents must leave for a planned change in land use or condemnation, plus notice of the first agency hearing at least seven days before it.

Because nothing requires your tenant to pass on papers delivered to the property, use the library's clause requiring the tenant to tell you of any proceeding to recover the property and hand over the notice ("Notice of Proceedings Against the Property" clause).

title: When the Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText:
No Utah statute says what happens to a residential lease when the property is taken by eminent domain: none ends the lease or the rent, lets the court cancel the lease, makes the lease's own condemnation terms control, or lets either side end the lease after a partial taking. Those questions are left to the lease and to case law, so put the answer in the lease ("Eminent Domain" clause).

In the condemnation case, the court values the property as a whole and each separate interest in it, and anyone occupying or claiming an interest may appear, so a tenant can claim the value of a leasehold. A lease term giving that value to you is common, but whether it binds a residential tenant is case law; the library's clause keeps relocation and improvement payments with the tenant either way.

Utah's Relocation Assistance Act protects people displaced by a taking, tenants included, and binds the condemning agency, not you: no one has to move from a residence until offered a comparable replacement dwelling, the agency must, as far as practicable, give at least 90 days' written notice before a required move, and an agency letting an occupant stay on short-term may charge no more than fair rental value.

Relocation payments go to the displaced person. A tenant who owns improvements it may remove is paid their value only if you disclaim any interest in them. A landlord whose only business at the site is renting to others does not qualify for the fixed business relocation payment. Mobile home parks: the nine-month land-use notice does not apply to a government condemnation.

title: Agreeing on Notice Methods
bodyText:
Utah's landlord-tenant statutes do not use an "actual notice" standard, and no statute lets the parties add a notice method across the board. Whether you may agree on another method depends on the notice.

Eviction notices (to pay or leave, to comply or leave, and notices to quit) must be served by a method the eviction statute lists: in person; by registered or certified mail or an equivalent means; if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the residence; or, only if no such person can be found there, by posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property. Text and email are not named, and whether either is an "equivalent means" is unsettled, so do not rely on them for these notices even if the lease names them; the federal and Utah electronic-signature laws do not change that.

Some Utah rules leave the method to the lease or to the tenant. The 24-hour entry notice applies except as the rental agreement provides, so the lease may say how entry notice is given. Your tenant may serve a notice of a deficient condition by a statutory method or by a method the rental agreement sets, and may report a dangerous condition by any reasonable means. You may send the deposit refund and itemization electronically by a means the tenant gave you.

Electronic notice works only between parties who have agreed to deal electronically, it must be in a form the recipient can keep and print, and a tenant who agreed may later refuse further electronic dealings; that right cannot be waived.

The library's optional clause is "Added Notice Methods" clause. The entry-notice and deficient-condition rules are in Utah's Fit Premises Act, which covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals; the eviction-notice methods apply to every tenancy.

title: Online Portals for Rent and Notices
bodyText:
No Utah statute bars you from offering, or asking a tenant to use, an online portal for rent, maintenance requests, signatures or notices, and none regulates portal fees for landlords.

Utah's electronic transactions law sets the limits. It applies only between parties who have each agreed to deal electronically, and a tenant who agreed may refuse to deal electronically in later transactions; that right cannot be waived in the lease. So a lease term requiring every signature or notice to go through the portal cannot bind a tenant who later refuses. Whether the same right reaches how rent is paid is unsettled, so keep at least one way to pay that does not need the portal.

An electronic signature counts where a signature is required, and an electronic notice counts where writing is required only if the tenant can keep and print it. If you send consumer notices the law requires in writing, the federal E-SIGN Act also asks for the tenant's informed consent first.

Never use the portal to serve a notice to pay rent or leave, a notice to comply or leave or a notice to quit: serve those by a method the eviction statute lists.

Any portal or card fee must be in the lease with its amount (on a month-to-month agreement a new fee needs 15 days' notice). The library's optional clause is "Online Portal" clause. These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Terms
bodyText: No Utah statute bars terms that are more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant, or the reverse, and none limits how much more rent you may charge for one kind of lease than another; cities and counties may not control rents ("State Preemption of Rent Control and Local Landlord Rules"). The lease type still changes the rules that apply. A fixed term ends on its last day without notice, while a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy ends on a notice served at least 15 calendar days before the end of a rental period ("Notice to End a Month-to-Month Tenancy" clause). And only on a month-to-month agreement may you add a fee the rental agreement does not include, after 15 days' notice; in a fixed term every fee must be in the lease from the start ("Fees Must Be in the Lease"). Whatever you offer, offer it on the same terms to every applicant in the same situation ("Utah Fair Housing Act"). Mobile home park leases must state whether the leasehold is for a term or periodic.

title: No Type-Size Rule for Utah Leases
bodyText: No Utah statute sets a minimum type size or font for a residential lease, and none makes a lease, or a term in it, unenforceable or inadmissible because the print is small.
