The type-size rules Utah does have are for other documents: a lender foreclosing on residential rental property must give tenants a notice in at least 14-point type, the cancellation notice for a direct-solicitation sale must be in at least 12-point bold type, and the automatic-renewal notice law, which requires larger or contrasting type, does not apply to rental agreements. Utah also has no plain-language rule for leases ("No Plain-Language Lease Law in Utah") and prescribes no lease layout ("What a Utah Lease Must Contain", "No Font or First-Page Lease Disclosure Rule"). Print the lease in a size an ordinary reader can read easily anyway: a term a tenant could not reasonably read invites a dispute over whether it was agreed, which is a question of case law.

title: No Lease Translation Duty in Utah
bodyText: No Utah statute requires you to translate a lease or any rental notice, to give a tenant the lease in the language you advertised or negotiated in, or prescribes verbatim lease text with a type size and translation rule, and none says which version controls if you sign a lease in two languages. Utah's translation duties are for other businesses: debt-management providers who communicate mainly in another language, solar retailers who market in another language (whose agreement is unenforceable without the translated copy), insurers, whose English version controls a dispute, and buyers of inheritance interests. Utah prescribes no form for the lease itself ("Forms Utah Prescribes for Rentals") and has no plain-language rule ("No Plain-Language Lease Law in Utah"). If you negotiate in another language, the cautious course is to give the tenant a translation and say in the lease which language version controls; how a court would treat a tenant who signed a lease in a language the tenant could not read is case law. Language practices must not become national-origin discrimination, which Utah's Fair Housing Act forbids ("Utah Fair Housing Act").

title: Lease-Option and Rent-to-Own Homes
bodyText: Utah has no statute governing a residential lease with an option to purchase, or a rent-to-own or lease-purchase arrangement for a home. Nothing sets the option's required terms, lets the tenant exercise early without penalty, gives a longer cure period for money defaults, protects option money from forfeiture, or requires a cancellation statement or recording. Utah has no general seller property-condition disclosure statute and no disclosure form triggered by an option. The one statutory condition disclosure, known current methamphetamine contamination, applies to a lease, a conveyance and any other transaction related to the property, so it covers the lease, the option and a sale on exercise ("Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure" clause). General rules still apply. A contract for the sale of land, or a lease for longer than one year, is void unless it or a memorandum of it is in writing signed by the party making the sale or lease, so put the option in a signed writing ("Leases Longer Than One Year Must Be Written"). An option is an interest in land that can be recorded, and an unrecorded interest may not bind a later buyer who records first. Utah's rental-purchase law covers rent-to-own of household goods, not homes. Whether option money is forfeited on default, or the arrangement is really a sale, is case law; have a lawyer draft any lease-option, and keep the option in a separate signed document so the lease's own terms stay clear.

title: Disclosures Utah Requires for a Rental
bodyText: Utah requires a short list of written disclosures for a residential rental, and no state form or first-page notice. Before you take an application fee: a good-faith estimate of rent and fixed fees, the type of each use-based charge, the availability date, your screening criteria and how money is refunded ("Written Disclosures Before Taking an Application Fee"). Before signing: a written condition inventory, a condition form, or a chance for a walkthrough ("Move-In Condition Record"). When you take a deposit: a written statement of any part that is nonrefundable ("Nonrefundable Deposits" clause). At or before the start of the term: the name, address and phone number of the owner or manager, or of the person authorized to receive notices ("Owner and Manager Disclosure" clause), an executed copy of a written lease and a copy of any rules ("Copy of Lease and Rules"). If you know of it: current methamphetamine contamination ("Methamphetamine Contamination Disclosure" clause). For pre-1978 housing, the federal lead-based paint disclosure, and for land under a recorded environmental covenant, the covenant notice ("Environmental Covenant Notice" clause). If you are a licensed real estate agent or broker, disclose in writing whether you are renting for yourself or for an undisclosed principal; any rule on its form is in the Real Estate Commission's rules. Utah has no notice of rent-regulation or just-cause coverage ("No Good-Cause Notice in Utah"), no rights statement ("No Truth-in-Renting Statement in Utah") and no seller disclosure triggered by an option to buy ("Lease-Option and Rent-to-Own Homes"). Mobile home park leases have their own required contents.

title: Emergency Contacts for Tenants
bodyText:
No Utah statute requires a lease to give an emergency or after-hours contact, a management website or a social-services hotline notice, and none requires you to post emergency contacts in the building.

Two rules make a working contact wise. At or before the start of the term you must give the tenant, in writing, the name, address and phone number of the owner or of the manager or person authorized to receive notices ("Owner and Manager Disclosure" clause). And a tenant may report a dangerous condition, one that risks imminent loss of life or significant physical harm, by any reasonable means, after which you must begin remedial action within 24 hours. So give tenants a number that is answered around the clock.

Asking the tenant for a personal emergency contact is not regulated; the library's optional clause limits how you use it ("Tenant's Emergency Contact" clause). These Fit Premises Act rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText:
No Utah statute regulates renter's insurance in a residential lease. You may require it, and nothing sets who chooses the insurer, a proof deadline, force-placed or landlord-bought coverage, an administrative fee, or a required notice that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings.

Utah's fee rule controls any money you collect for it: you may not charge a cost the rental agreement does not include, or more than the amount it states. If you buy coverage when the tenant fails to show proof and want the tenant to repay it, the lease must say so in advance and fix the method, such as the premium the insurer actually bills you for that coverage, with no markup or added fee and a copy of the bill; on a month-to-month agreement a new charge needs 15 days' notice. An unpaid insurance charge may come out of the deposit at move-out only if the lease provides for it.

The library's Utah clause requiring renter's insurance and saying your insurance does not cover the tenant's property is "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause.

In a condominium or homeowners' association, the association's insurer does not waive its claims against your tenant ("Tenant Insurance Claims and Subrogation"), which is one more reason to require liability coverage. These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: No Landlord Insurance Requirement
bodyText: Utah does not require a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to tell tenants what insurance it carries, or to buy a fire policy with a relocation benefit for displaced tenants. The state's limits on city rental licensing do not list insurance as a licensing condition, and whether a particular city's business license asks for it is a local question ("Local Rental Licensing and Good Landlord Programs"). If you rent a condominium unit or a home in a homeowners' association, the association must carry its own property and liability insurance, and when a loss is covered by both the association's policy and yours, the association's policy is primary but you as unit owner are responsible for a share of the association's deductible, measured by the damage to your unit. Insurance remains your protection against claims by tenants and guests; Utah has no statute limiting lease terms that shift liability ("Clauses Limiting Your Liability").

title: Tenant Insurance Claims and Subrogation
bodyText: No Utah statute says whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's own insurance, or how a tenant's claim affects the tenancy. Two rules shape what you can do. Your repair duties under the Fit Premises Act are yours unless an explicit written agreement signed by both of you allocates a duty to the tenant, so do not make a tenant's insurance claim a condition of repairs you owe ("Tenant-Performed Duties" clause). And any cost you pass to the tenant, such as your deductible for tenant-caused damage, must be in the lease with its amount or method ("Fees and Charges" clause); liability for tenant-caused damage is in "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause. An insurer that pays a loss may sue in its insured's name to recover it. In a condominium or homeowners' association, the association's insurer waives that right only against the unit or lot owner and people living with an owner who lives there, so a tenant of an owner who does not live there is not protected and may be pursued if the tenant causes a loss. Whether your own insurer can pursue a negligent tenant is case law. These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Rentals After a Declared Disaster
bodyText: No Utah statute says what a declared disaster does to a residential lease: nothing ends the tenancy, stops rent while the unit cannot be reached, sets debris or hazard clean-up duties, or pauses evictions. The ordinary rules decide it. You may not rent a unit that is not safe, sanitary and fit, and the Fit Premises Act's notice and remedy process applies to damage the disaster causes: if your tenant serves a notice of deficient condition and the unit is not fit for occupancy, you may decide not to repair and end the lease by telling the tenant in writing before the corrective period ends; you must then refund prorated prepaid rent and any deposit due within 10 calendar days, and the tenant has at least 10 calendar days after your notice to leave. The library's optional casualty clause ends or reduces rent for a destroyed or partly unusable unit ("Fire or Other Casualty" clause), and the cautious course is not to charge rent for days the tenant cannot occupy the unit ("Rent for Condemned or Unfit Premises"). During a declared state of emergency, Utah's price-gouging law bars providing a service, including a rental, that people need because of the emergency at more than 10% above the highest price you charged in the 30 days before the declaration, inside the affected area. Whether that reaches an ordinary lease or a rent increase is unsettled, so while a declaration lasts, do not raise rents or price vacant units above that level for people displaced or affected by the disaster. The governor and local officials can issue emergency orders with the force of law, order evacuation of premises and, by executive order, suspend enforcement of a statute for up to the life of the declaration; check current orders when an emergency is declared. Mobile home park spaces are not covered here. The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Housing People Displaced by a Disaster
bodyText: No Utah statute lets a tenant house people displaced by a fire, flood or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, limits how long such guests may stay, or says that a displaced person staying in a hotel or someone's home does not become a tenant. Your lease terms apply as written: a tenant may not increase the number of occupants above the number the rental agreement specifies without your written permission, and your guest rules bind the tenant ("Guest Policy" clause, "Guests and Visitors"). If a tenant asks to take in displaced family or friends, the practical course is a short written permission that names them and sets an end date, so they stay guests rather than becoming occupants or tenants; whether a long stay creates a tenancy is case law. Apply the same approach to everyone who asks ("Utah Fair Housing Act"). Public housing authorities may house disaster victims notwithstanding their usual admission and occupancy rules. These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: No Tenant Right to Buy on Sale
bodyText: Utah gives tenants no right to buy, or to receive an offer on, a rental property you plan to sell, and no right of first refusal; there is no District of Columbia-style tenant opportunity to purchase law. Utah also has no statewide rent cap or just-cause eviction law, and cities and counties may not control rents, so no lease notice about rent limits, just-cause coverage or a purchase right is required ("No Good-Cause Notice in Utah", "State Preemption of Rent Control and Local Landlord Rules"). When you sell, the lease and the deposit obligations pass with the property ("Selling the Property or Changing Managers", "Deposits When the Property Is Sold"). Mobile home parks are the nearest case: residents may form an association to buy all or part of the park and may limit its membership to home owners for that purpose, but the park owner has no duty to sell to it; a planned change in land use needs nine months' mailed notice ("Converting a Rental Building").

title: No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Exemption Notice
bodyText: Because Utah has no statewide rent cap, no just-cause eviction law for houses and apartments and no tenant right to buy, there is nothing for a property to be exempt from, and no lease or notice statement of exemption is required. Cities and counties may not control rents ("State Preemption of Rent Control and Local Landlord Rules"), and the library's Utah rows on just cause and purchase rights say the same ("No Just-Cause Eviction Rule", "No Tenant Right to Buy on Sale"). Leave other states' exemption notices out of a Utah lease: a statement about a law Utah does not have only confuses the tenant. Mobile home park space leases are different, because a park may end a lease only for causes the Mobile Home Park Residency Act lists, and the lease must disclose that protection conspicuously.

title: No Expiring Tenant Laws in Utah
bodyText: As of November 8, 2026, none of Utah's core landlord-tenant statutes is scheduled to expire: the Fit Premises Act, the deposit statute, the eviction statute, the Fair Housing Act, the Mobile Home Park Residency Act and the ban on local rent control carry no repeal date, and none appears in the Code's lists of sunset and repeal dates. One change is dated: a new version of the section on crime victims' new locks and domestic violence lease termination takes effect January 1, 2027 ("Domestic Violence Lease Termination", "New Locks for Crime Victims"). Utah has no tenant protection act like California's to expire. The Legislature can still amend these laws in any session, so the library rechecks them after each one.

title: Rent Increases Written Into the Lease
bodyText:
Utah has no statute on rent escalation clauses. Nothing sets how much or how often rent may rise, no statute sets notice for an increase, and cities and counties may not control rents. Utah also has no general retaliation statute, so no safe harbour for an increase depends on what the lease says.

During a fixed term, rent changes only as the lease provides. Write any increase into the lease as a stated new amount and the date it starts, or as an objective formula such as a published price index. Utah's fee rule bars charging a cost in an amount greater than the rental agreement states; whether rent counts as such a cost is a question for the courts, so the library does not offer a clause letting you raise rent mid-term by notice in an amount you choose then.

Before you take an application fee, your written good-faith estimate of the rent should show any scheduled increase: if the lease amount differs from the estimate, a prospective renter who has not signed or moved in may demand all money back within five business days.

To raise rent on a month-to-month tenancy, get the tenant's signed agreement or end the tenancy with at least 15 calendar days' notice before the end of a rental period and offer new terms ("Changing Terms of a Periodic Tenancy" clause, "No Rent-Increase Notice Rule"). These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

Mobile home park spaces have their own rules: a periodic increase needs 60 days' mailed notice, and no increase is allowed after a notice of a planned change in land use. The library's optional escalation clause is "Scheduled Rent Changes" clause.

title: Passing Tax and Insurance Increases to Tenants
bodyText:
No Utah statute addresses passing a property-tax or insurance increase to a residential tenant. Nothing requires or forbids a tax escalation clause, sets the tenant's share, or requires you to refund an abatement. Utah's fee rule still controls how you do it: you may not charge a cost the rental agreement does not include, or more than the amount it states, except that on a month-to-month agreement you may add a charge after 15 days' notice.

So a fixed-term lease must contain the clause from the start, with an objective method: the tenant's stated percentage of the increase over a base year shown on the county's tax bill or the insurer's premium notice, a copy of the bill given, and no markup or added fee. Refund the same share of any later reduction or abatement so the tenant never pays more than the method gives.

An unpaid share may be taken from the deposit at the end of the tenancy only if the lease provides for it. Before you take an application fee, list the charge and how it is figured in your written pre-application disclosure.

These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals. The library's optional clause is "Tax and Insurance Increases" clause; rent increases are covered in "Rent Increases Written Into the Lease".

title: Property Rules and Changing Them
bodyText:
Utah makes the tenant's duty to follow your rules part of the Fit Premises Act: a tenant must comply with each rule, regulation or requirement of the rental agreement, including any smoking rule, and the rental agreement includes any agreement, written or oral, that sets or changes the rules. At or before the start of the term, give the tenant a copy of any rules that apply to the unit.

A tenant who breaks a rule that is part of the agreement can be served a 3-calendar-day notice to comply or leave, and a tenant out of compliance loses the Fit Premises Act repair remedies.

Utah has no statute setting a reasonableness test for rules and none letting you change the rules on your own during a tenancy. In a fixed term, the cautious course is that a new or changed rule binds the tenant only if the tenant agrees to it in writing or it becomes part of a renewal ("Rules and Regulations" clause). On a month-to-month tenancy, propose the change in writing and get the tenant's signed agreement, or end the tenancy and offer new terms ("Changing Terms of a Periodic Tenancy" clause).

Any fine or fee in the rules must state its amount, because the rules are part of the rental agreement and you may not charge more than it states; on a month-to-month agreement a new charge needs 15 days' notice. Apply rules evenly to all tenants ("Utah Fair Housing Act"). These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

Mobile home parks have their own statute: rules must relate to health, safety, conduct or upkeep, may not be unconscionable, and a new rule requiring exterior improvements takes effect only 60 to 120 days after it is issued, depending on cost.

title: Billing Tenants for Electricity or Gas
bodyText: No Utah statute requires a lease disclosure when you submeter electricity or natural gas to a tenant, and none is written for landlord submetering. The open question is a different one: whether a landlord that bills tenants for electricity or gas it buys from the utility becomes a public utility regulated by the Public Service Commission. Utah's utility law treats a person that furnishes electricity or gas to consumers for domestic use, for payment, as a public utility. It leaves out electricity generated on or distributed by a producer solely for its own use or its tenants' use and not for sale to the public generally, and gas made or produced on private property and distributed by the producer solely for its own or its tenants' use and not for sale to others. Power from an on-site renewable system that you give tenants without charge is expressly exempt, and so, under conditions, is on-site renewable power used by occupants of property you own or control. Whether a landlord that resells electricity or gas bought from the utility, by submeter or by formula, is covered is not settled by the Code; the Commission's rules and the utilities' tariffs may answer it, and the library does not hold them. Until they are checked, the cautious course is not to bill tenants for electricity or gas measured by your own submeter or allocated by formula: have each tenant hold the account for a utility-owned meter serving only the unit, or pay the service yourself as part of the rent. If you bill a tenant for any utility, the lease must state the charge or the method for figuring it, and your written pre-application disclosure must list its type. Mobile home parks have their own rules: a park lease must fully disclose every utility cost the park charges and how each resident's bill is calculated, including costs allocated from a master-metered bill and submetered costs, the park must give a yearly disclosure of how utility charges were calculated, and a park using a single-service meter must show the resident's utility charges on the bill. Charging for electric vehicle charging is treated differently ("Electric Vehicle Charging at a Rental"); water, sewer and trash allocation is in "Splitting Shared Utility Bills".

title: No Meter-Based Efficiency Charge Rule
bodyText: No section of the Utah Code or Constitution lets a utility attach an energy-efficiency repayment charge to a meter so that it follows the premises to the next customer, requires you to tell a new tenant about such a charge, or gives the tenant a rent deduction for one. Utah's efficiency laws work differently. The Public Service Commission may approve a line-item charge on the bills of all of an electric utility's customers to pay for its demand-side management programs, so a tenant who holds the electric account pays it like any other customer; it is not tied to a particular meter or upgrade. A commercial property assessed clean energy (C-PACE) assessment can finance efficiency, clean-energy or vehicle-charging work on a building with more than four rental units, but only with the owner's voluntary consent, and it is an assessment on the property with the same lien priority as a property tax; nothing in the act passes it to tenants. If you want a tenant to pay any part of an energy charge you pay, the lease must state the charge or its method, as with any other charge; a charge the lease does not include is allowed only on a month-to-month tenancy after 15 days' notice. Any on-bill program in a utility's tariff is outside the library, which does not hold the commission's rules or the tariffs. Utah also has no statute regulating how a landlord bills submetered water; see "Splitting Shared Utility Bills".

title: Utility Allowances and Rebilled Utilities
bodyText:
Utah has no statute capping what you may charge a tenant when you rebill a utility, and no statute on utility allowances, except in mobile home parks, where a park's yearly income from service charges may not exceed its actual cost of providing the services.

For other rentals the fee rule controls: you may charge a tenant only a charge the lease includes, in the amount or by the method the lease states; on a month-to-month lease you may add one after 15 days' notice. An allowance with a tenant-paid overage is lawful if the lease fixes the allowance and measures the overage by the provider's actual bill, with no markup or added fee, and you give the tenant a copy of the bill ("Utility Allowance with Tenant-Paid Overage" clause).

List the overage as a use-based charge in your written pre-application disclosure. For electricity or natural gas, use an allowance only where a utility-owned meter serves only the unit ("Billing Tenants for Electricity or Gas").

If the tenant leaves owing an overage, you may take it from the deposit because the lease provides for it. Don't cut off service to collect it ("Interrupting a Tenant's Utilities"). These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Splitting Shared Utility Bills
bodyText:
Utah has no statute that bars you from charging a tenant for a utility that is not separately metered to the unit, or that regulates how you divide a shared bill among units, whether by submeter, floor area, occupants or another formula.

Three rules shape it. First, the fee rule: the charge must be in the lease, with the method for figuring it, or you can't collect it (on a month-to-month lease you may add one after 15 days' notice), and your written pre-application disclosure must list the type of each use-based charge.

Second, cities may not interfere with your contract with a tenant about paying utility or municipal service costs, but a city or special district may still make you, as owner, sign for and pay all water and sewer service, so you stay liable to the provider whatever the lease says.

Third, for electricity and natural gas the cautious course is not to allocate or submeter at all ("Billing Tenants for Electricity or Gas").

For water, sewer, storm water and trash, use "Shared Water, Sewer and Trash Charges" clause: it states the method, passes through only what the provider bills, and gives the tenant a copy of each bill.

A city or county may prohibit a separate meter for an internal accessory dwelling unit, so an ADU lease should say how shared costs are split. Mobile home parks must disclose master-meter allocations and submetered costs in the lease ("Billing Tenants for Electricity or Gas"). These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Utility Charges in the Pre-Application Disclosure
bodyText: Utah requires no utility attachment to a lease: no prescribed form on how a shared bill is split, no billing history or average-cost statement, and no submeter certificate. What it does require comes before the lease. Before you accept an application fee or any other payment from a prospective tenant, you must give a written disclosure that includes a good-faith estimate of the rent and of each fixed non-rent charge (a flat monthly utility or service fee, for example) and the type of each use-based non-rent charge (a water or trash charge that varies with use, for example). The estimates may be given in the rental application, a deposit agreement or a written summary. If the lease then states a different amount, or adds a use-based charge you did not disclose, the applicant may demand in writing, within five business days after receiving the lease and before signing it or moving in, the return of everything paid, and you must refund it within five business days. The lease itself must still state each utility charge and how it is figured ("Splitting Shared Utility Bills"), and the library's clauses say who pays which utility ("Utilities Paid by Tenant" clause, "Utilities Paid by Landlord" clause). Mobile home parks must put full utility-cost disclosures in the lease itself and give a yearly disclosure ("Billing Tenants for Electricity or Gas"). These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Copies of Utility Shutoff Notices
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code lets a landlord, or a tenant on the landlord's behalf, designate someone to receive a utility's notice of pending disconnection, and none requires a utility to copy a landlord on a shutoff notice. Any such third-party notice program for electric, gas, water or sewer utilities would sit in the Public Service Commission's rules or the utility's tariff, or, for city or district water and sewer, in local ordinances.

What the Code does say: a special district may not suspend service at the request of a private third party who is not the customer, and a public utility may not disconnect basic utility service for an account holder's failure to pay third-party charges billed through the utility.

You may still ask your tenant to authorize you as an additional contact on the tenant's accounts; the optional clause "Authorization for Utility Notices to Landlord" does that without making you liable for the tenant's bills, and it works whatever the utility's rules allow, because it binds only the tenant. Where a city or district makes you, as owner, the account holder for water and sewer, you receive its notices directly ("City Water and Sewer Bills").

title: Interrupting a Tenant's Utilities
bodyText:
Utah has no utility-interruption rules written for submetered or landlord-billed electricity, and the library's cautious course is not to submeter electricity or gas at all ("Billing Tenants for Electricity or Gas").

The general rules apply to any interruption you cause. Every covered rental must have electrical systems, heating, plumbing and hot and cold water, and you must maintain them; a loss of an essential service you are responsible for can be a deficient condition the tenant may give you notice to correct, and a dangerous condition requires you to begin repairs within 24 hours.

You may not willfully exclude a tenant except by court process ("No Lockouts Without a Court Order"); whether shutting off a utility counts as exclusion is a question for the courts, so treat it as unlawful and never interrupt service to collect money or to make a tenant leave.

Water and sewer special districts may suspend service only to their own nonpaying customers: an owner may ask for a temporary shutoff for maintenance, but not for debt collection, eviction or any other unlawful purpose. Planned interruptions for repairs are lawful if kept short and announced in advance ("Planned Utility Interruptions" clause); give the entry notice your lease requires if you must go inside.

A tenant who, to avoid paying the utility, reconnects a service the provider has lawfully disconnected, or tampers with a meter, commits theft of a utility service. The habitability and repair rules are in Utah's Fit Premises Act, which covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals; the lockout, shutoff and theft rules apply to every tenancy.

title: Utility Accounts in the Landlord's Name
bodyText: When the water, sewer or other utility account for a rental is in your name, you are the customer, and Utah law lets the provider look to you. A city that runs a water or sewer system may require the owner to sign the application and agree to pay for all water and sewer service to the property, whether the owner or a tenant lives there, and may shut off service if the owner does not pay; a special district has the same powers and may also certify past-due fees as a lien on the property, collected on the property tax notice. A provider may not hold a past-due bill against a later owner unless a special district lien was already established. A special district may suspend service only to its own nonpaying customer: it may not do so at the request of a private third party who is not the customer, and you may ask it to suspend service only temporarily for maintenance, never for debt collection or eviction. If service is cut because you did not pay, your tenant has the Fit Premises Act remedies: every covered rental must have electrical systems, heating, plumbing and hot and cold water, and the tenant may give you a notice of deficient condition and, if you do not act, end the lease with a refund or correct the condition and deduct up to two months' rent; whether paying your utility bill counts as correcting the condition is for the courts. No Utah statute gives tenants a separate right to pay your utility bill and deduct it, a utility-specific receivership, or liquidated damages, and the Code sets no utility rules on notice to each unit before a building-wide shutoff or on shutting off tenants for a landlord's unpaid bill; any such rules would be in the Public Service Commission's rules or the provider's tariff or ordinances, which the library does not hold. Keep landlord-held accounts paid, and if the lease makes the tenant pay you for the service, state the charge or its method in the lease ("Splitting Shared Utility Bills"). The Fit Premises Act rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Utility Disconnection Rules in Utah
bodyText: The Utah Code contains no rules on when an electric, gas, water or sewer utility may disconnect a residential customer for nonpayment: no winter moratorium or winter extension of the notice period, no medical or life-support protection, and no bar on disconnection during a declared storm or other emergency. Those protections, if Utah has them, would be in the Public Service Commission's rules for the utilities it regulates, or in a city's or district's own ordinances or rules for water and sewer; the library does not hold them. What the Code does say: a city or special district that supplies water or sewer service may make the property owner sign for the service and may shut it off for nonpayment, but may not hold one owner's unpaid bill against a later owner ("Utility Accounts in the Landlord's Name"); a special district may not suspend service at a private third party's request; and a public utility may not disconnect or threaten to disconnect basic utility service because the customer has not paid third-party charges billed through the utility. Low-income tenants who hold their own electric or gas accounts may qualify for bill payment assistance programs run through the utilities. For your own conduct as landlord, see "Interrupting a Tenant's Utilities": never cut off or ask a provider to cut off a tenant's service to collect money or to make the tenant leave.

title: Submetering and Separate Utility Billing
bodyText: Outside mobile home parks, no Utah statute regulates submetering or separate utility billing of a rental: there is no prescribed lease disclosure, no type-size or separate-page rule, no unit threshold, no regulator registration for water submetering, no cap on billing fees, no special late-fee cap, and no rule against eviction or disconnection for unpaid utility charges. The general rules control instead. The lease must state each utility charge and the method for figuring it, or you can't collect it; on a month-to-month lease you may add a new charge after 15 days' notice, but you can't add one to a fixed-term lease mid-term. Your written pre-application disclosure must list the type of each use-based charge, and an applicant may get back everything paid if the lease adds one you did not disclose. A late fee, if the lease applies one, is capped by the general late-fee limit. For water, sewer and trash, "Shared Water, Sewer and Trash Charges" clause bills by submeter reading or formula at the provider's charge with a copy of the bill. For electricity and natural gas, the cautious course is not to submeter ("Billing Tenants for Electricity or Gas"). Never cut off service to collect a utility charge ("Interrupting a Tenant's Utilities"). A mobile home park's lease must fully disclose utility costs, including submetered and master-metered allocations and how each bill is calculated, with a yearly disclosure and the charges shown on each bill. These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: No Utility Transfer Rule
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution sets a deadline for a tenant to put utility accounts in the tenant's own name, or lets you shut off a utility left in your name because the tenant did not transfer it. Make the transfer a lease duty instead: the optional clause "Transfer of Utility Accounts" requires the tenant to open or transfer each tenant-paid account by a date you choose, makes the tenant repay what the provider actually charged for any period the account stayed in your name, against a copy of the bill, and promises that you will not cut off service over it.

That promise matters in Utah: locking a tenant out without a court order is unlawful, whether cutting a utility counts is a question for the courts, and a water or sewer special district may not act on an owner's request to discontinue service for debt collection or eviction.

Some cities and districts require the owner to sign for water and sewer service, so those accounts may have to stay in your name; bill the tenant for them only as the lease states ("Splitting Shared Utility Bills") or include them in the rent. Ask the tenant to show the transfer was made ("Evidence of Utility Payment" clause).

Whether an electric or gas utility will close an account in your name while a tenant lives there, and what notice it must give the occupants, is set by the Public Service Commission's rules and the utility's tariff. The limit on charges is in Utah's Fit Premises Act, which covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals; the lockout and special-district rules apply to every tenancy.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging at a Rental
bodyText:
Utah gives tenants no right to install an electric vehicle charger ("No Tenant EV Charging Right"), and no statute requires a landlord to provide charging or EV-ready parking. Whether to allow a charger is your decision, made in the lease ("Tenant-Installed EV Charging System" clause).

Three sets of rules can still apply. If you own a condominium unit or a lot in a homeowners association, the association may not prohibit you, as owner, from installing or using a charger in a parking space assigned to your unit or lot or a limited common area space for your exclusive use, but it may require an application, a licensed electrical contractor, compliance with reasonable design rules and building codes, a reasonable review charge, reimbursement of any insurance increase for a charger in a common area, and payment of installation, metering, electricity and damage costs; your tenant has no such right against the association, so any tenant installation must go through you and the association's process.

If you sell charging to tenants or others, you are not a public utility so long as you buy the electricity from the local utility under its tariff, but if your charger delivers power to vehicles for a fee (per kilowatt-hour, per hour or by subscription) you are a charging station operator: you must collect Utah's 12.5% electric vehicle charging tax, give an itemized invoice showing the tax on its own line, and remit it with your sales tax returns. Whether a charger that bills by the kilowatt-hour must also be registered or tested under the weights-and-measures rules is not settled in the Code.

Charging fees in a lease must state the amount or the method, like any other charge; a charge the lease does not include is allowed only on a month-to-month tenancy after 15 days' notice.

title: EV Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: No Utah statute says who owns a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends, or requires the tenant to remove it or restore the space. The only Utah rule is for owners in condominium and homeowners associations: unless the owner and the association or declarant agree otherwise, a charger an owner installs is the owner's personal property, and before selling the unit or lot the owner must remove it and restore the premises unless the buyer accepts it with the related responsibilities; the owner must also disclose the charger to a prospective buyer. Between you and your tenant, the lease decides. The installation clause "Tenant-Installed EV Charging System" lets you choose, before any installation, whether the tenant removes the system and repairs the damage or leaves it in place as your property. Settle it in writing: whether equipment wired into the building belongs to you or the tenant without an agreement is a fixtures question for the courts. If the tenant leaves without removing a charger the lease required removed, you may apply the deposit to repair damage beyond reasonable wear and tear and to other costs the lease provides for, itemized as the deposit statute requires ("Deposit Return Penalty Process"); property left after an abandonment follows the abandoned-property procedure ("Handling of Property Left Behind" clause). If the property is in an association, its rules on chargers bind you as owner.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking Areas
bodyText:
No Utah statute gives a tenant a right to install an electric vehicle charger in a shared parking area, or sets terms for one. In your own building or lot, a charger in a space other tenants use is allowed only on the terms you set in the lease ("Tenant-Installed EV Charging System" clause, "EV Charger in a Shared Parking Area" clause). If you reserve the space for the tenant or charge for it, state the amount in the lease; a "reasonable fee" set later is not an amount agreed.

In a condominium or homeowners association, the rules bind you as owner: the association must allow an owner's charger in a space assigned to the unit or lot or a limited common area space for the owner's exclusive use, but need not allow one elsewhere in the common areas; for a charger in a common area the association may require you to reimburse the actual increase in its insurance premium, and it may make you pay for damage to common areas, limited common areas or another owner's exclusive-use area caused by installing, using, maintaining, repairing, removing or replacing the charger.

Pass those costs to your tenant only as the lease states, with the association's bill as the measure ("Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause). If you install shared chargers and charge users a fee, the charging tax and public-utility rules in "Electric Vehicle Charging at a Rental" apply.

title: Satellite Dishes, Antennas and Cable Access
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution gives a tenant a right to install a satellite dish or antenna, to choose a cable, satellite or internet provider, or to get provider access to a rental building, and none bars a rent difference for tenants who subscribe to a service. The rule most likely to govern dishes and antennas is federal: the Federal Communications Commission's over-the-air reception devices rule.

Don't ban dishes or antennas outright; require consent and placement terms that yield to any federal or state right, as the optional clause "Television, Satellite and Internet Service" does.

Two Utah rules touch the subject. A cable company that wants to run its lines along a utility's easement across your private property needs your consent, unless the easement is a dedicated public utility strip. And a tenant who connects to a building's cable distribution without the cable company's authority commits theft of cable service. A satellite dish or antenna is not cable service for that crime.

title: Plug-In and Balcony Solar Devices
bodyText:
Utah gives tenants no right to install a plug-in, balcony or portable solar device, and no statute limits a lease term that prohibits or conditions one.

What Utah's 2025 law does is free these devices from the electric utility's rules: a portable solar generation device (movable, no more than 1,200 watts, plugged into a standard 120-volt outlet, meeting the current National Electrical Code and certified by Underwriters Laboratories or an equivalent lab) must have a feature that stops it from energizing the building's wiring during an outage, is exempt from interconnection and net metering requirements, and an electrical corporation may not require approval, a fee or extra equipment for it.

That limit binds electrical corporations; a city-owned power system is not a corporation under the utility code, so its own rules may differ. None of this binds you as landlord. You may prohibit the devices or allow them on your terms ("Portable Solar Devices" clause).

Utah's other solar laws protect owners, not tenants: in a homeowners association only the declaration may prohibit an owner's solar energy system on a detached home (or, in limited cases, an attached one), adding such a prohibition takes a 67% owner vote, and other rules may only restrict it; owners may grant recorded solar easements; and a city or county may refuse to approve a subdivision whose covenants bar reasonably sited solar collectors. No Utah statute voids a lease or other instrument that restricts solar.

title: Property Tax and Your Tenants
bodyText: No Utah statute requires you to tell a tenant how much of the rent goes to property tax, to give an annual property-tax statement, or to give one on request for a tax credit. Two property-tax rules still touch your tenants. First, Utah's renter's credit, for renters who are 66 or 67 and older (depending on birth year) or qualifying surviving spouses, with limited household income: the tenant must give the Tax Commission reasonable proof of rent paid and the name and address of the owner or managing agent, so an older tenant may ask you for a rent receipt or statement. Nothing requires you to provide one, but it helps the tenant. The credit counts only rent for occupancy, not utilities, services or furniture you supply under the rental agreement; if the rent includes electricity or natural gas and the statement does not itemize it, the commission deducts 7% of the rent for one of them or 13% for both, so a statement that shows the utility amount can matter. Second, the 45% residential exemption: a home rented as a tenant's primary residence qualifies, but not one used for short-term or other transient stays. Before the county allows it, each owner must file a written declaration, under penalty of perjury and on the commission's form, that the property will be used as a tenant's primary residence; the assessor may then ask you for a current lease signed by the tenant, and if that is not enough, your insurance policy and then your tax filing showing rental income or loss, but may not ask your tenant for information. Furniture and appliances you own that are used only in the tenant's primary residence count as residential property too. Neither rule requires you to pass the tax saving to the tenant.

title: Parking Rules, Towing and Booting
bodyText:
Utah has no statute written for residential parking rules: nothing prescribes a heading, requires delivery of the rules before the lease is signed, limits mid-term changes or the vehicle information you may ask for, or ties a parking permit to the lease term. Three general rules apply.

First, if your parking rules are part of the rules for the rental, you must give the tenant a copy of them at or before the start of the tenancy, and the tenant must follow them; attaching them to the lease does both ("Parking Rules" clause).

Second, towing: you may adopt and enforce parking rules, but a tow you request from a private lot needs the vehicle owner's consent, state-format signs at each entrance, or a written 24-hour warning notice placed on the driver's side window; no signs or notice are needed for a detached single-family home or duplex, places where parking is illegal (fire lanes, near hydrants, disabled spaces), places plainly not open to parking, gated or attended lots, vehicles blocking access, or repossessions, and a city may add requirements ("Towing from Rental Property"). Utah has no special waiting period for a tenant's car with expired registration.

Third, booting: in a building of more than eight units, a vehicle may be booted without the owner's knowledge only where signs show where parking is subject to immobilization and give a contact name and number, and the removal fee is capped at $75 for the first day plus $25 a day, $150 in all.

Your rules may not bar a tenant from keeping a lawful firearm locked out of sight in a vehicle unless you offer free alternative parking or secure storage nearby ("Firearms Stored in Vehicles"), and any charge for tags or decals must be in the lease ("Parking & Vehicle Requirements" clause). These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText:
No section of the Utah Code or Constitution requires you to price parking separately from rent, forbids it, or regulates a separate parking charge. Some cities reduce or remove parking requirements for housing near transit or for senior housing as part of their moderate-income housing plans; those are local land-use rules, not landlord-tenant rules.

If you charge for parking separately, the fee rule applies: the charge must be in the lease with its amount, you may not raise it above that amount during the term, and on a month-to-month lease you may add a new charge only after 15 days' written notice. List the parking charge's amount in your pre-application estimate of fixed non-rent charges.

The optional clause "Optional Parking Not Included in Rent" sets this up as a separate parking license that either party may end on notice; an assigned space included in the rent is "Assigned Parking Space(s)" clause, and parking rules are in "Parking Rules" clause. These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText:
Utah's entry rule is a default the lease may change: unless the rental agreement provides otherwise, you must give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice before entering. So the lease may set a different notice, or none, for regularly scheduled services such as filter changes, pest treatment or smoke alarm checks. Utah does not require the term to be conspicuous, separately signed or limited to certain hours.

Because the lease is the only source of a scheduled-services right, write the schedule into it: the optional clause "Entry for Regularly Scheduled Services" lists each service and its schedule, sets the hours and the advance notice for each visit, and requires a knock before entry.

Tenants may not unreasonably refuse entry for repairs. A failure to give the required notice does not by itself give the tenant a claim under the Fit Premises Act or excuse the tenant from the lease, but entering beyond what the lease allows can still lead to other claims, so follow the schedule you set. Your general entry clause is "Landlord's Right of Entry" clause. These rules cover a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Out-of-State Owners and Entity Landlords
bodyText: Utah does not make an owner who lives outside Utah appoint a Utah agent, name one in the lease, or file anything before renting or suing, and it does not make your tenant withhold income tax from rent paid to an out-of-state owner. What every owner must do, wherever you live, is tell the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name, address and telephone number of the owner or of the person authorized to manage the unit (or, if the manager cannot receive notices, of the person who can receive notices and perform the owner's duties). The library's owner and manager disclosure clause does this. That duty is part of the Fit Premises Act, which covers a renter's principal residence and not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or recreational property rented occasionally. Where an out-of-state owner can be stopped is business filings. (1) An LLC, corporation, limited partnership or other entity formed by a filing in another state may not do business in Utah until it registers with the Division of Corporations and Commercial Code, and while it does business here unregistered it may not maintain an action or proceeding in Utah, an eviction included. Its leases stay valid and it may still defend a suit. Owning real property is listed as not doing business, but renting it out is not on that list, so whether a rental business is doing business in Utah depends on the facts; the law here turns on case law, so register before you rent or file. A registered foreign entity must keep a registered agent in Utah. (2) Anyone, individual or entity, who rents under a name other than its own legal name must file a D.B.A. certificate with the Division within 30 days after starting, naming a Utah registered agent, and may not bring a court action as the D.B.A. until it complies. A corporation or LLC renting under its own true name does not need one. (3) If a nonresident doing business here has not appointed a Utah registered agent, court papers may be served on anyone employed by or acting as an agent for the nonresident, such as your property manager. And owning, using or possessing Utah real estate lets a Utah court hear claims arising from it, with the papers served on you outside Utah. Keep your contact details current with your manager and tenants. You may also give a city, in writing, the name and address of a person to receive all its correspondence about the property, and the city must then send its correspondence to that person; this is optional, not a required agent. (4) If you own through a partnership, an LLC taxed as a partnership or an S corporation, the entity itself must pay or withhold Utah income tax on the Utah income of its owners, except for owners who are Utah resident individuals and a few other listed cases; that is the entity's own tax duty, not your tenant's, and the amount is set by State Tax Commission rule. The same filing rules sit with local rental licensing in "Local Rental Licensing and Good Landlord Programs", and the reporting duties that bind every person, landlords included, are in "Reporting Duties and Police Cooperation".

title: Rules Outside the Landlord-Tenant Laws
bodyText: These questions are answered across the whole Utah Code and Constitution, not only the landlord-tenant chapters. (1) Squatters: present. Since 2025 an owner, or the owner's authorized agent, can ask local law enforcement to remove at once a trespasser (someone who never had any right to possession) by presenting a verified statutory complaint attesting that the person entered unlawfully, the property was not open to the public when they entered, and the person has been told to leave. It is not available against a current or former tenant under a written rental agreement, an immediate family member of the owner, or where litigation over the property is pending between you, and wrongful use exposes you to actual damages, triple the fair market rent, costs and attorney fees ("Removing Trespassers and Long-Term Guests"). Tenants are removed only by eviction. (2) Cash receipts: present, in a general statute. Anyone who pays money is entitled to a receipt from the person paid and may demand a properly signed receipt as a condition of paying, so give a signed receipt whenever a tenant asks, and for every cash payment as a matter of practice ("Receipts for Rent"). (3) Registration before eviction: no Utah statute requires a statewide landlord registration, and none makes registration, a rental license or a city business license a condition of filing an eviction or getting a judgment for possession. A city's licensing ordinance is local law; check the city's own rules ("Local Rental Licensing and Good Landlord Programs"). Business filings can still stop a suit: an out-of-state LLC, corporation or other filed entity doing business in Utah unregistered may not maintain an action, an eviction included, and a person renting under an unregistered business name may not bring an action under that name until it files. Neither failure voids the lease ("Out-of-State Owners and Entity Landlords"). (4) Suing or serving someone outside Utah: owning, using or possessing Utah real estate, or doing business here, lets a Utah court hear claims arising from it, so a tenant who has moved away can still be sued here for rent or damages, and papers can be served outside Utah ("Out-of-State Owners and Entity Landlords"). (5) Reporting duties that bind every person, landlords and their staff included, such as reporting suspected child abuse or abuse of a vulnerable adult and reporting certain deaths, are in "Reporting Duties and Police Cooperation".

title: Construction Liens for Tenant Work
bodyText:
Utah's construction lien law lets a contractor, worker or supplier who is not paid claim a lien on the property interest of the person who hired the original contractor. When your tenant hires the work, the tenant is that person, and the lien attaches only to the tenant's interest (the leasehold), not to your ownership.

There is one exception: the lien can reach your ownership if the contractor shows that you authorized the work and that it gives you a substantial benefit lasting beyond the lease. Whether a lease clause or a general consent to alterations counts as authorizing the work is a question for the courts, so treat any consent you give to a lasting improvement as a possible exposure: consent in writing to specific work only, and require proof of payment or lien waivers before you consent to large projects.

Utah has no notice of nonresponsibility, so there is nothing you can post or record to disclaim work your tenant orders. A contract cannot waive or limit a lien right, and a contract term that tries to is void, so a lease sentence saying your interest "will not be subject to liens" does not bind a contractor; use the library's tenant payment and release clause ("Tenant-Ordered Work and Liens" clause) instead, which only allocates the duty and cost between you and your tenant.

Any person may ask the State Construction Registry to be notified of filings for a project, and a contractor or supplier who wants a lien must file a preliminary notice with the Registry within 20 days after starting work (a late notice covers only later work); a lien notice must be recorded within 180 days after the work is finally complete (90 days after a notice of completion is filed), a copy must be mailed to the record owner within 30 days, and the lien is void unless a suit to enforce it is filed within 180 days after the lien notice.

When you are the one who orders the work on a single-family home or duplex that you or your tenant will occupy within 180 days after the work ends, a separate protection applies: if you contract in writing with a licensed contractor and pay that contractor in full, subcontractors and suppliers cannot keep a lien on the home or win a judgment against you for what the contractor failed to pay them, and for a contract of $5,000 or less subcontractors are barred whether or not the contractor is licensed.

title: Restricted Foreign Entities and Leases
bodyText: Utah bars a "restricted foreign entity" from acquiring any interest in land in Utah. The law defines an interest in land as any right, title, lien, claim, interest or estate with respect to land, so a lease is covered, and there is no exception for short leases or for homes. A restricted foreign entity is: a company the U.S. Secretary of Defense must list as a Chinese military company under federal defense law; an entity that the government of China, Iran, North Korea or Russia owns or directly controls; an affiliate, subsidiary or holding company of either; the countries whose industrial base such an entity is part of, and their states, provinces, cities, agencies and departments; and any entity in which one of these holds at least 25%. The rule is about entities and governments, not people: a person's nationality, citizenship or national origin does not make the person restricted, and refusing to rent to someone because of national origin is illegal housing discrimination ("Utah Fair Housing Act"). An interest a restricted foreign entity obtains in violation must be given up within one year after it is acquired; if it is not, the state sells it at public auction. The law does not say the lease itself is void. Separately, any person who knowingly buys or leases an interest in land on behalf of a restricted foreign entity, using its money or acting under its direction, commits a third degree felony. The law puts no duty on you to investigate tenants, but the Department of Public Safety keeps a public list of restricted foreign entities. If your prospective tenant is a company, or a company is paying for or directing a lease for someone else (for example staff housing), check the list and do not lease to a listed entity or on its behalf. An individual who buys (not leases) land must disclose to the county recorder any service in the military of a restricted foreign entity. Utah has no other alien land law: no Utah statute bars a nonresident alien from leasing, and none requires a lease to a foreign person to state the person's name and address or to be approved or recorded.

title: When Illegal Use Voids the Lease
bodyText: Two Utah statutes void a lease because of how the premises are used. (1) Alcohol: if a tenant uses the premises, or any part of them, in maintaining an alcohol nuisance (a place where alcoholic products are kept, sold, made, given or otherwise handled in violation of Utah's alcohol laws), or knowingly lets someone else do so, the lease is void and the right to possession reverts to you, with the remedy the law gives for forcible detention of the premises. If you know or have reason to believe your property is used as an alcohol nuisance, the property can be subject to a lien for the fines and costs, and knowingly permitting the use, or failing to take proper steps after written notice of it, is itself a crime. (2) Pornography and obscenity: if a tenant or occupant is convicted of an offense under Utah's pornographic and harmful materials chapter for an activity on the property, the conviction makes the lease void at your option, once all direct appeals are over. You exercise the option by written notice, and your right to possession returns 10 days after the notice; a tenant who does not leave within 10 days commits a class A misdemeanor. If the county or city attorney notifies you in writing that a convicted tenant is still using the property for those purposes and you do not exercise the option within 10 days, you commit a class A misdemeanor, and any fine becomes a lien on the property. For other illegal uses no statute voids the lease; you end the tenancy by eviction: three calendar days' notice to quit where the tenant carries on an unlawful business, keeps a nuisance or commits a criminal act on the premises ("Utah Eviction Notices by Tenancy Type"), or a nuisance-abatement eviction ("Nuisance Abatement by Eviction"). Do not lock the tenant out even where the lease is void; use the court process ("No Lockouts Without a Court Order"). Separately, knowingly renting or making premises available for making, storing, distributing or using illegal drugs is a second degree felony, and leasing or permitting a place you control to be used for prostitution is a crime. The library's residential-use clause ("Residential Use Only" clause) limits the premises to residential use.

title: Entering to Care for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText:
Utah gives you no special right to enter a rental to feed, check on or remove a tenant's animal when the tenant is hospitalized, detained or otherwise away, and no procedure for taking custody of it.

Your ordinary entry rule applies: for a tenant's principal residence covered by the Fit Premises Act you must give at least 24 hours' notice before entering unless the rental agreement provides otherwise, so the lease itself can set a different rule. The library's optional animal-care clause ("Animal Care in Tenant's Absence" clause) uses that room: the tenant names a person to care for or remove the animals and consents in advance to your letting that person in, and if no one can be reached you may ask animal control, a peace officer or a shelter to take charge.

If you believe an animal is being neglected, call animal control or the police rather than removing it yourself: a peace officer or animal control officer may take possession of an animal involved in a cruelty offense, and anyone who has custody of an animal and fails to provide necessary food, water, care or shelter, or abandons it, commits a crime.

Two narrower rules exist: when an eviction order is carried out, a pet goes to the tenant if present and otherwise animal control must be notified to take custody ("Tenant Property and Animals After an Eviction"); and when a tenant abandons the premises you do not have to store pets left behind, but handle them through animal control, not by disposing of them yourself.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Utah does not require you to give a tenant a state fact sheet or notice about pets and eviction, with the lease or at any other time, even when you know the tenant has a dog or cat. What Utah does have is a rule for the day an eviction order is carried out (since September 1, 2026): a personal animal on the premises (a dog, cat, rabbit, bird or other animal kept solely as a pet, not a production animal) goes to the tenant if the tenant is present. If the tenant is not present, the sheriff, constable or you must notify the local animal control authority, which must come to take custody within one business day and post a notice at the premises saying where the animal was taken, and you must give animal control the tenant's name and last known contact information ("Tenant Property and Animals After an Eviction"). Telling a tenant facing eviction about this rule is good practice but not required.

title: Passing Government Fines to a Tenant
bodyText:
No Utah statute bars you from making a tenant reimburse a fine, penalty or abatement charge a government imposes on you, and none limits that to fines the tenant caused; equally, no statute makes a tenant liable to you for one by default. So a tenant owes you a government fine only if the lease says so.

For a tenant's principal residence covered by the Fit Premises Act, Utah's fee rule decides how: you may not charge a fine or other cost that is not included in the rental agreement (unless the tenancy is month to month and you give 15 days' notice of the charge), or more than the amount agreed, so the lease must state the amount or a fixed method, such as the amount the government charged you, shown by a copy of the citation, order or bill. The library's optional clause ("Fines Caused by Tenant" clause) does that and covers only fines and abatement charges for conditions the tenant, the household or the tenant's guests caused or permitted.

How cities collect: when a city inspector finds weeds, garbage, a public nuisance, an illegal structure or hazardous materials, the written notice goes to the owner of record, and may also go to a non-owner occupant or a manager or agent where you do not live there and the city's ordinance puts a maintenance duty on that person. If the notice is not complied with, the city may abate the condition and bill the owner of record; unpaid costs can become a lien collected with your property taxes, or the city can sue you.

The bill comes to you even when your tenant caused the condition, which is why the reimbursement must be in the lease. A city may not stop you from passing a rental license fee or disproportionate rental fee on to the tenant. Fines from a homeowners or condominium association are not government fines ("Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause).

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText:
No Utah statute says whether a tenant who rents a home with farmland or acreage gets the right to hunt or fish there, or keeps that right with you unless you grant it in writing, so the lease decides.

Utah's hunting trespass law matters here: a hunter or angler may not enter private land that is cultivated or properly posted without permission, and permission must be a signed document from "the owner or person in charge" naming the person, the dates and the property. Utah does not define who is "in charge", so a tenant in possession of the land may be able to give that permission, and only someone who owns or legally controls land may post it.

If you want to keep hunting, fishing and trapping for yourself, say so in the lease: the library's optional clause ("Hunting, Fishing and Trapping Reserved" clause) reserves those rights to you and bars the tenant from letting others hunt without your written agreement.

A few related rules: shooting within 600 feet of a house, other building, barn or corral needs written permission from the owner or person in charge of the property, and because your tenant may be the person in charge of the rented house, keep your own hunting party beyond 600 feet of it or get the tenant's written permission; a landowner or lessee may kill big game damaging cultivated crops only after asking the Division of Wildlife Resources to act and meeting the statute's notice conditions; and an owner, which for this purpose includes a tenant or lessee, who lets people hunt or fish on the land without charge owes them no duty to keep the land safe, except for willful or malicious conduct or where a charge is made.

title: Housing Your Own Employee
bodyText: Utah has no statute on housing you provide to your own employee, such as a resident manager, caretaker or farm worker. Nothing requires a signed disclosure of the conditions for occupying and vacating the unit, nothing requires you to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, and the Fit Premises Act and the eviction chapter have no employee exception. The eviction chapter does not mention employees or caretakers either: it covers a "tenant", which includes any individual except a person with no legal right to the premises. So treat an employee who lives in your unit as a tenant. Put the arrangement in a written rental agreement that states the rent (or that the housing is part of the pay), the term, and what happens when the job ends, and if the employee will not leave, end the tenancy by the right notice and an eviction, not a lockout ("Utah Eviction Notices by Tenancy Type", "No Lockouts Without a Court Order"). The fast law-enforcement removal for trespassers does not fit: it is for someone who never had a right to possession. Nor is an employee who works in exchange for the housing a "long-term guest" under the criminal trespass law, which excludes anyone who has agreed to provide labor instead of paying. For the unit's condition, the Fit Premises Act applies to the employee's principal residence like any other rental. Construction and labor camps are covered by state sanitation rules. Wage, tax and benefit rules for housing given as pay are outside this library.

title: Trying to Settle Before Court
bodyText:
No Utah statute requires, permits or limits a lease term that has you and your tenant try to settle a dispute informally before going to court, so such a term is an ordinary contract term. Keep it non-binding and keep possession out of it: a step that delayed an eviction or a statutory notice could be challenged, and the effect of such terms is case law.

The library's optional clause ("Informal Dispute Resolution" clause) does this: either party gives written notice of a dispute and offers to meet within 10 days, possession and emergency actions are excluded, and no deadline, notice or remedy is delayed.

Binding arbitration is a different thing and the library does not offer it in Utah ("Arbitration Clauses in Utah Leases").

Two Utah rules sit nearby. A court may refer a case to mediation under the court's program, and a party may object for good cause; a mediated settlement can be filed and enforced as a judgment, and communications in a mediation are generally privileged. And in a mobile home park, before ending a resident's lease or suing over a park rule violation (other than certain serious conduct or nonpayment), the park must give a written notice of noncompliance, and if the resident disputes it in writing the park must meet the resident in person to try to settle.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Utah property law does not use; the word appears nowhere in the Utah Code or Constitution, so the civil-law rules about leases granted by a usufructuary do not apply here. The closest Utah interest is a life estate, for example a parent who deeded a house to the children but kept the right to live in it for life. Utah law says a life estate ends when the holder dies, and the end can be put on the record by an affidavit with the death certificate. No Utah statute says what happens to a lease the life tenant granted when the life estate ends, whether it binds the people who then own the property, or what the life tenant must tell the tenant; that is left to case law. If you rent out property you hold only for life, the cautious course is to tell the tenant in the lease that you hold a life estate, and either have the holders of the remainder sign the lease too or make the lease end when your estate ends.

title: Special Districts and Your Tenant
bodyText: No Utah statute requires a lease to state that a rental sits in a special district (such as a water, sewer, improvement or fire district), a special service district, a public infrastructure district or an assessment area, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges or rules. The one disclosure Utah has runs the other way: when residential property inside a public infrastructure district is sold, the seller must disclose the expected annual cost of the district's tax at or before closing. It does not apply to leases. Tenants have no special role in district decisions because they rent: where a district's creation, annexation or withdrawal turns on property-owner petitions or protests, the "owner" counted is the fee title owner on the county records, so your tenant does not sign in your place. Board members of most special districts must be registered voters who live in the district, so a tenant who lives there can qualify like any other resident. If a district offers an income-based residential fee credit, it must offer it to residential tenants as well as homeowners. If a district bills you as owner for water or sewer service your tenant uses, see the utility rows ("Utility Accounts in the Landlord's Name").

title: Leasing Tribal or Trust Land
bodyText: No Utah statute requires a government officer to approve a lease of communal, tribal or Indian-owned land before it is valid, and none says what happens to rent or possession before approval. Utah has no communal land system of its own. Land in Utah held in trust by the United States for a tribe or an individual Indian, or subject to a federal restriction on transfer, is governed by federal law, and Utah's own Indian-jurisdiction statute says nothing in it authorizes the alienation or encumbrance of that property or lets the state decide who owns or may possess it. Utah's Constitution likewise leaves lands held by Indians or Indian tribes under the jurisdiction and control of Congress until the United States extinguishes their title. Federal leasing law and the tribe's own law are where an approval rule for such land would sit. If you are asked to rent, or to rent out, a home on tribal trust or restricted land (for example on the Navajo, Ute, Goshute, Paiute or Shoshone lands in Utah), treat the lease as needing the approval federal and tribal law require, and get that confirmed with the Bureau of Indian Affairs agency and the tribe before you sign or collect rent. A lease of ordinary privately owned land in Utah needs no government approval, whoever the parties are (see "Recording a Lease in Utah" for recording).

title: Things Utah Law Does Not Address
bodyText: These are the questions in this group that Utah law does not answer, across the whole Utah Code and the Utah Constitution, not only the landlord-tenant chapters. Where a row is named, it gives the detail and what Utah does have nearby. (1) Out-of-state owners: no Utah statute makes an individual owner who lives outside Utah appoint a Utah agent, name one in the lease or file one before suing, and none makes a tenant withhold income tax from rent paid to an out-of-state owner ("Out-of-State Owners and Entity Landlords"). (2) Registration before eviction: no Utah statute makes landlord registration, a rental license or a city business license a condition of filing an eviction or of a judgment for possession ("Rules Outside the Landlord-Tenant Laws"). (3) Construction liens: Utah has no notice of nonresponsibility and no statute letting a lease keep the owner's interest free of liens for tenant work ("Construction Liens for Tenant Work"). (4) Foreign persons: apart from the restricted-foreign-entity law, no Utah statute bars a nonresident alien from leasing, requires a lease to a foreign person to name the person or be approved or recorded ("Restricted Foreign Entities and Leases"). (5) Illegal use: outside the alcohol-nuisance and obscenity statutes, no Utah statute voids a lease because of how the premises are used ("When Illegal Use Voids the Lease"). (6) Animals: no Utah statute gives a landlord a right to enter to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal, and none requires a pet or eviction fact sheet ("Entering to Care for a Tenant's Animal", "No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet"). (7) Government fines: no Utah statute bars passing a government fine to a tenant, limits it to fines the tenant caused, or makes a tenant liable for one by default ("Passing Government Fines to a Tenant"). (8) Hunting on rented land: no Utah statute allocates hunting or fishing rights between owner and tenant ("Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land").
