(9) Employee housing: no Utah statute requires an occupancy disclosure for housing given to an employee, an offer of a rental agreement when the job ends, or a special eviction rule for caretakers ("Housing Your Own Employee"). (10) Pre-suit resolution: no Utah statute requires, permits or limits a lease term asking the parties to try informal resolution before court; mobile home parks have their own statutory dispute meeting ("Trying to Settle Before Court"). (11) Usufruct and life estates: Utah has no usufruct and no statute on what happens to a lease granted by a life tenant when the life estate ends ("Leasing as a Life Tenant"). (12) Special districts: no Utah statute requires a lease to disclose a special district or gives a tenant a district role because of the tenancy; the public infrastructure district disclosure applies only to sales ("Special Districts and Your Tenant"). (13) Tribal land: no Utah statute requires approval of a lease of communal, tribal or Indian land; federal and tribal law may ("Leasing Tribal or Trust Land"). An absence here means no statute.

title: Association Documents and Tenants
bodyText:
Utah has no statute requiring a lease of a condominium or homeowners' association unit to describe the association's obligations or to give the tenant the association's documents.

Two other rules reach the same ground. Under the Fit Premises Act you must give the tenant, at or before the start of the term, a copy of any rules and regulations that apply to the unit ("Copy of Lease and Rules"); the Act does not say whether that includes association rules, so the cautious course is to give the tenant the association rules that bind the unit.

And association documents can bind your tenant directly: condominium tenants are subject to the condominium act, declaration and bylaws, and a condominium or community association's governing documents may require each tenant to follow them and hold you and your tenant jointly and severally liable for a violation.

An association may require you and your tenant to sign its lease addendum, but may not require its approval of the tenant or the lease or require its own lease form.

If you fall more than 60 days behind on assessments and the association's declaration, bylaws or rules allow it, the association may, after giving you notice and 15 days to pay, direct your tenant in writing to pay the rent to it; you must credit those payments as rent and may not sue the tenant for them ("HOA and Condominium Rental Rules"). The Fit Premises Act covers a tenant's principal residence, not boarding or rooming houses, mobile home lots or occasional recreational rentals.

title: Property Manager License from 2027
bodyText: An individual may not, for consideration, manage residential or other real estate owned by another person (advertising or arranging rentals, collecting rent, or signing leases or addenda with tenants) unless licensed under Utah's real estate licensing law. Managing others' property for pay is already a principal broker's act, so today it needs a principal broker, associate broker, sales agent or dual broker license. From January 1, 2027, Utah adds a separate property manager license, which covers residential rental units only. Applicants must complete the state's education program and examination (with shortcuts for those licensed in another state or already holding a broker or sales agent license) and submit fingerprints for a state and FBI background check with ongoing monitoring. An individual needs no license to manage property that individual owns or leases; whether an entity owner's own staff need one is not settled by the text (Real Estate Commission rules not held), so check before relying on it; members of the owner's immediate family, unlicensed or remote assistants of a property manager, people who only do maintenance and repairs or bookkeeping, and regional managers or corporate officials of a rental agency who do none of the management acts are also exempt. Hotel management and stays of under 30 days in tourist accommodations are not property management.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Utah follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Utah Code Ann. § 70A-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Utah Code Ann. § 70A-1a-308(2)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Utah's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (the Utah Fit Premises Act, the deposit statute and the eviction statutes searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Utah's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
